title: AdaBIMBA: Adaptive Token Compression for Long Endoscopy Video Understanding
reviewer_1_strengths: AdaBIMBA outperforms 7 other models on this test set over different question types. These models do not include GPT-4o that was used to generate the questions. The 581 full-length video dataset for training and testing was annotated by domain experts, with boundaries for six anatomical segments and the Mayo Endoscopic score for each segment. The technical novelty is in the token scorer, which assigns a high score to important frames and a low score to less important frames. More query tokens are allocated to the high-score frames, and vice versa. An ablation study was done to show the impact of each component of AdaBIMBA. The presentation is nicely done, with diagrams showing the components of AdaBIMBA, example questions and answers, question types, video length distribution, and the distribution of different question types.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper does not list the domain experts’ experience (e. g. , years of experience or the number of colonoscopies performed) who did the labeling. Did multiple domain experts review the same video segments? This information would help readers judge the quality of the dataset. There was no mention of whether the LLM-generated questions were verified by the domain experts. A sample subset of the question set can be verified by domain experts. There was no statistically significant testing to show that the improvement of AdaBIMBA is statistically significant. It would be good to have the distribution of the number of anatomical segments with different MES scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3.This would help with the evaluation of Table 3. Because the number of questions for each category is not the same, how is the average computed? Does each category get the same weight? There was no measurement of how many tokens were actually reduced when compared to BIMBA. The paper does not mention whether the code and dataset will be available, which will enhance reproducibility and impact of the work.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has a number of appealing aspects. The problem setting is important and clinically relevant, as the work moves beyond static images or short clips and instead considers full-procedure endoscopy videos, which is closer to how these data are encountered in practice. The proposed method is also reasonably motivated. The authors build on the observation that clinically important abnormalities in endoscopy are often brief and sparse, and use this to justify an adaptive compression strategy based on frame importance; this is a sensible design choice for the task. I also appreciate that the paper does not rely solely on a single end-to-end result: the two-stage training procedure, the question-conditioned scorer, and the ablations suggest a genuine attempt to examine the contribution of different components. In addition, the evaluation covers several task types, including summarization, severity scoring, reasoning, and temporal grounding, which makes the empirical study fairly broad.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The Introduction does not provide a sufficiently complete discussion of the most relevant literature on long-video compression and adaptive selection. Characterizing prior approaches mainly as “uniform frame sampling” is somewhat inaccurate and unfair, as many existing works already explore adaptive sampling or adaptive compression. I would encourage the authors to present a more balanced review and clarify the actual distinction of this work from prior studies. 2.The idea of first estimating importance and then allocating compression accordingly is intuitive and well motivated. However, the current comparisons do not convincingly isolate the contribution of the proposed method itself. AdaBIMBA uses a maximum of 1024 frames, compared with 512 for BIMBA and 128 for Qwen3-VL. While the average score improves from 50.8 to 54.7 over BIMBA, this gain is obtained with twice as many visible input frames. Although the paper repeatedly emphasizes the “same memory budget,” it does not yet provide sufficient evidence that the improvement mainly comes from the adaptive allocation strategy rather than simply from seeing more frames. 3.Another concerning observation is that AdaBIMBA performs worse than BIMBA on the most severe category, with MES=3 dropping from 53.5 to 49.6.Since higher MES corresponds to more active inflammation, and the paper positions clinically realistic endoscopy understanding as a key motivation, this degradation on the most critical cases deserves closer attention. I would encourage the authors to provide a more careful analysis of why the method underperforms on severe cases and discuss the potential implications.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The main strength of this study is the construction of a long-duration endoscopic video dataset derived from clinical trials. Unlike conventional short, fragmented data, it captures the full examination process with high-quality expert annotations, enabling learning of full procedural context. 2.Another key strength is that the proposed method performs adaptive, frame-wise compression based on estimated frame importance, rather than relying on uniform frame subsampling. This enables efficient processing of long sequences while minimizing information loss.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The description of the dataset is insufficient. In particular, the class distribution of the Mayo score, the data split proportions, and whether the split was performed at the patient level are unclear. These factors directly affect the reliability and reproducibility of the evaluation and should be clarified. 2.It is unclear to what extent the estimated importance aligns with clinically relevant content. The relationship between the model’s internal importance scores and clinical utility is not well established. Furthermore, the potential risk that adaptive frame compression may lead to the omission of clinically relevant information is not sufficiently discussed. 3.The efficiency gains from the proposed frame compression are not clearly quantified. In particular, reductions in computational cost, such as memory usage and inference time, are not sufficiently demonstrated. 4.While AdaBIMBA shows overall performance improvements, the reason for the performance decline in MES 3 is not explained. The analysis is insufficient, particularly regarding potential factors such as class imbalance and its interaction with frame compression.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their constructive feedback. We appreciate recognition of our method’s novelty(R1,3), clinical relevance(R2,3), broad evaluation and ablations(R1,2). 1) R2—Are gains simply due to more frames? To isolate frame-count from adaptive compression, we trained/evaluated AdaBIMBA with the same 512-frame input as BIMBA. AdaBIMBA scores 66.6/67.4/55.4/40.5/37.3/47.8 on Local/Global/Scoring/Reasoning/Event/Segment, outperforms BIMBA across all categories and improvs average 50.8 → 52.5 (paired t-test p=0.0045), confirming gains are not solely due to higher frame count. At 1024 frames, AdaBIMBA shows its second advantage: expanded temporal coverage under the same 2×80GB memory budget. BIMBA compresses 512 frame-tokens to ~128; AdaBIMBA compresses 1024 to ~132, maintaining nearly identical downstream token counts while doubling temporal coverage, further improving average to 54.7.Gains arise from both adaptive allocation at matched frame count and broader procedural coverage from efficient token utilization, without additional memory. 2) R1,2,3—MES=3 subgroup analysis The MES=3 drop is not statistically significant (p=0.335) with overlapping CIs. In different seeds AdaBIMBA (52.9,54.7) also matches or exceeds BIMBA (51.8,50.3), similarly under matched 512-frame (54.7 vs 53.5), suggesting variance in a smaller subgroup rather than systematic degradation. In contrast, AdaBIMBA shows significant improvements for MES=0–2 (p=0.001/0.010/0.005) and overall F1 (p<0.005), indicating stronger broader-cohort performance. A plausible explanation is that mild–moderate disease has sparse/localized findings benefiting more from adaptive allocation, while severe disease often involves diffuse pathology already captured in shorter windows. We will clarify this limitation and add future validation on larger MES=3 cohorts. 3) R2—Positioning relative to BIMBA and prior adaptive methods We revised Related Work to clarify AdaBIMBA’s contributions: (i) learnable question-conditioned Token Scorer for fine-grained per-frame adaptive compression; (ii) gradient-supervised two-stage training compatible with FlashAttention. Unlike heuristic saliency methods (e.g. LongVU), AdaBIMBA learns task-specific importance via QA supervision; unlike global compression (e.g. Dynamic-VLM), it adapts compression per frame; unlike keyframe selection (e.g. AKS), it preserves frames while reallocating token budget toward clinically relevant regions. 4) R1,3—Statistical significance, average weighting, efficiency Paired t-tests show significance across all categories (Event p<0.02; others p<0.005). Averages are unweighted, with consistent gains in weighted average (46.8→50.3). Token Scorer adds only ~1.21% parameters. Under identical pre-compression frame input generating 128 tokens, Qwen3-VL/BIMBA/AdaBIMBA take 28.7/12.7/6.54s (77% and 48.5% speedup; see 1) for token efficiency). 5) R1,3—Dataset details/reproducibility The dataset is split at patient level into 10,153/3,545 QAs from 441/140 train/test videos, preventing leakage. MES 0-3 counts are: train 766/562/539/467, test 280/185/212/166.Each video is annotated by up to 6 clinicians (3–8+ years experience, 59.7% MES inter-rater agreement). Scoring/Reasoning/Segment QA labels are directly derived from expert annotations; clinician validation of other QA categories is ongoing. Due to regulations, full data access will be case-dependent; but we will release detailed pseudocode, QA samples, dataset-construction and implementation details for reproducibility. 6) R3—Token importance and omission risk Fig 5 is intended to show the reliability of AdaBIMBA’s adaptive allocation rather than direct clinical utility. It shows less compression in question-relevant video regions, grounding answers in correct temporal evidence. While any compression may omit information, AdaBIMBA mitigates this vs. uniform BIMBA by retaining more information in important frames, instead of treating all frames equally.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The comparison with BIMBA is confounded by frame budget (1024 vs. 512), so it is unclear whether gains come from adaptive allocation or simply from more visible frames. Second, the drop on MES=3 needs a careful explanation, including any interaction with class imbalance. Third, several dataset clarifications are needed: MES class distribution, train/test split proportions, and whether splits are patient-level, annotator experience and inter-rater agreement, and whether the generated QA pairs were verified by clinicians. Finally, the positioning relative to prior work on adaptive sampling and compression should be clarified. | The authors provided a strong rebuttal and answered the previously raised points. The paper is well-written and the method thoroughly validated. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The initial reviews nevertheless identified several substantive weaknesses. R2 raised the most important methodological concern: the main comparison with BIMBA was confounded by different visible-frame budgets, since AdaBIMBA used up to 1024 frames whereas BIMBA used 512.This made it difficult to determine whether the gains came from adaptive allocation or simply from seeing more frames. R2 and R3 also noted the degradation on the MES=3 subgroup, which is clinically important. R1 and R3 requested additional dataset information, including patient-level splitting, MES class distribution, annotator experience, inter-rater agreement, and whether LLM-generated QA pairs were clinically verified. Additional concerns included limited positioning with respect to prior adaptive compression/sampling methods, lack of statistical testing, limited efficiency quantification, and incomplete reproducibility details. The rebuttal substantially improved the assessment. The authors clarified that AdaBIMBA also outperforms BIMBA at the same 512-frame input budget, reported statistical testing, explained the 1024-frame setting as increased temporal coverage under a similar downstream token/memory budget, and provided additional analysis of the MES=3 subgroup. The rebuttal also clarified the patient-level split, MES distributions, annotator experience, inter-rater agreement, average weighting, inference time, and release plan for pseudocode/QA samples. These clarifications directly address many of the concerns raised by R1, R2, R3, and the initial meta-review. However, some of these clarifications include additional analyses not fully present in the submitted paper, so they should be interpreted primarily as evidence that the original claims are plausible rather than as a complete replacement for clearer controls in the manuscript. The remaining limitations are important but not sufficient to warrant rejection. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a novel method, and its performance was demonstrated through the experiments. Therefore, I believe this paper is worthy of acceptance.

title: AffordTissue: Dense Affordance Prediction for Tool-Action Specific Tissue Interaction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1)The paper introduces a novel dataset that covers a large number of videos from diverse sources, which is valuable for advancing research in this area. 2)The ablation study is comprehensive and evaluates the contributions of the proposed components in a systematic manner. 3)The overall structure of the paper is clear, and both the methodology and experimental setup are well described.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1)The reported DICE score is relatively low (0.124), which raises concerns about the effectiveness of the method. It would be helpful to understand why this is the case, especially in comparison to SAM-based approaches that achieve higher DICE scores. Additionally, more details are needed on how SAM (or SAM3) is prompted in this context. 2)How about alternative dense prediction baselines? For example, will standard architectures such as U-Net be able to be adapted to this task and how they compare with the proposed method? 3)From a clinical perspective, the definition of the affordance regions is not entirely clear. Since this is a newly introduced dataset, more details are needed regarding the annotation protocol, including how consistency and reliability are ensured across videos/annotators.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Framing tissue affordance prediction as a dense heatmap estimation task is a genuinely novel and well-motivated formulation that bridges surgical scene understanding and robot safety, going meaningfully beyond existing semantic segmentation approaches. The large benchmark dataset is a substantial contribution in its own right and could enable future research in this area if released. The design choice of conditioning on tool-action language prompts rather than hardcoding tool categories is principled and enables generalization to unseen instrument-action combinations. The ablation studies are thorough and cover language encoder choice, vision backbone, decoder type, temporal context, and prompt structure, giving a clear picture of what each component contributes. The dual-mode safety application is well-articulated and clinically meaningful and repurposing the AdaLN decoder from diffusion modeling for dense heatmap prediction is an interesting and practical architectural adaptation that is clearly explained.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Annotation Protocol Is Insufficiently Rigorous for a Safety-Critical Task: The ground truth affordance regions are defined by four manually annotated keypoints forming a polygon, from which a Gaussian heatmap is generated centered at the polygon centroid. This annotation protocol raises several concerns: (1) four keypoints are a very coarse representation of a tissue interaction zone, particularly for irregular or elongated anatomical structures, (2) the paper provides no information about annotator qualifications; whether annotations were performed by surgeons or trained laparoscopic experts, how many annotators were used, or what inter-annotator agreement looks like. For a task explicitly framed around surgical safety, the reliability and clinical validity of the ground truth is paramount. If affordance regions are inconsistently or inaccurately annotated, any model trained on them inherits those errors, and the safety claims become difficult to defend. Recommendation: Report inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., keypoint displacement variance or IoU between annotators) if annotated by humans, specify annotator qualifications, and consider whether four keypoints are sufficient to capture the geometry of the affordance region or whether a more expressive annotation format such as a freehand polygon or brush mask would be more appropriate. 2.The Comparison Against Baselines Is Not Fully Fair: The proposed model is a task-specific architecture trained end-to-end on 15,638 annotated clips for the exact task of tissue affordance heatmap prediction. The baselines (Molmo-VLM, QWEN-8B, and SAM3) are general-purpose foundation models fine-tuned only with regression heads for vertex prediction or segmentation, and their outputs are post-hoc converted to heatmaps via Gaussian centering. This comparison is inherently asymmetric: the proposed model has a significant architectural and training advantage by design. Furthermore, the heatmap conversion from predicted polygon vertices introduces an additional source of error for the baselines that does not apply to the proposed model. The conclusion that “task-specific architecture outperforms large-scale foundation models” is expected and unjustifiable given this setup and does not tell us much about the core architectural choices. Recommendation: Include at least one more competitive baseline, for example, a simpler task-specific model such as a UNet or ViT-based heatmap predictor trained on the same data, to isolate the contribution of the specific architecture choices (AdaLN decoder, SigLIP conditioning, Swin backbone) from the benefit of task-specific training in general. 3.The Proposed Task Is Restricted to a Single Procedure and Six Tool-Action Pairs: The entire framework, dataset, and evaluation are scoped exclusively to laparoscopic cholecystectomy, covering only four instruments and six tool-action pairs. While the authors frame cholecystectomy as a good starting point, the broader claims about safe surgical automation and policy guidance are much harder to support when the system has only been demonstrated on one procedure. Surgical affordance needs vary substantially across procedures: robotic prostatectomy, colorectal surgery, and nephrectomy involve very different tissue types, instrument interactions, and safety constraints. The current scope also means the dataset’s tool-action pairs are heavily imbalanced: dissect-hook accounts for over 10,000 clips while cut-scissors has only 343, which may bias both training and evaluation. Recommendation: Discuss the procedure-specificity as an explicit limitation, analyze performance broken down per tool-action pair to expose the effect of class imbalance, and outline a concrete plan for extending the benchmark to additional procedures or robotic platforms as future work. 4.Temporal Context Ablation Suggests Its Contribution Is Modest, Undermining a Core Design Claim: One of the paper’s key architectural choices is the use of 256 past frames (approximately 10.6 seconds of context) encoded by the Video Swin Transformer to capture tool motion and tissue dynamics. However, Table 5 shows that removing temporal context leads to only a moderate ASSD increase of 21.48% and HD increase of 7.73%, while removing tool specification in the text prompt causes a much larger ASSD increase of 32.81%. This suggests that the single-frame image features, combined with language conditioning, carry most of the predictive signal, and that the temporal context, despite being the most computationally expensive component, provides relatively limited additional benefit. This is not adequately discussed or explained. Recommendation: As an ablation study, provide a more thorough analysis of when temporal context helps and when it does not; for example, by comparing performance on early pre-action frames (where temporal cues should matter most) versus late pre-action frames, and by visualizing what the Swin encoder actually attends to across the temporal window. 5.The Dice Score Anomaly Is Not Adequately Explained: Table 2 shows that SAM3 achieves a higher Dice score (0.18) than the proposed model (0.124), which is an inconsistency the manuscript acknowledge but dismiss by noting that SAM3 tends to predict nearly the entire tissue region. However, this explanation is not supported by any quantitative analysis, for instance, one would expect a comparison of predicted heatmap coverage area or a breakdown of Dice by tool-action pair. More importantly, the proposed model’s own Dice score of 0.124 is quite low in absolute terms, and the paper’s explanation, that it is caused by intensity distribution differences rather than boundary misalignment, is unconvincing without supporting evidence. A low Dice score in a safety-critical application is not something that should be casually set aside, as it reflects poor probabilistic calibration of the output heatmap. Recommendation: Provide a quantitative breakdown of Dice scores per tool-action pair, and address whether the low dice score has implications for the proposed safety-layer use case. 6.Safety Claims Are Not Empirically Validated: The paper’s core motivation is surgical safety, specifically, using affordance predictions as a conditioning signal for learned policies and as a safety layer to trigger early robot stopping. These are strong and clinically meaningful claims. However, the paper provides no empirical validation of either use case. There is no simulation or real-robot experiment showing that a policy conditioned on the predicted affordance maps performs better or more safely than one without, and no experiment demonstrating that the predicted heatmaps can reliably detect instrument deviation from safe zones before harmful contact occurs. The entire safety argument rests on the assumption that accurate affordance prediction translates to safety benefit, which may be plausible but unverified. Recommendation: Include at minimum a proof-of-concept simulation experiment demonstrating one of the two proposed safety modes, either policy conditioning or early stop triggering, using the predicted affordance maps, even in a simplified or synthetic setting. Without any empirical grounding, the safety claims remain speculative and should be toned down or clearly labeled as future work.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The concept of the paper as a whole is novel and is clinically very important. 2.The paper is well presented and the concept is exposed in sufficient detail. 3.The paper provides sufficient ablations to highlight the contributing components in the proposed method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: As such there no major technical weakness that the reviewer could identify in this work. However, there are some minor clarifications required along with few questions and suggestions to the authors which are listed in the other comments section.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for acknowledging our strengths﹣the novel task formulation (R4, R5), clinical importance (R4, R5), unique architecture and ablations (R1, R4, R5), novel dataset (R1, R4, R5), and clarity (R1, R5)﹣and for their feedback. 1.Clarity on annotation protocol (R1, R4, R5) Interaction zones are defined using task-specific keypoints﹣4 or 10 (grasping) points depending on action﹣to capture geometry accurately. We employed a two-stage annotation pipeline: medical/engineering students performed primary annotations, and audited by a core research team in consultation with clinicians. Quality/reliability is additionally enforced through a mandatory onboarding process (30 successfully completed cases). To minimize variance, we utilize semi-automatic tools (point tracking) which anchor predictions to anatomical landmarks and strictly reject “drift” (where points follow instruments instead of tissue). While affordance is annotated as uniformly safe polygons, we model them as gaussian distributions for dense prediction, where distance to boundary represents a transition toward non-affordance. Critically, this probability gradient is a mathematical modeling choice, not a reflection of varying safety levels. Therefore, the task is satisfied if the model recovers the area of the region, even if intensities deviate from the gaussian prior. 2.Affordance definition (R1, R4, R5) Tool-tissue affordance is the determined contact area on a tissue surface for a specific tool-action pair. We envision it to navigate the instrument toward regions where it can optimally and safely act to successfully execute an action. 3.Additional baseline (R1, R4) U-Net performs worse under the same training setup, validating efficiency of our architectural design. Model | ASSD | HD U-Net | 44.39 | 98.24 4.DICE score clarity (R1, R4) The DICE score discrepancy arises because SAM3’s binary output is post-hoc fitted to a Gaussian, a mathematical artifact that artificially matches the target distribution. Our model, however, predicts continuous probability values directly. While our model accurately localizes the affordance areas (low ASSD, HD), it receives a lower DICE score because it does not perfectly replicate the idealized Gaussian distribution. We argue the intensity mismatch that lowers our DICE score is a mathematical artifact from design choice, not a failure, and precise spatial localization is far more critical for surgical safety than the exact fit of a probabilistic prior. 5.Dataset collection and model generalizability (R4, R5) We distinguish between case: full recordings from unique operation and clip: temporal windows extracted from cases to represent singular tool-action pairs. Each case (that includes all its clips) is assigned exclusively to either the training / test set to prevent data leakage. Because each case is an independent table-top study, they represent a diverse distribution. This variety allows for a robust validation of model generalization, as the individual procedures present unique environmental conditions that make a leave-one-source-out evaluation redundant. 6.Role of temporal context (R4, R5) Our temporal window captures tool-tissue dynamics across viewpoints to model deformation and intent, also providing robustness against occlusions and motion blur. Our analysis shows that temporal context is critical in the early pre-action phase: a single-frame model suffers a 39% degradation in ASSD and 19% in HD. Model | ASSD | HD Baseline Model with Temporal Context on early pre-action frames | 22.93 | 85.71 Model w/o Temporal Context on early pre-action frames | 31.95 | 102.70 This proves temporal context is essential for providing reliable guidance at the start of a maneuver.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces tissue affordance prediction as a dense heatmap estimation task conditioned on tool–action language prompts, alongside a sizable benchmark curated from laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos. Reviewers agree that the task formulation is novel and clinically meaningful, and that the dataset and ablation studies represent a solid contribution. However, several issues limit the strength of the current claims. The annotation protocol lacks sufficient clinical rigor for a safety‑motivated task (coarse keypoint polygons, unclear annotator expertise, no agreement analysis), and the baseline comparisons are asymmetric, comparing a task‑specific model against general‑purpose foundation models. Absolute performance remains problematic, particularly the low Dice score, which is insufficiently analyzed despite being critical in a safety context. The work is also restricted to a single procedure with heavy class imbalance, and the claimed safety applications (policy conditioning, early stopping) are not empirically validated, leaving a gap between motivation and evidence. To strengthen the paper, the authors should ensuring the claims are fully supported by the evaluation, clarify and justify the annotation and evaluation choices, discuss the limitations of procedure scope and metrics. They should also refrain from grand safety claims and over emphasis on robotic automation unless supported by concrete validation. Authors should address each concern raised by the reviewers. | While the authors clarified the annotation pipeline, added a U‑Net baseline, and better explained temporal modelling, some concerns remain unresolved. In particular, the low Dice score is not convincingly addressed, annotation reliability lacks inter‑annotator agreement evidence, generalization is unsupported (no cross-source evaluation), and the safety claims remain unvalidated. Overall, reviewers lean towards Acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers’ concerns have been successfully addressed in the rebuttal, making the work a solid contribution especially for what concerns methodological applications in CAI.

title: AGGRNet: Selective Feature Extraction and Aggregation for Enhanced Medical Image Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: They proposed AGGRNet based on YOLOv11 backbone, with a novel FEA block as the key module for extracting informative and non-informative features, while capturing global spatial dependencies. This network is appropriately designed and sound.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1)The evaluation experiments are somewhat ambiguous. On different datasets, the authors compared AGGRNet with different methods using different metrics. Why can’t they adopt a unified comparison strategy? Also, is this comparative design fair? Did the authors performed the comparisons under the unified experimental settings or just adopted the results in the original papers of these methods? (2)In table 3, the Acc values of YOLOv11 backbone + C2PCA + FEA@1,2 and YOLOv11 backbone + C2PCA + FEA@1 are not higher then that of YOLOv11 backbone + C2PCA. I think the author needs to provide an explanation for this result.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The “informative/non-informative” split is produced by combining spatial and channel attention, thresholding the result, and then feeding the masked tensors into a custom attention block. It looks like a modest repackaging of existing attention machinery with a hand-crafted masking rule. Likewise, replacing YOLOv11’s C2PSA with a channel-attention variant called C2PCA is incremental.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: -The paper presents AGGRNet as a unified solution for severity grading and disease subtype classification, but both are still standard image classification tasks in this context. Prior work already addresses these applications, including CDW-CE for ulcerative colitis severity estimation [15], SATOMIL for ordinal UC grading [19], and HiFuse for medical image classification [7]. -The comparative methods are not recent; for example, newer approaches such as Mamba-based models or recent hybrid transformer architectures are not included, which weakens the comparison. -The ablation study in Table 3 does not evaluate the most important design choices, such as hard vs. soft masking, the threshold parameter itself, or alternative Q/K/V definitions. -Much of the paper combines previously proposed modules. For example, separating “informative” and “non-informative” features is closely related to existing attention-based feature reweighting methods such as CBAM [24]. Similarly, combining local features with global representations has already been explored in works like HiFuse [7], Conformer [12], and UniFormer [8].
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The motivation is clear and I think it is clinically relevant. Distinguishing between diagnostically important regions and irrelevant background is a genuine challenge in medical imaging, especially for things like ulcerative colitis grading where adjacent severity grades can look almost identical. The paper explains this problem well and the reader understands from the beginning why this matters.The mathematical formulation of the cross-attention in FAM is one of the more interesting parts. Using the sum and difference of informative and non-informative features as Q and K respectively is a creative way to build an attention bias toward relevant regions. The authors also provide a mathematical breakdown of why this works which I appreciated, even if it could be explained more intuitively.Testing across five different datasets from different medical imaging domains is a strength. It gives at least some evidence that the approach is not just overfitting to one specific problem or dataset.The ablation study is done properly. Each component is added one at a time and the accuracy is tracked at each step. This makes it easy to see what is actually contributing to the final result.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My biggest concern is the binary thresholding in the FEM module. The authors use a hard threshold tau to split features into informative and non-informative using a binary mask. This operation is not differentiable. I have not seen any explanation in the paper of how gradients are supposed to flow through this step during backpropagation. This is not a minor detail, it is a fundamental question about whether the module can actually be trained end-to-end the way the authors describe. The rebuttal must address this clearly. The choice of YOLOv11 as a classification backbone is unusual and I think it is not well justified. YOLO architectures are designed for detection tasks and using them for pure classification in medical imaging is not standard. I have noticed that some of the performance gains might simply come from the YOLOv11 backbone being a stronger starting point than the older baselines like ResNet18 or even HiFuse, rather than from the FEA module itself. A fairer comparison would be to plug FEA into a standard classification backbone and show the gains independently. The baseline comparisons are not always up to date. On LIMUC for example most baselines are from 2021 and 2022.There are more recent methods that are missing. Claiming state-of-the-art on all five datasets while comparing against older baselines is a strong claim that is hard to fully trust. There is no report of inference time or computational overhead from the FEA module. For clinical deployment this matters and the paper completely ignores it. There is also no experiment on cross-dataset generalization or domain shift. All five datasets are evaluated independently. In real clinical settings models often have to deal with data from different scanners or institutions and there is no discussion of this at all. One small but notable issue: the paper title in the PDF header reads “Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length” which is a LaTeX formatting error that should have been fixed before submission.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback and insightful comments and for recognizing the novelty of the FEA design, its clear clinical motivation and the consistent performance gains demonstrated across diverse datasets. R1: As stated in Section 3.3, metric selection for each dataset follows those reported in SOTA literature. Although we evaluated AGGRNet across all metrics, we report only those aligned with prior work to ensure direct comparability. A unified retraining of all baselines may introduce inconsistencies with established standards; thus, we adopt results from original papers. For Table 3, we agree that clarification is needed. The observation that partial FEA placement (e.g., FEA@1 or FEA@1,2) does not outperform the backbone validates our design principle (Sec. 2.2): FEA is effective when applied hierarchically across multiple depths. Only FEA@1,2,3 enables proper multi-scale aggregation, where deep semantic and shallow spatial features interact effectively. R2: We clarify that our contribution is not redefining classification tasks, but introducing an architecture-agnostic feature extraction mechanism applicable across diverse medical imaging scenarios. “Unified” refers to: (1)handling both ordinal severity grading(LIMUC, RetinaMNIST) and multi-class classification (ISIC, Kvasir, PathMNIST), (2)requiring no task-specific modifications (unlike CDW-CE or SATOMIL) and (3)generalizing across modalities (endoscopy, dermoscopy, histopathology, retinal imaging). Regarding recent models, Table 2 includes recent hybrid methods SATOMIL’25, HiFuse’24, UniFormer’23, etc. Mamba-based approaches (eg, XFMamba) target multi-view datasets, while AGGRNet focuses on single-view medical imaging. Extending to multi-view settings is an important direction for future work. We conducted additional ablations (omitted in the paper due to space): (a)Hard vs soft masking: nearly identical performance; hard masking chosen for efficiency and interpretability. (b)Q/K/V variants: multiple alternatives were tested; our formulation consistently performed best with mathematical justification in Sec 2.1.While prior works (CBAM, HiFuse) perform feature reweighting or fusion, FEA differs fundamentally with explicit feature segregation, cross-attention between informative and non-informative features and contrast-based interaction (Eq. 6), enabling richer representation learning. R3: We use a Straight-Through Estimator (STE) that backpropagates gradients through non-differentiable operations. We employ hard binary masking in the forward pass and approximate the backward pass with an identity mapping (gradients bypass binarization), enabling end-to-end training. Empirically τ converges to meaningful values, and similar performance with soft masking confirms stable gradient flow. To address concerns on backbone bias, we demonstrate architecture-agnostic gains with FEA (Table 3), ResNet18 (+1.5%) and YOLOv11+C2PCA (+1.4%). These confirm improvements stem from FEA, not the backbone. YOLOv11 was chosen for its efficient multi-scale design (C3K2, SPPF), providing a strong testbed. We include recent baselines (e.g., SATOMIL 2025, HiFuse 2024), while older models demonstrate generalizability across CNN, transformer, and hybrid architectures. For efficiency, we report parameter counts in Table 2.AGGRNet (38.65M) is more compact than HiFuse-Base (127.8M). While parameters and FLOPs are not strictly proportional, lower parameterization generally implies reduced computational and memory overhead. AGGRNet was validated on five public datasets spanning diverse modalities, acquisition settings and clinical tasks with some datasets inherently reflecting inter-hospital variability. Eg, ISIC 2018 includes multi-institutional data, capturing real-world variation in skin lesion appearance. These results indicate generalizability and robustness of AGGRNet across diverse medical imaging settings. We will fix the LaTeX formatting issue in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a method for medical image classification. All reviewers commented about the method contributions. However, there are several important questions that should be addressed in the rebuttal, including the gradient flow through the binary mask in the FEM module, the choice of YOLOv11 as a classification backbone, baseline comparisons, validation of design choices, and the novelty of the method. | Two reviewers have recommended accept while one reviewer recommended reject. The initial comments about more comparison with more recent methods were addressed in the rebuttal. One of the reviewers is still concerned about limited novelty. Considering the efficiency of the method, general applicability on different backbones, and good performance across multiple datasets, this paper might be accepted. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper presents a medical image classification framework with feature separation and aggregation modules, and the reported results across multiple datasets are promising. However, after considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend rejection because the current submission remains below the acceptance threshold for a methodological contribution. 1) The methodological novelty is limited. The core idea of separating informative and less-informative features through spatial/channel attention and then aggregating them is closely related to existing attention-based feature reweighting and fusion mechanisms. The C2PCA modification is also an incremental replacement of self-attention with channel attention. The rebuttal clarifies the authors’ intention, but does not sufficiently establish a clearly new technical contribution beyond a recombination of existing attention and feature fusion designs. 2) The baseline comparison is not sufficiently convincing. The paper compares different methods across different datasets using dataset-specific metrics and, in several cases, appears to rely on results from prior papers rather than a unified retraining protocol. Some baseline sets are also not up to date or not directly comparable to the proposed YOLOv11-based classifier. This makes it difficult to determine whether the gains come from the proposed FEA module, the backbone choice, or differences in training/evaluation settings. 3) The key design choices are not adequately validated. The ablation study does not systematically evaluate hard versus soft masking, the thresholding strategy, alternative Q/K/V definitions, or the sensitivity of the learned binary mask. These are central to the proposed FEA module. The explanation in the rebuttal, including the use of a straight-through estimator, is useful but should have been part of the submitted manuscript and supported by stronger experimental evidence. 4) The claim of a unified solution for medical image classification is somewhat overstated. The evaluated tasks remain standard image classification problems, and there is no cross-dataset or domain-shift evaluation to demonstrate robustness in realistic clinical deployment settings. Given the incremental nature of the method, stronger and more controlled evidence would be needed to justify this broad claim. Overall, although the paper is clearly motivated and reports competitive results, its technical novelty and experimental rigor are not sufficient for acceptance as a methodological MICCAI paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is recommended for acceptance based on its compelling clinical motivation, sound methodological formulation, and comprehensive validation across diverse medical imaging domains. Reviewers recognized the structural novelty of the Feature Extraction and Aggregation (FEA) module for effectively separating informative disease morphology from non-informative background cues.

title: Attenuation-Resilient Alternating Optimization for Laparoscopic Liver Landmark Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper tackles an important and clinically relevant problem in laparoscopic liver surgery. The motivation is clear and well-justified, particularly regarding illumination issues and structural continuity. The proposed architecture is coherent and integrates complementary ideas (appearance enhancement + geometric modeling). The alternating optimization between segmentation and curve modeling is interesting and addresses a known limitation of segmentation-based approaches. The method is evaluated on multiple datasets with consistent improvements. The ablation study is thorough and demonstrates the contribution of individual components. The paper is technically sound and well-positioned within the literature.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The performance gains over strong baselines (e. g. , D2GPLand+) are relatively modest (~1–2%), raising questions about practical significance. The proposed framework is complex, combining multiple modules (IFC, FOSF, ASCO, depth estimation, SAM encoder), but lacks analysis of computational cost and inference time. There is no discussion on real-time applicability, which is critical for intraoperative surgical use. The evaluation is limited to segmentation metrics (DSC, IoU, ASSD), without demonstrating clinical impact or integration into AR navigation systems. Curve-based methods are excluded from comparison, which is questionable given the explicit curve modeling contribution. The illumination compensation component appears incremental relative to existing enhancement approaches. The paper lacks analysis of failure cases and robustness under challenging conditions (e. g. , occlusion, bleeding, specular reflections).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper presents and explains the method clearly. 2.Ablations in Tab2, clearly show the importance of various components in the method. 3.The scope of the current work is stated well to a certain extent. 4.Comparison to piror-works and networks is well established in Tab1 and visually supposed in Fig1,3.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There as such no weakness of the paper, however some sections need clarifications which are mentioned in the additional comments section below.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Well-motivated and clearly structured problem formulation. The paper identifies two concrete, practically relevant failure modes — illumination attenuation and the localization-continuity tradeoff — and designs dedicated modules for each. The introduction provides clear visual examples (Fig. 1) of blue-circle attenuation errors, yellow-circle segmentation false positives, and pink-circle endpoint localization failures that motivate the approach. S2.Technically sound module design with principled foundations. Each component is technically well-motivated and clearly described: the IFC block builds on a reflectance-illumination decomposition assumption (akin to Retinex, though the paper does not use that term) with a learnable intensity collapse (Eq. 1); the FOSF module combines Haar wavelet frequency analysis with Gabor orientation filtering; and the ASCO decoder models landmarks as Bezier curves with soft rasterization (Eq. 4) and differentiable control-point updates (Eq. 5). The interplay is well-articulated: IFC addresses appearance, FOSF addresses feature-level texture suppression, and ASCO addresses the output-level geometry gap. S3.Thorough ablation study demonstrating component complementarity. Table 2 systematically isolates the contribution of each module (IFC, L_illum, FOSF, ASCO, L_curve) through six progressive variants, showing that each addition yields measurable improvement. Adding L_illum to IFC (V1→V2) yields the largest single-step DSC gain (+2.22%), and further combining with FOSF (V2→V4: +2.03%) produces a substantial cumulative improvement, validating the complementarity of illumination compensation and frequency filtering. S4.Comprehensive baseline comparison. The paper benchmarks against 16 methods across three categories (general segmentation, SAM-based adaptation, task-specific detection), providing a well-contextualised evaluation landscape. The consistent improvement across all three datasets and all three metrics (DSC, IoU, ASSD) lends credibility to the approach. S5.Clean mathematical exposition. The equations are well-defined and the notation is consistent throughout. The paper makes the training pipeline clear (end-to-end with joint supervision, Eq. 6) and specifies all key hyperparameters.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1.No uncertainty estimates or statistical significance tests. (General Review Consideration §5, §6) The paper reports single-point performance numbers throughout Tables 1 and 2 with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Given that the improvements over D2GPLand+ are modest — 1.85% DSC on L3D-2K, 0.69% DSC on L3D, and 0.87% DSC on P2ILF — it is not possible to assess whether these gains are statistically meaningful. The number of training runs, random seed policy, and variance across seeds are not disclosed. Without at least a paired test or multi-seed standard deviation, the evidence for superiority over D2GPLand+ is incomplete. W2.Notable validation–test performance gap unexplained. The ablation study (Table 2) is conducted on the L3D-2K validation set, where the full A2ONet achieves DSC 45.16% / IoU 33.76%. However, Table 1 reports DSC 53.51% / IoU 38.32% on the L3D-2K test set — an 8.35% DSC gap favouring the test set. This is unusual (typically validation and test performance are comparable or test is slightly lower) and warrants explanation. Possible causes include different data characteristics between splits or overfitting to validation-set early stopping, but the paper does not discuss this discrepancy. W3.No inference time or model complexity analysis. (Clinical significance — General Review Consideration §1) The paper motivates A2ONet for intraoperative anatomy guidance and AR-guided laparoscopic interventions, so reporting runtime, parameter count, or FLOPs would help assess practical deployability. Yet no inference speed (FPS), parameter count, or FLOPs are reported. The architecture includes a ResNet-34 encoder, a frozen SAM-b encoder, Depth Anything V2 for monocular depth estimation, Haar wavelet transforms, Gabor filtering, and a multi-stage ASCO decoder with cross-attention — these components together likely carry a non-trivial computational cost. Without runtime analysis, the practical applicability for the stated clinical use case remains unclear. W4.Minimal discussion of limitations and failure cases. (General Review Consideration §8) The conclusion mentions no limitations at all. A brief sentence states A2ONet “provides a stable and robust prerequisite for AR-guided navigation,” but no failure case analysis is provided. Given the moderate absolute performance on L3D-2K (53.51% DSC), understanding where and why the method fails — for example across landmark types, illumination conditions, or unusual anatomy — would be valuable. W5.P2ILF evaluation protocol is non-standard. The paper acknowledges that P2ILF’s official testing set is unavailable, so it subdivides the 167-image training set into 124 train / 43 test. This means (a) results are not directly comparable with future work that uses the official test set, and (b) 43 test images is very small, amplifying variance concerns (further supporting W1). The paper does not discuss this limitation. W6.Curve-based evaluation absent. The paper acknowledges excluding “curve-only methods” because their evaluation protocol “precludes fair benchmarking against mask-based predictors.” However, since a core contribution is the explicit Bezier curve modeling (ASCO), it would strengthen the paper to report curve-specific metrics (e.g., endpoint localization error, Frechet distance between predicted and ground-truth curves) that directly validate this contribution. Relying solely on mask-based metrics (DSC, IoU, ASSD) may not fully capture the benefit of curve modeling. W7.Data diversity and label quality not discussed. (General Review Considerations §3, §4) The three datasets are from the same clinical domain (laparoscopic liver surgery), but the paper does not discuss patient demographics, inter-annotator agreement for landmark labeling, or how annotation noise might affect the thin curvilinear structures being detected. Given that the paper does not report inter-rater agreement, annotation protocol details, or label uncertainty for thin curvilinear landmarks, this omission is notable. W8.Depth estimation dependency not ablated. The paper uses Depth Anything V2 for monocular depth estimation as input to the frozen SAM encoder. This is a significant design choice, yet no ablation examines A2ONet’s sensitivity to depth quality or compares against using no depth input. The absence of such analysis leaves the depth modality’s contribution and the method’s robustness to depth estimation errors unclear.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for recognizing the clinical relevance and motivation (R1, R3), clear presentation (R2), and consistent multi-dataset improvements (R1, R3) of our work. We address the remaining concerns below: Q1.Statistical significance (R1, R3): We have performed significance tests against D2GPLand+ on all three datasets, confirming our statistically significant improvements. We will report the mean±std results. Beyond DSC and IoU, A2ONet also substantially reduces ASSD, supporting improved boundary localization. Q2.Model complexity and efficiency (R1, R3): Although A2ONet integrates multiple modules, its trainable components are lightweight, relying mainly on convolutions and gating operations. The computational cost and inference speed are comparable to other SAM-based methods, reaching real-time inference. Q3.Curve-based evaluation (R1, R3): Our current comparison focuses on mask-based metrics to ensure consistency with existing segmentation benchmarks, but we agree that they may not fully reflect the benefit of explicit curve modeling. In future work, we will develop more comprehensive landmark evaluation metrics, including curve-specific metrics, to enable fairer comparison between mask- and curve-based methods. Q4.Design of IFC block and visualization (R1, R2): Unlike general low-light enhancement, our setting mainly suffers from spatially non-uniform laparoscopic illumination, with central saturation and peripheral attenuation. IFC is therefore designed as a lightweight task-oriented module to compensate this specific attenuation pattern without introducing heavy enhancement networks, preserving clinical efficiency. We sincerely thank R2 for this suggestion. The illumination-perturbation ablation would be helpful to assess prediction stability under different illumination settings. Q5.Depth-modality justification (R3): Our encoder design follows D2GPLand+, whose depth-modality ablation (Table 10) demonstrates that adding depth features clearly improves performance over RGB-only input, and using a stronger depth estimator further improves the results. This supports that depth provides useful geometric cues for landmark detection. Q6.Parameter clarification and convergence (R2, R3): We will clarify that the logit function is: logit(x)=log(x/1−x), where x is clamped to [10^−6, 1–10^−6] for numerical stability. We will also specify all hyperparameters, including λcurve=0.2, λillum=0.1, and the top-K=16.Ablations on key parameters and curve-update convergence will be included in future extended work. Q7.Dataset protocol and characteristics (R3): The validation-test gap on L3D-2K is mainly due to the distribution difference between the patient-level validation and test set. Similar gap are also observed in D2GPLand+ under the same dataset setting, as reflected in Table 2 (test set) and Table 4 (validation set). For P2ILF, we will release our code to facilitate future comparison. Despite the small test set, our improvements remain statistically significant. We will also discuss data diversity, annotation quality, and label uncertainty in journal version. Q8.Limitations and clinical validation (R1-R3): Due to the inherent difficulty of curvilinear structure segmentation in laparoscopic liver images, the absolute segmentation metrics leave room for improvement, especially in failure cases such as ambiguous junctions between silhouettes/ridges and ligaments, and false predictions under tissue or instrument occlusion. Our method is robust against reflections and there are few bleeding incidents in current datasets. We will further validate the detected landmarks in downstream pre-to-intraoperative 2D-3D liver registration to assess their clinical utility for AR guidance in the future.

title: B-spline Activations as Intrinsic Uncertainty Estimators in Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Novelty - The application of KAN activations as a signal of support is novel, to the best of my knowledge. Applicable method - Authors claim the FPS supports real-time deployment.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Statistical evaluation - the E-AURC table would benefit from std values and a statistical support for claims and comparisons should be added. Unclear scope - While the authors show that the uncertainty signal carried by B-spline activation reflects distributional coverage, they do not explain if there is a relation between distributional coverage and model confidence, and in particular whether pixel, segment, or boundary reliability capture the true confidence that can be useful in practice. For example, it is not clear if the per-pixel uncertainty represented by entropy in B-spline activations can be calibrated to inform decisions beyond the ranking task that is demoed in the paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper proposes a novel perspective on uncertainty estimation by linking activation dispersion in KAN layers to prediction uncertainty. The interpretation of local B-spline support as a proxy for data density is intuitive and provides a clear conceptual foundation. The proposed Residual KAN Head is lightweight and can be incorporated into existing segmentation architectures with minimal overhead, without requiring repeated inference or modifications to the training objective. Efficient single-pass uncertainty estimation: The method enables uncertainty estimation in a single forward pass and is substantially faster than multi-pass approaches such as MC Dropout and test-time augmentation, making it attractive for real-time applications. The approach achieves competitive or superior uncertainty estimation performance across multiple datasets and backbones, while preserving segmentation accuracy. No degradation of primary task performance: In contrast to some alternative single-pass methods, the proposed approach maintains segmentation accuracy across all evaluated settings. The method is validated on several medical imaging benchmarks and backbone models, supporting its general applicability. Initial ablation analysis: The paper includes an ablation study investigating architectural components (e.g., the role of the KAN head and grid size), providing initial insight into the behavior of the method. The figures are very well designed and help to illustrate the core ideas of the paper effectively.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While an ablation study is provided, it is relatively narrow in scope and does not sufficiently disentangle the contribution of key design choices (e.g., spline order). The current analysis (e.g., Table 4) remains limited and could be better structured to provide clearer insights. While the method is significantly faster than multi-pass approaches, it is slightly slower than other single-pass methods. This trade-off is not clearly discussed, which somewhat weakens the efficiency argument. Certain aspects of the training procedure and integration of the Residual KAN Head (e.g., whether training is fully end-to-end or partially frozen) are not explicitly described, which makes the method harder to fully assess. Some sections lack sufficient explanation (e.g., the “Inference Efficiency” section contains little to no descriptive text), and certain tables or formatting choices (e.g., Table 4 structure) reduce clarity.

reviewer_3_strengths: Major strengths: the technique presented in the paper is tested on 4 data sets, which is a good approach (enough to be convincing) this technique needs a very small number of additional parameters which shows that it is powerful this method is shown to be around 7 times faster than well-known TTA, deep ensembles, and MC DropOut, which seems very promising for real time applications the main ways to compute uncertainty are recalled in the state of the Art (MC Dropout, deep ensembles, and Test Time Augmentation for multiple pass algorithms and single pass algorithms), so it seems complete the ablation study is correctly done in this context

Is it the epistemic one ? or the random one ? this should be recalled and detailed. it seems hard to understand the way the uncertainty can be computed in only one pass, some diagrams or pictures might be be missing I see no picture of spline activation function with a finite/Local support, so it is hard to understand exactly how they are utilized and why it is so important here to have a local support. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the feedback. We address the AC’s convergent themes below. 1.SCOPE OF UNCERTAINTY [R1, R3, AC]. Our signal captures an epistemic component of predictive reliability arising from limited training-data coverage, not a full Bayesian decomposition. Local-support B-spline bases concentrate activation where inputs are well-covered during training and disperse it where coverage is sparse. Fig. 3 supports this: misclassified pixels show significantly higher activation entropy than correct ones (Cohen’s d up to 1.61, all p<0.001), and boundary pixels exceed interior ones (d up to 1.43)—confirming coverage-to-reliability and pixel-level discriminability. We will clarify in Sec. 2.1.2.STATISTICAL EVALUATION [R1, AC]. Per-cell ±std (3 seeds) computed; std on best cells is small (e.g., ISIC/UNet 18.7±1.2). Wilcoxon signed-rank across 12 backbone×dataset settings: Ours significantly outperforms Softmax (11/12, p=0.0015) and achieves statistical parity with the strongest multi-pass baselines (TTA×8 p=0.42, MC Dropout×10 p=0.79) as well as EDL (p=0.79), while running 6.9–8.9× faster than multi-pass methods and preserving Dice unlike EDL. Full results will be added to Table 2.3.APPLIED FRAMING [R1, AC]. Our framework targets selective prediction (Sec. 2.3): uncertainty ranks images so unreliable cases can be deferred for clinician review. Ranking and calibration address distinct clinical needs—ranking supports triage prioritization (our focus); calibration supports threshold-based automation. Fig. 4 demonstrates the practical sufficiency of ranking: at 50% coverage, our curve approaches the oracle on ISIC/UNet and clearly outperforms TTA/MC Dropout, confirming frame-level uncertainty supports the “defer top-k uncertain cases” workflow without absolute confidence thresholds. Because activation entropy is a continuous scalar, it remains compatible with post-hoc calibration (e.g., temperature scaling) if threshold decisions are needed. 4.LOCAL SUPPORT VISUALIZATION [R3]. Fig. 2 shows per-basis activation intensity but not Bk(x) themselves. We will add a compact-support Bk(x) inset and a brief B-spline definition in Sec. 2.1.The one-pass mechanism: during a standard forward pass, the KAN layer evaluates B-spline bases for each input feature; we read the distribution of these already-computed values as uncertainty, no additional computation needed. 5.COMPUTATIONAL PERFORMANCE [R2, R3, AC]. Our claim concerns sequential repeated inference in latency-sensitive workflows (not all multi-pass methods). Table 3: TTA 100.69 ms; MC Dropout 129.48 ms; ours 14.60 ms. Among single-pass methods, our 1.1× overhead (14.60 vs. 12.79 ms) is slightly above Softmax (13.12) and EDL (13.5). However, Softmax ranks significantly worse (p=0.0015); EDL requires loss modification and degrades Dice up to 2.5%. Ours maintains Dice (<0.3%) without altering training, matching EDL in win count (6/12 each) while preserving accuracy across all settings. 6.ABLATION SCOPE AND TRAINING [R2]. Table 4 isolates grid size G and residual structure, the two largest empirical factors. We fix S=2 and acknowledge spline-order sensitivity is not experimentally disentangled. Mechanistically, G directly controls the resolution of the basis decomposition (K=G+S) and is the dominant factor, as the G=5→3 effect (E-AURC 82.1→50.8) confirms. Training is fully end-to-end with no frozen components. 7.REPRODUCIBILITY AND MINOR ISSUES [R1, R2, R3]. Upon acceptance we will release code, checkpoints, and config files with a reproducibility checklist; we will also expand Sec. 3.4, update arXiv refs, simplify Table 4, and fix Sec. 3.3 formatting. We hope these clarifications address the reviewers’ and AC’s concerns; all promised revisions will be incorporated in the camera-ready.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes an uncertainty estimation method for image segmentation using b-spline activation functions. The reviews diverge in appreciation, note potential relevance to the field, but also converge on major concerns: unclear scope of uncertainty and motivation of application, limitations in the experimental evaluation, concerns on computational performance. A rebuttal should clarify these points with realistically minor changes to the manuscript. For these reasons, the recommendation is to request a rebuttal. | The rebuttal was helpful in addressing the reviewer concerns on a statistical validation, computational efficiency, and methodological scope. A consensus has been reached to recommended for acceptance due to the practical value and novelty of its single-pass uncertainty estimation approach. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend rejection. The paper studies an interesting direction—using B-spline/KAN activation patterns as a single-pass uncertainty signal for medical image segmentation—but the current evidence is not sufficiently convincing for acceptance. The central claim that B-spline activation dispersion serves as an intrinsic uncertainty estimator remains largely heuristic and empirically under-validated; the pixel-level statistics show correlation with errors/boundaries, but do not establish reliable uncertainty estimation, calibration, or density-awareness. Experimentally, the results are mixed. The proposed method achieves the best E-AURC in only 4 of 12 settings, while multi-pass baselines often outperform it despite higher cost. The advantage over single-pass alternatives is also not decisive, as EDL is competitive or better in several cases. Important uncertainty baselines discussed in the paper, such as DUQ, SNGP, DDU, or deep ensembles, are not evaluated. The validation sets are also small for some datasets, and the paper lacks stronger statistical testing, calibration analysis, OOD/domain-shift evaluation, and broader ablations. Overall, while the idea is potentially useful, the novelty and empirical support are currently insufficient. The claims about intrinsic uncertainty estimation and clinical real-time applicability are stronger than what the presented results justify. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a useful single-pass uncertainty quantification method with competitive performance. The authors have properly addressed reviewers’ concerns, including outlying the scope and significance of their results.

title: Bayesian Temporal Pose Networks for Uncertainty-Calibrated Laparoscopic Tool Pose Tracking
reviewer_1_strengths: A key strength of the work is the dual contribution of both a new methodology and the curation of specialized datasets for validation. By incorporating kinematic motion knowledge via a hierarchical temporal transformer, the model effectively addresses the challenges of monocular tracking. Furthermore, the inclusion of Bayesian uncertainty provides a critical layer of reliability, offering a calibrated confidence metric that is essential for the transition toward objective, automated skill assessment in clinical training.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Ground Truth Validation and EM Sensor Calibration There are significant technical omissions regarding the use of Electromagnetic (EM) sensors for ground truth. The manuscript does not detail the calibration procedure used to align the EM motion sensors with the video coordinate domain. Furthermore, the inherent accuracy and error margins of the sensors themselves are not reported. A critical concern is the sensor placement on the tool shaft to estimate the position of the tool tips; this extrapolation can introduce significant kinematic errors, especially if the tool experiences any flexing. Additionally, of metallic interference on EM sensor may impact readings. 2.Clarification of Temporal Resolutions and Labeling The authors introduce a Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT) with resolutions categorized as “micro-gesture,” “medium,” and “global. “ However, it is unclear whether these categories are supported by explicit gesture labeling or if they are merely theoretical designations for specific temporal windows. The distinction between the “medium” and “global” window masks is particularly ambiguous. The methodology for these temporal scales is primarily conveyed through a model diagram, which lacks the detail necessary for a systematic technical analysis. 3.Model Reproducibility To ensure reproducibility more granular detail on the model parameters and architecture is required. Given the complexity the model , I believe a formal commitment to publishing the source code would be very important
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors contribute a novel formulation that enables accurate 7-DoF pose tracking for non-robotic laparoscopic instruments using only monocular video, effectively eliminating the reliance on unavailable geometric or CAD priors by substituting them with a self-supervised kinematic foundation model trained on electromagnetic data. This methodological innovation is rigorously substantiated by a thorough ablation study in Table 2b, which quantitatively isolates the contribution of each architectural component. For instance, removing the kinematic prior degrades position RMSE from 6.8 mm to 25.3 mm, clearly demonstrating that the kinematic foundation model provide distinct, necessary value rather than redundant processing.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Clarity of Architecture Visualization: While Section 2.3 describes the network components, Figure 2 is densely packed with numerous modules, making it difficult to trace the exact data flow without significant cognitive load. A step-by-step walkthrough in the caption or a simplified schematic alongside the detailed diagram would improve accessibility for readers attempting to replicate the method. 2.Incomplete Justification for Dataset Limitations: While Table 1 indicates missing jaw annotations for Dataset C with a dash, and Table 2c reflects this as “N/A,” the manuscript does not explicitly explain why this data is unavailable. Providing specific context on whether Dataset C utilized instruments without magnetic jaw sensors would clarify the scope of Out-of-Distribution testing and improve reproducibility for future researchers attempting to replicate these benchmarks.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The major strength of the paper is the proposed bayesian temporal pose network that fuses visual and kinematic cues to provide accurate 6DoF pose estimation including calibrated uncertainties.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weaknesses are missing details in the description and limited comparison to state of the art methods. These make it difficult to judge the novelty and validity of the approach. Authors should include more information on the dataset, how accurate the ground-truthing EM sensor works and how the data was prepared for training or testing of visual or kinematic models. I could not find any information related to the self-supervised training of the kinematic foundation model. Likewise, it is not described how the visual and kinematic features are fused by the BTPN. Figure 2 is laden with low level details that make it hard to read but seemingly is missing important high level details like how the different models are fused. The state of the art comparison seems incomplete. Authors only compare to one published paper [9] and then some other reference architectures that they implemented themselves. It is not described how authors trained the comparison methods on their dataset. Authors should include more published references for 6DoF pose estimation such as https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icte.2024.01.002 or 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3647882
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the valuable comments and feedback. Major concerns are grouped by theme: 1.Clarification of Temporal Resolutions (R1#2) Sec 2.3 details resolutions as “local for micro-gestures (grasp onset, release timing), medium for purposeful actions (reach, transfer, place) and global for the full sequence”. The dataset contains explicit gesture labelling, though not used in this work, with durations: reach (~1.07s), grasp (~1.22s), transfer (~2.40s) and place (~2.01s). These clinical actions supported the motivation of the medium resolution, with local micro-gestures within these longer phases. 2.Clarity of Architecture Visualization (R2#1, R3#3, MR#1) Whilst Sec 2.3 already gives the high-level flow, we agree with the reviewers that more could be done to simplify the diagram. Redundant information such as the grey text could easily be removed, without changing the figure’s meaning. For clarity, we will add detailed captions to explain every component with high-level details in the BTPN. The code will be released and allow exact method replication. Foundation model is pre-trained with masked-frame reconstruction (see Sec 2.5). The fine-tuning is used to predict the next coordinates given previous frames, primarily learning encoding embeddings for the different temporal resolutions. Fig 2 also shows the use of multi-head attention, utilising visual embeddings as queries and kinematic embeddings as keys and values, to obtain a fused visual-kinematic 256D embedding. We will clarify these in the revised paper. 3.Limited Comparison (R3) Both suggested papers were considered. Shabir et al., cited as [18], collects its data from a robotic arm moving a single instrument at a fixed centre-of-motion. They recover tip position and shaft-axis vector under a cylindrical-shaft assumption. However, our data is bimanual, marker-less, EM-tracked, human-free peg-transfer videos. Running their method requires rebuilding both the data-acquisition assumption and the geometric pose head, effectively making it a new method rather than a comparison. Similarly, Lu et al. output 2D pixel coordinates, so the output space is not directly comparable to our 3D pose metric. We compared with ART-Net [9] as it is the closest in setting to ours, making it a fair representative of the geometric-prior class. Due to data novelty, we further implemented 4 common temporal architectures and 4 component ablations to benchmark each design choice. 4.EM Sensor Validation (R1#1, R3#2, MR#2) Sec 2.1 states using the NDI Aurora system to obtain ground truth kinematics. It has a manufacturer-specified 0.48mm RMSE position and 0.3deg RMSE orientation. We performed calibration by 1) rotating the tool about the shaft axis to obtain offset of sensor from central and rotation tool shaft axes, 2) apply pointed cap to end of the tool with known distance from axis we wish to calibrate to (jaw hinge) and then a pivot calibration, 3) finally fix shaft in flat position compared with a world reference to get axial rotation around shaft. All trials were recorded on a non-ferrous box trainer, keeping metallic interference well below the system’s published drift threshold. The rigid tool shafts and light peg-transfer loads produced no measurable bending and kept a fixed transformation between the coils and tooltips. 5.Dataset Limitations and Reproducibility (R1#3, R2#2, MR#3) Datasets were collected over a period of 3 years, with jaw angle sensors added only after the 1st dataset collection (unavailable in Dataset C). We marked it as OOD due to observed shifts from differences in the training box, camera, tools, and insertion angles. Due to the dataset’s large size, we were unable to make it available anonymously. However, we confirm that the full code, weights and datasets will be released on acceptance, as stated in the submission. We believe these clarifications resolve all major concerns without altering any experiments, data, or claims.
