title: BRAIN: Bi-directional Motion Reasoning with Dynamic Memory Pruning for Surgical Video Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper is motivated by realistic challenges in surgical videos, which are indeed common in clinical surgical navigation settings. Addressing these issues enhances the practical relevance of the work. 2.The proposed framework is clearly organised, with complementary modules (BMR and DM) that target different aspects of the problem. The overall design is coherent and easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not engage sufficiently with recent related work in surgical video segmentation using large foundation models, such as EndoMamba: An Efficient Foundation Model for Endoscopic Videos via Hierarchical Pre-training, Memory-Augmented SAM2 for Training-Free Surgical Video Segmentation, and ReSurgSAM2: Referring Segment Anything in Surgical Video via Credible Long-term Tracking (all MICCAI 2025). This weak positioning makes the claimed novelty less convincing. Also, the limited experimental comparison (in Table 1) with recent related methods further reduces confidence in the paper’s contribution relative to the current state of the art. 2.The method involves several key hyperparameters (e. g. , thresholds for motion consistency, weighting factors, and memory pruning criteria), but the paper does not provide systematic ablation or sensitivity analysis. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness and reproducibility of the design choices.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The use of bidirectional tracking (Kalman filtering combined with RTS smoothing) and memory diversity-based pruning provides a reasonable and interpretable design. The method demonstrates consistent and significant improvements over SAM2 and related baselines on EndoVis benchmarks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The method involves multiple critical hyperparameters, including τ, γ, k, λ, L, and β. However, only β is studied in the ablation (Fig. 4), while all other parameters are fixed without sensitivity analysis. The lack of systematic analysis raises concerns about robustness and reproducibility. 2.The appearance score used in Motion-Guided Mask Reselection is not clearly compared to standard feature matching approaches in ReID literature. Its differences and potential advantages are not sufficiently explained. 3.When motion inconsistency is detected, especially under abrupt shifts or long-term absence, the memory bank itself may contain corrupted, occluded, or misidentified entries. In such cases, relying on appearance-based reselection may reinforce existing errors rather than correct them. This critical dependency is not analyzed or validated. 4.It is unclear which prompting strategy (among those described in Table 1) is used for the results reported in Table 2.5.In the BMR module, the contribution of bidirectional reasoning is not isolated. In particular, the effect of RTS backward smoothing is not independently evaluated, making it unclear whether the gains come from forward Kalman tracking or backward smoothing. 6.Although BRAIN introduces the BMR module on top of SAM2, the paper does not analyze the additional computational cost or complexity, which is important for practical deployment.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The problem formulation is precise and clinically grounded. Unlike vague claims about “surgical challenges,” the authors define concrete phenomena: motion inertia (Fig. 1) and instrument absence quantified via IAR (Instrument Absence Ratio). The safety argument—that misidentification could cause unintended robotic manipulation—is specific and credible. Fig. 2 showing baseline collapse at IAR > 60% is compelling evidence that current methods fail exactly where they matter most. 2.The bidirectional motion reasoning is elegant and well-motivated. Using RTS backward smoothing to detect inconsistencies with forward predictions is a classic signal processing technique [19], but the application to surgical instrument tracking is thoughtful. The Mahalanobis distance-based consistency score (J_t) provides a principled way to detect “teleports” or abrupt re-entries. The dynamic weighting scheme, which decays motion trust as a function of absence duration, is intuitively motivated: an instrument unseen for 50 frames should not be trusted for motion predictions. 3.The memory pruning mechanism addresses a real SAM2 limitation. SAM2’s fixed-length memory bank (initial frame + 6 recent frames) is known to struggle with long occlusions. The dissimilarity-based pruning with minimum retention policy (always keep reference frame, max 6 additional frames) is simple but effective. Fig. 6’s visualization showing memory bank composition under different settings is genuinely helpful for understanding why this matters. 4.Strong empirical results on challenging classes. Table 2 shows massive improvements on historically difficult categories: Clip Applier (+20.62%: 45.29% → 65.91%) and Ultrasound Probe (+35.63%: 25.62% → 61.25%). These are instruments that frequently disappear and reappear, so the gains directly validate the method’s design intent. The ablation in Fig. 7 showing BMR and DM are complementary. 5.Honest about building on SAM2 rather than claiming novelty from scratch. The paper clearly positions itself as extending SAM2 and SurgSAM2, not replacing them.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The core components are largely classical, not novel. Kalman filtering for object tracking dates to the 1960s, RTS smoothing is from 1965, and memory management in visual tracking has been extensively studied (e.g., SAMURAI uses motion-aware memory, MoSAM does spatial-temporal memory selection). The specific combination is new, but the individual pieces are well-established. The paper cites some related work but doesn’t clearly articulate what BRAIN does differently from these concurrent SAM2 adaptations. 2.The “dynamic” memory pruning is less dynamic than claimed. The dissimilarity-based selection (Sec. 2.2) uses a fixed threshold β=6 and fixed maximum memory size (6 frames). This is essentially static pruning with a dissimilarity heuristic, not truly adaptive to scene complexity. A more dynamic approach might adjust memory capacity based on estimated occlusion duration or instrument motion predictability. The ablation in Fig. 4 shows performance vs. β but doesn’t explain why β=6 is optimal or how to set it without validation data. 3.Missing comparison to non-SAM2 surgical trackers. Table 2 compares BRAIN to task-specific methods (ISINet, TraSeTR, S3Net, MATIS, LACOSTE) and SAM-based approaches, but these are mostly single-frame or category-level methods. There’s no comparison to modern surgical video tracking methods that explicitly handle occlusion, such as TraSeTR’s temporal consistency or LACOSTE’s stereo-temporal fusion. The claim that BRAIN “surpasses strong task-specific models” is partially true but conflates different problem settings (instance-level vs. category-level, video vs. single-frame). 4.The appearance score during reselection is underspecified. When J_t ≥ τ (motion inconsistent), BRAIN switches to appearance matching using “cosine similarity between the embedding vector extracted from M_{t,i} and that of the most confident mask in the memory bank.” But if the instrument has been absent for 100 frames, the memory bank contains only old embeddings. How does appearance matching work when the instrument reappears with different orientation, lighting, or occlusion? The paper doesn’t analyze failure modes where appearance changes drastically during absence. 5.Limited analysis of IAR-specific performance. The paper defines IAR and shows baseline collapse (Fig. 2), but doesn’t report BRAIN’s performance stratified by IAR bins. Does BRAIN maintain 80%+ accuracy at IAR > 60%? The abstract claims “significant outperformance” but without IAR-stratified results, we can’t verify that the gains come specifically from handling high-absence cases versus general improvement. 6.The evaluation protocol has gaps. They “exclude the first and last frames of each sequence” following standard protocol, but surgical videos often have the most instrument entry/exit at boundaries. This exclusion might artificially inflate performance. Also, using SurgSAM2’s instance-level annotation protocol for evaluation is fine, but the comparison to category-level methods in Table 2 is unfair—these methods weren’t designed for instance tracking. 7.No discussion of computational cost. Adding Kalman filtering, RTS smoothing, and dissimilarity computation to SAM2’s per-frame inference adds overhead. Is BRAIN real-time? SAM2 is already computationally heavy; the extra modules might push it beyond practical deployment limits for robotic surgery. Given the safety framing, latency analysis is relevant.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for the constructive comments. We are encouraged that BRAIN is recognized as “well-motivated” (R3), “easy to follow” (R1), and “clearly organised” (R1,2), with “significant improvements” (R2,3) and “quantifying critical real-world challenges” (R4). We will release code upon acceptance. 1 Computational cost (R2,3,4). BRAIN (46.75 FPS, 0.02 s/frame, 3.23 GB) adds negligible overhead over SAM2 (52.18 FPS, 0.02 s/frame, 3.14 GB) on A800, since extra modules use simple matrix computation, RTS uses a short temporal window (L=15), and DM prunes redundant frames to further speed up the process. 2.1 Hyperparameter sensitivity (R1,2,3). BRAIN is insensitive to γ, k, L; τ and β are interpretable. λ=e^-n adjusts dynamically with n, not manually tuned. We evaluated τ/γ/k∈{0.1,…,0.9}, L∈{10,12,15,17,20}, and β∈{3,…,7}. BRAIN is stable to score fusion (γ), tracker-update gating (k), RTS window (L) with 0.06/0.05/0.09% IoU variation. τ and β are more influential, with 1.26/1.32% variation. τ controls motion-inconsistency detection: small τ over-triggers appearance reselection and large τ misses abrupt shifts. β controls memory pruning: small β over-prunes context, large β keeps redundant memories. Thus,τ=0.5,β=6 balance best. “Dynamic” means dynamic memory-frame selection, not capacity adjustment; dynamic capacity yields comparable Dice (86.48%) but lower efficiency (29.07 FPS). Failures mainly occur when both cues vanish, e.g., severe lens occlusion/blur, or strong camera shake, a shared open challenge. 2.2 BMR ablation (R2). We isolate BMR: Kalman improves Dice from 83.44% to 85.13%, and RTS further improves it to 86.51%, confirming both contributions. 3.1 Reselection (R2,3). Appearance reselection uses the most confident memory embedding (0.13% high-confidence errors), so corrupted, occluded, or misidentified frames do not dominate the appearance score. As analyzed in Fig. 6, DM suppresses empty, low-confidence, and redundant absent frames, enabling robust appearance matching after many absent frames. BMR improves current-frame mask quality and reduces drift; together, BMR and DM reduce repeated use of erroneous memories. When re-entry involves orientation, lighting, or occlusion but no abrupt positional shift, BRAIN selects mask using both motion and appearance cues. With IAR > 60%, including occluded re-entries, appearance matching localizes the target in 91.2% of cases. 3.2 Embedding/ReID (R4,2). Embedding is a SAM2 feature-pooled mask-level semantic vector. Appearance score is L2-normalized cosine similarity to the most confident memory embedding. BMR considers both motion and appearance scores, differing from ReID methods that recognize identities by simply fusing all frames. 4.1 Novelty (R1,3). Although SAMURAI, MoSAM, EndoMamba, Memory-Augmented SAM2, and ReSurgSAM2 improve surgical video representation or tracking, they ignore long instrument absence with abrupt positional shifts, a critical cause of performance reduction. Instead of simply combining Kalman and RTS like previous methods (SAMURAI), we innovatively propose BMR to correct mask selection under abrupt positional shifts and DM to remove redundant long absent frames, jointly enabling SOTA performance (e.g., SAMURAI, 79.69% Dice). 4.2 IAR-stratified (R3). For low/mid/high IAR (<30%, 30–60%, >60%), BRAIN obtains 87.43/81.85/93.30% IoU, compared with SAM2’s 83.23/79.85/52.15% and SurgSAM2’s 85.17/81.47/65.06%. The largest gain at high IAR confirms that BRAIN targets long-absence/re-entry failures. 5 Prompt/ Fairness (R2,3,4). Table 2 uses the full-mask prompt. Table 1 is the fair comparison, where SAM2, SurgSAM2, and BRAIN use the same instance-level protocol and prompt setting. The standard VOS first/last-frame exclusion changes performance by only 0.03%. Table 2 is a broad reference covering category-level, prompt-free setting. In the same instance-level setting, BRAIN beats occlusion-aware trackers e.g., LACOSTE/TraSeTR (85.6/81.0% Dice)
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal should address four decision-affecting concerns. First, runtime, FPS, and GPU-memory analysis, which is critical given the safety framing and is currently absent. Second, a systematic sensitivity analysis of the multiple hyperparameters τ, γ, k, λ, L, β—of which only β is currently studied—and an isolated ablation that disentangles forward Kalman tracking from backward RTS smoothing within the BMR module. Third, an explicit specification of the embedding vector and similarity metric used in the motion-guided mask reselection, together with a discussion of long-absence re-entry behaviour, raised by R3: how appearance matching works when the instrument reappears after long absences with corrupted or stale memory entries. Fourth, IAR-stratified performance to substantiate the central claim that the method specifically improves the high-absence regime, and clearer positioning with respect to concurrent SAM2 adaptations such as SAMURAI and MoSAM, and to recent surgical-video foundation models such as EndoMamba, Memory-Augmented SAM2, and ReSurgSAM2. | The paper proposes bidirectional motion reasoning combined with dynamic memory pruning for surgical video segmentation on the EndoVis benchmarks. The reviewers raised four decision-affecting concerns: missing runtime and memory analysis given the safety framing; insufficient sensitivity analysis of multiple hyperparameters and a lack of an isolated ablation that separates forward tracking from backward smoothing; the unspecified embedding vector and similarity metric used in the motion-guided mask reselection, along with a question about behavior under long-absence re-entry; and positioning relative to concurrent SAM2 adaptations and recent surgical-video foundation models. The rebuttal substantively addresses the first three concerns, providing efficiency numbers, a hyperparameter sweep with reported sensitivities, isolating the contributions of the forward and backward components, explicitly specifying the embedding and similarity, and providing a stratified analysis under high-absence regimes. Two reviewers explicitly endorsed acceptance after the rebuttal. The remaining Reject concerns the positioning of related work, which the camera-ready version must improve. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, there are two Accept and one Reject. The other reviewer did not update. After reading the paper as well as the reviews and author rebuttal, I think the paper is a good work with good performance and method design. Major concerns include limited engagement with recent related work and incremental novelty. Pros outweigh cons and therefore the recommendation is Accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors managed to provide satisfactory answers.

title: Breaking Teacher’s Mean Regression Bias: Boundary-Aware Contrastive Distillation for Endoscopic Super-Resolution
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The study explicitly pointed out the problem of bias inheritance that occurs when applying knowledge distillation to super-resolution tasks. 2.Experimental results demonstrate that the reconstructed images clearly reproduce clinically significant microvascular structures and mucosal textures, which directly contribute to improved accuracy in lesion segmentation. 3.The paper proposes a novel and unique contrastive learning method. It extracts positive and negative examples that serve as upper and lower bounds from the teacher network and uses them for contrastive learning.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.There are some exaggerated statements. While Section 2.1 presents a theoretical formulation, it does not provide a proof. Although the explanation is convincing, it remains largely intuitive. Furthermore, Sections 2.2 and 2.3 use the terms “lower bound” and “upper bound,” but these do not strictly guarantee that the best or worst possible samples will be drawn. 2.There is no mention of computational cost. Since gradient-based input optimization is performed to generate positive examples, the training cost is expected to increase. 3.While the improvements in LPIPS and downstream performance are substantial, the improvement in PSNR is only slight.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A major strength of the paper is its rigorous and well-structured theoretical formulation. The authors carefully develop a boundary-aware learning strategy within the framework of knowledge distillation, supported by clear mathematical derivations. This principled approach enhances the clarity and soundness of the method, making the proposed formulation both interpretable and technically convincing.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although the paper reports significant performance improvements, it does not provide quantitative analysis of real-time performance, such as FPS or inference latency. This makes it difficult to assess the practical applicability of the method in real-time settings. Including such evaluations would improve the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This paper introduces a novel and insightful problem formulation by identifying that Knowledge Distillation (KD), which is typically assumed to be beneficial, can in fact exacerbate the mean regression issue in super-resolution. 2.The paper proposes a boundary-aware reformulation of the optimization objective, which is a significant conceptual innovation. Instead of relying on conventional point-wise regression that tends to produce averaged solutions, the method constrains the solution space using both lower and upper bounds. 3.The method demonstrates originality in how it constructs supervisory signals, particularly through the use of gradient-based teacher-optimized inputs as an upper bound. This goes beyond directly using teacher outputs and instead extracts richer high-frequency priors from the teacher model, effectively turning it into a more informative source of guidance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the paper claims that Knowledge Distillation (KD) exacerbates the mean regression problem, this insight may not be entirely novel. Prior works in super-resolution and image restoration have already discussed the over-smoothing effect induced by pixel-wise losses and the limitations of KD in preserving high-frequency details. 2.The proposed boundary-aware contrastive framework, while intuitively appealing, appears to be conceptually related to existing contrastive and hard-sample mining strategies. The idea of pushing representations away from degraded or low-quality samples and pulling them toward high-quality counterparts resembles contrastive formulations widely used in low-level vision. 3.Another limitation lies in the construction of the upper bound using gradient-based teacher-optimized inputs. While this is an interesting idea, the paper does not fully analyze its computational overhead or stability. Gradient-based input optimization can be expensive and sensitive to hyperparameters, especially in high-resolution medical images. Without a clear discussion or ablation on efficiency and robustness, it is difficult to assess whether this component is practical for real-world deployment, particularly given the paper’s emphasis on lightweight models and limited computational resources.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs for their constructive comments and for recognizing the strengths of our work. We address the main concerns below. Regarding the theoretical formulation and the use of “lower/upper bound” (R1-W1), we agree that Sec. 2.1 is an analytical formulation rather than a formal theorem. Our intention is not to claim a strict global guarantee over the HR solution space, but to explain why standard KD can further suppress high-frequency variance when the student is constrained by both the GT loss and a variance-suppressed teacher output. Thus, “lower/upper bound” refers to operational boundary anchors obtained by controlled probes of the frozen teacher, rather than globally worst/best possible samples. The degraded teacher response serves as a negative anchor, while the optimized teacher response serves as a positive anchor. The ablation study supports this interpretation: the naive positive anchor causes manifold mismatch, whereas the optimized positive anchor gives the best PSNR–LPIPS trade-off. Regarding novelty relative to prior over-smoothing, contrastive learning, and hard-sample mining work (R3-W1, R3-W2), we agree that over-smoothing in SR and contrastive objectives in low-level vision have been studied before. Our contribution is more specific: we identify a distillation failure mode in which the teacher is already a smoothed estimator, and rigidly mimicking it makes the lightweight student inherit and amplify this mean-regression bias. BACD also differs from conventional contrastive or hard-sample mining methods in anchor construction. Instead of selecting positives/negatives from the dataset or using generic degradations, BACD probes a frozen teacher to generate teacher-specific boundary anchors: a degraded teacher response and a gradient-optimized teacher response. This turns the teacher from a fixed point-wise target into a source of boundary-aware contrastive supervision. Regarding computational cost, stability, and real-time applicability (R1-W2, R2-W1, R3-W3), we acknowledge that gradient-based input optimization adds training-time computation. Since the rebuttal instructions do not allow new experimental results, we do not report additional timing numbers here, but clarify the mechanism. The extra cost is limited because optimization is applied only to the input tensor, the teacher is frozen, no extra teacher training is performed, and only K=3 steps are used. More importantly, all extra components are training-only. At inference, BACD does not require the teacher, input optimization, VGG feature extraction, or the contrastive branch. The deployed model is exactly the standard lightweight student architecture, so BACD introduces no additional inference latency. Under the same student settings, BACD outperforms competing KD baselines and improves clinically relevant reconstruction quality, supporting its practical value for lightweight clinical deployment. Regarding the modest PSNR gain (R1-W3), this is consistent with the perception–distortion trade-off in SR: perceptual improvement often comes at the cost of PSNR, while PSNR-oriented methods tend to over-smooth textures. BACD is meaningful because it improves perceptual quality without sacrificing PSNR. It achieves the best PSNR among student models while substantially improving LPIPS; in several settings, its LPIPS even surpasses the teacher, indicating that the student is not merely copying the teacher’s smoothed output but recovering more faithful structures. This is particularly important for endoscopic SR, where microvascular and mucosal details may not be fully reflected by PSNR. The downstream segmentation results further show that the improvement is clinically useful rather than only visually pleasing. We appreciate the reviewers’ suggestions. These clarifications address the main concerns while preserving the central contribution of the submitted paper.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a boundary-aware contrastive distillation framework to prevent the student model from inheriting the teacher model’s mean regression bias. The paper makes innovative contributions in terms of problem formulation and the proposed solution. Despite some conceptual similarities with existing contrastive learning approaches and boundary-aware methods, the paper is a good fit for the MICCAI audience.

title: CMSA-Net: Causal Multi-scale Aggregation with Adaptive Multi-source Reference for Video Polyp Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: Directly targets key VPS pain points—low contrast (weak semantics) and large inter-frame motion/scale changes. CMA is a solid technical contribution: Multi-scale feature aggregation with a causal (time-ordered) attention constraint to reduce cross-frame feature contamination. DMR is practical and efficient: Dynamically maintains multiple reference frames using separability + confidence cues, avoiding brittle fixed references and heavy memory banks. Convincing empirical support: Comprehensive SUN-SEG evaluation (Easy/Hard, Seen/Unseen) with clear ablations validating each design choice. Real-time orientation: Reports complexity/speed and designs for clinical feasibility rather than purely offline accuracy.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: DMR can be brittle because it is self-scored from the model’s own predictions. Both “semantic separability” (prototype distance via masked pooling) and “confidence” (entropy) are derived from p_t. This risks selecting wrong-but-confident frames as references and amplifying errors over time; the paper lacks drift/stability analysis. The “causal / real-time” story is not fully pinned down by the evaluation protocol. The method is presented as causal and suitable for real-time use, but experiments are described on fixed clips (e. g. , 6 frames). The paper should explicitly define a strict streaming inference setup (no future access under any sliding window) and report latency/long-sequence behavior. Insufficient implementation detail for reproducibility. CMA’s attention tokenization and tensor shapes (how multi-scale features are concatenated/flattened, exact masks, Q/K/V formation) and DMR’s update mechanics are not specified to the level needed for easy reimplementation. Writing/typos and notation issues reduce clarity. “Casual” appears where “Causal” is intended, and there are minor formula/notation inconsistencies (e. g. , the attention scaling term is written in a nonstandard way). These don’t change the idea, but they hurt readability and confidence in exact implementation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem, namely video polyp segmentation under weak semantic contrast, large spatio-temporal variation, and real-time constraints. 2.The proposed method is technically coherent: CMA and DMR are complementary, with CMA enhancing temporally causal multi-scale aggregation and DMR improving the quality of reference information. 3.The experimental evaluation is relatively solid, including comparisons with multiple prior methods, ablation studies, and efficiency analysis on different SUN-SEG subsets (easy/hard, seen/unseen). 4.The paper demonstrates a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, which is valuable for practical deployment in colonoscopy scenarios.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The novelty appears moderate rather than highly significant. While the method is effective, it can be viewed as a structured extension of existing VPS designs that already exploit temporal aggregation, reference frames, or long-/short-term interaction, such as PNS/PNS+, SALI, MAST, and STDDNet. 2.The empirical evidence is mainly based on a single benchmark (SUN-SEG). Therefore, claims regarding robustness and generalization should be stated more cautiously. 3.Some methodological details remain unclear and affect reproducibility, including the exact handling and number of references in DMR, whether dynamic updates are applied during training and/or inference, and several notation inconsistencies in the paper. 4.Although the method consistently improves over prior baselines, some gains over the strongest same-backbone baselines are relatively modest on certain subsets, so the empirical advantage is solid but not overwhelmingly large.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper provides a clear and detailed description of the proposed network architecture, including its individual modules and the rationale for their design. This level of transparency makes the method easy to follow and reproducible, and helps the reader understand how the different components contribute to addressing spatio-temporal challenges in video-based polyp segmentation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited Novelty in Multi-Scale Feature Fusion The proposed multi-scale feature fusion module offers limited novelty, as similar approaches have been extensively studied in prior work. Moreover, the design appears relatively simple compared to more recent and advanced fusion strategies, some of which have demonstrated superior performance. 2.Marginal Performance Gains over Recent Methods Despite extensive comparisons with existing approaches, the reported improvements are incremental, particularly when compared to recent methods such as STDDNet (ICCV 2025). Additionally, results in Table 3 indicate that GELOP achieves higher performance than the proposed method (R) on certain metrics, which weakens the claim of consistent superiority. 3.Missing Ablation on Loss Components While the paper includes ablation studies on architectural modules, it lacks a detailed analysis of the loss design. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of individual loss components, either for the segmentation loss or for the overall objective, making it difficult to assess their effectiveness. 4.Inconsistency Between Quantitative and Qualitative Results The qualitative results do not convincingly reflect the quantitative improvements reported in the paper, particularly compared with STDDNet. The visual examples fail to clearly demonstrate the claimed performance gains, raising concerns about the consistency of the evaluation.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive comments and for recognizing the importance of video polyp segmentation, the coherence of CMA+DMR, and the solid SUN-SEG evaluation. We address the main concerns below. Novelty (R2,R3). We agree that temporal aggregation, reference frames, and multi-scale features have been explored in VPS. Our novelty lies in their causal and role-aware integration. Existing methods often rely on fixed/single references or aggregate frames without explicitly modeling the causal relations among reference, adjacent, and current frames, which may cause feature contamination or unreliable guidance under large variations (Fig. 1). CMSA-Net addresses this via (1) CMA, which performs multi-scale aggregation under a time-ordered attention constraint, and (2) DMR, which maintains compact multi-source references using complementary separability and confidence cues. Table 4 shows that removing CMA or DMR leads to clear degradation, especially on Hard-Unseen, supporting their complementary roles. DMR stability (R1). We appreciate the concern about self-reinforcement. DMR includes several safeguards. First, it uses two complementary cues (separability and confidence) rather than a single score. Second, both scores incorporate temporal consistency, preventing selection based solely on entropy or prototype distance. Third, cooldown intervals limit frequent updates. Finally, DMR maintains a compact reference set instead of accumulating all historical frames, which constrains error propagation. The strong Hard-Unseen results and the “w/o DMR” ablation in Table 4 indicate that DMR improves robustness in the submitted evaluation. Causal/real-time setting (R1). CMSA-Net is causal by design. In Sec. 2.1, an adjacent frame at time t only attends to reference frames and past frames up to t; the current frame uses only reference and past adjacent frames within the window. No future information beyond the prediction target is used. The 6-frame clip is the implementation of this causal window rather than an offline setting. Table 3 reports 38/47 FPS with PVTv2-B2/Res2Net-50, supporting real-time feasibility. Single benchmark (R2). We agree that more datasets would strengthen generalization claims. Nevertheless, SUN-SEG is the largest and most widely used VPS benchmark, with 49,136 annotated frames and diverse clinical conditions (low contrast, fast motion, illumination changes, instruments, etc.). It is also the standard benchmark used by representative works such as PNS+, SALI, MAST, and STDDNet. Thus, we believe SUN-SEG provides a rigorous basis for evaluation. Magnitude of gains (R2,R3). We agree that gains over strong baselines (e.g., STDDNet) are sometimes moderate. However, consistent improvements across subsets and metrics remain meaningful. More importantly, CMSA-Net shows clearer advantages in difficult settings (Hard-Seen/Hard-Unseen and challenging qualitative cases), which directly correspond to the targeted clinical challenges. Loss ablation (R3). Our contribution focuses on architecture rather than loss design. We adopt standard segmentation losses (Dice, weighted IoU, weighted BCE), consistent with prior VPS works. Thus, improvements mainly reflect the effect of CMA and DMR, and Table 4 already isolates the main architectural components. Reproducibility and notation (R1,R2). We acknowledge that some details and notation could be clearer. The manuscript specifies multi-scale features, Q/K/V construction, attention heads, clip length, and DMR cooldown intervals. We will correct typos (e.g., “Casual” → “Causal”) in the camera-ready version and release code and models upon acceptance. We thank the reviewers again for their valuable feedback.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes CMSA-Net, a video polyp segmentation framework that leverages causal multi-scale aggregation to model temporal dependencies and improve semantic discrimination across frames. Three reviewers (R1, R2, R3) vote for weak accept. The work is above the acceptance threshold and is suitable for acceptance. That said, several important issues should be addressed in the final manuscript to strengthen clarity, rigor, and reproducibility: R1 raises a meaningful concern that DMR relies on model predictions, which may introduce a feedback loop where incorrect but confident predictions are reinforced. R2 notes that evaluation is limited to a single dataset and novelty is moderate. R3 highlights the lack of detailed ablation studies on the loss function.

title: CoGE: Sim-to-Real Online Geometric Estimation for Monocular Colonoscopy
reviewer_1_strengths: -A major strength of this work is that the methodological design is well aligned with the main challenges of colonoscopy videos, rather than being a loosely combined set of generic components. Specifically, the Structure-Aware Perception (SAP) block is designed to capture both structural and local texture information, the Illumination-Aware Supervision (IAS) module explicitly addresses unstable illumination and specular artifacts, and the memory forgetting mechanism is intended to reduce redundant information in long temporal sequences. Overall, these components form a coherent and task-specific framework for sim-to-real geometric estimation in colonoscopy. The evaluation covers one simulated dataset and two real-world datasets, with comparisons against both colonoscopy-specific approaches and recent 3D geometric estimation baselines. The reported quantitative and qualitative results are consistently competitive. In monocular depth estimation, the proposed method outperforms strong baselines including Spann3R, MonST3R, CUT3R, and STream3R across SimCol, C3VD, and C3VDv2.In 3D reconstruction, the paper further reports improved reconstruction accuracy over STream3R, CUT3R, and MonST3R. The fact that these results are obtained while training only on simulated data is an important practical strength of the work.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The ablation study on the memory forgetting mechanism is currently not sufficient to fully justify the specific design in Eq. (6). In particular, the filtering rule depends on two empirically chosen thresholds: a memory token is retained only if at least 5% of feature tokens assign it an attention score above 5×〖10〗^(-4). However, the current experiments only compare the model with and without the memory forgetting module, without any sensitivity analysis for these thresholds. As a result, Table 2 supports that the module is helpful, but does not yet establish that this particular filtering rule is robust or well justified. It therefore remains unclear whether the observed gains come from a generally effective design or from a relatively fragile heuristic choice.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The core insight is well motivated: conventional two-stage sim-to-real pipelines, which combine style translation with downstream geometric estimation, are limited by both inference inefficiency and residual domain mismatch. Exploring an end-to-end feature-level domain generalization strategy is therefore a meaningful and clinically relevant direction for colonoscopy. 2.The experimental evaluation is relatively comprehensive. The method is assessed on both the simulated SimCol3D dataset and the real-world C3VD/C3VDv2 datasets, and the reported results on depth estimation and 3D reconstruction demonstrate competitive performance against several recent foundation-model-based baselines.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The claimed technical novelty appears limited and somewhat overstated. The method is largely a task-specific extension of an existing online 3D perception pipeline, combining DUSt3R-based initialization, CUT3R-style geometric supervision, and memory designs reminiscent of Spann3R. Its additional components, including wavelet-based feature decomposition, Retinex-inspired illumination modeling, and heuristic memory pruning, seem more like incremental work. 2.The formulation around the low-frequency branch is unclear. The text states that low-frequency information is extracted from the low-low branch using attention, whereas Eq. (2) defines it from hh rather than from the low-frequency feature, which appears inconsistent and may be a typographical error. In addition, several recent 3DGS-based methods, including Wavelet-GS (ACM MM 2025), EndoWave (BIBM 2025), and PCR-GS (ICCV 2025), should be discussed in the related work, or the differences from them should be clarified. 3.The reference list includes Endo3R (MICCAI 2025), a unified online reconstruction method for dynamic monocular endoscopic video, yet this method is absent from the quantitative comparisons. 4.The ablation study in Table 2 provides only limited support for the effectiveness of the proposed modules. For example, on C3VD, removing the SAP block increases Abs Rel only from 0.085 to 0.089, while removing the IAS module increases it to 0.087.It would be helpful to provide a more comprehensive ablation study, including the baseline model and different combinations of the proposed modules, to more clearly assess the individual and joint contributions of each component. 5.The manuscript still contains a number of language and presentation issues. For example, in Figure 1, “Common Structrual Features” should be corrected to “Common Structural Features.” The phrase “to pretend interference of redundant memory” should be “to prevent interference from redundant memory.” Similarly, in Section 1 (Contributions), “to pretend the influence of diverse illumination” should be replaced with “to prevent” or “to mitigate ” The formatting of the piecewise function in Eq. (6) is also non-standard and difficult to read. In addition, there are many missing or incorrect articles (a/an) in the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Using only synthetic data is a promising direction, as it can substantially reduce annotation cost and may still yield strong generalization, consistent with recent findings in related vision tasks. 2.The method shows relatively clear empirical improvements over the compared baselines. 3.The design motivation is reasonable: the illumination-aware and structure-aware modules are well aligned with two key challenges in colonoscopy imaging, namely lighting variation and structural perception.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Although the paper reports quantitative results on C3VD and C3VDv2, these datasets are primarily phantom-based rather than true in-vivo clinical datasets. As a result, the evidence for generalization to real clinical colonoscopy remains limited, especially since the in-house clinical examples are only qualitative. 2.The paper describes CoGE as a “foundation model-based framework,” but this framing seems somewhat overstated. In practice, the method is trained on only 24 simulated VR-Caps sequences, initialized from DUSt3R, and optimized for 10 epochs. 3.The paper is motivated by robustness to illumination variation and sim-to-real deployment, yet the evaluation does not systematically examine several clinically important failure cases. This is also consistent with the authors’ own conclusion, which notes performance degradation under motion blur, acute dynamic changes, and lesion tissue.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers; each section first quotes the criticism. (1) “Gemini-3 wins, so the benchmark is biased toward Gemini” [R1, R2]. To refute the bias hypothesis, we tested a recently released non-Gemini control: open-source Gemma 4 31B achieves 63.8 / 59.9 / 85.1 / 47.2 on Prompted-VQA / Unprompted-VQA / Classification-Acc / Seg-mIoU, almost matching Gemini 3 Pro (top of Table 3) . (2) “How are adversarial VQA distractors generated for debias?” [R1]. Distractors come from a Gemini-3 call seeing only the question and correct answer (not the video), emitting 4 length, style, and specificity-matched alternatives; positions are re-randomized. Blind text-only LLM accuracy drops from ~70% (naive distractors) to ~20% (random), confirming text cues are not exploitable. (3) “Human-expert verification and VQA content are under-specified” [R1, R2]. All windows were reviewed by the authors with Dr. J.H., a surgeon with over 30 years of GI/colonoscopy practice (11.6% expert-rejection, Fig.1). Lesion descriptions are AI-generated by the verification agent; the expert accepts/rejects the window+annotations+description package. Two tiers: Prompted (bbox, no time refs) and Unprompted (no bbox, time-referenced queries); questions cover lesion type, size, location, interventions, and process descriptions. Up to 10% of VQA pairs were manually checked by the authors with 98% correctness (supp. mp4). (4) “Table 2 Precision/recall 55.4 / 48.6 indicate a noisy benchmark” [R1, R2, R3]. Specificity 94.4% is the relevant reliability indicator. The 55.4 / 48.6 figures compare our 14-category annotations against REAL-COLON’s polyp-only labels from a commercial detector flagging ~12% of REAL-COLON’s frames; most of our categories (ulcers, bleeding, angiectasia, etc.) are absent from this reference, so the labels mismatch by definition. Table 2 will be reframed for R3’s false-negative concern; we target representative lesion-spectrum coverage, not exhaustive frame-level recall. (5) “No release commitment” [R1, R2]. Dataset, code, prompts, SKILL.md, and Jsons will be released on Hugging Face and GitHub on acceptance. Detailed methodology was in a supplementary PDF disallowed by MICCAI 2026 this year and will fold into the camera-ready. (6) “Missing EndoBench (NeurIPS 2025)” [R1]. EndoBench (Dec 2025) is concurrent with our Feb 2026 submission and will be cited. It evaluates static-image VQA on general endoscopy. Colon-Bench is the first video colonoscopy benchmark: dense video segmentation, binary lesion classification (over a 14-category lesion spectrum), and prompted/unprompted video VQA. Disjoint scope. (7) “Inconsistent units: 60 vs 528 vs 1,597 in Table 1 & Sec. 2.2 “ [R1, R2, R3]. 60 source recordings are full-procedure videos scanned end-to-end; 528 = annotated lesion windows extracted from them (duration: median 59.9 s, mean 87.9 s, std 83.2 s); 264 clips in segmentation benchmark. 1,597 = VQA clip pool: Prompted (bbox) + Unprompted (no bbox) renderings of accepted windows + confirmed non-lesion distractors. Table 1 will add duration stats; Sec.2.2 will spell out the 528/264/1,597 relation; “full-procedure” softened to “representative full-procedure coverage”. (8) “Pipeline and Colon-Skill are under-specified” [R1, R2]. Each agent uses a JSON-templated prompt; t_p = window duration (s) for temporal grounding. The AI-cued confirmation agent ingests the clip with bbox+description overlay and outputs accept/reject + rationale. Colon-Skill aggregates up to 20 common errors per lesion category (a design choice) into anti-error rules (e.g., “a flat lesion on a haustral fold without a fibrous tether is Sessile”). +9.7% gain across model families. In sum: bias is refuted (Gemma 4 control + debiasing Q/A); verification was by a 30+ year senior surgeon, including the VQA check; reproducibility committed; precision/recall are cross-taxonomy. We respectfully ask R1 to reconsider, citing their own “potential to be highly impactful” assessment.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers commonly raise concerns that the dataset contribution and scale are overstated, since Colon-Bench is derived from REAL-COLON and appears to consist of curated clips/windows rather than full-procedure videos, with unclear and inconsistent reporting of dataset units and counts. They also emphasize that the annotation and VQA generation pipeline lacks sufficient methodological detail, human-expert verification, reproducibility information, and error analysis, while the relatively low reported annotation quality and heavy reliance on Gemini may introduce noise and bias into the benchmark. | Most of the concerns raised by the reviewers (human expert confirmation, Bias on Gemini, …) were addressed in the author’s feedback. Dataset, code, prompts, SKILL.md, and Jsons will be released on Hugging Face and GitHub on acceptance. Furthermore, the authors will make their dataset and codes publicly available. It will contribute to the community’s progress. This manuscript is worthy of acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received Reject, Reject, and Accept. The paper makes a real contribution in dataset curation and annotation: 528 lesion windows extracted from REAL-COLON’s 60 full-procedure videos, spanning 14 lesion categories (vs prior single-polyp datasets) with 300k bounding boxes, 213k segmentation masks, and 133k words of clinical descriptions, and the dataset is publicly released; however, the two post-rebuttal Rejects raised structural concerns that the rebuttal did not fully resolve: the pipeline-evaluation circularity (Gemini models generate the lesion proposals, bounding boxes, lesion descriptions, and VQA questions, and Gemini 3 Pro/Flash then top all four benchmark tasks), the dataset-size misrepresentation in Table 1 (528 lesion windows compared against REAL-COLON’s 60 full-procedure videos), and the limited human verification of the AI-generated VQA pairs (10% sample by the authors themselves). My decision to accept rests on the dataset’s tangible value to the community (14 lesion categories vs prior single-polyp datasets, dense multi-modal annotations, and confirmed public availability), and is conditional on the authors severely addressing the remaining concerns in the camera-ready. The authors must (1) explicitly disclose the Gemini-dependence throughout the annotation and VQA-generation pipeline and discuss the resulting benchmark bias as a known limitation; (2) correct Table 1 to compare like with like (lesion windows vs lesion windows, full-procedure videos vs full-procedure videos) and add duration statistics for the 528 windows; (3) acknowledge the limited human verification (10% sample by the authors) as a known limitation rather than a quality endorsement; (4) add EndoBench (NeurIPS 2025) to the related work and discuss the disjoint scope (static images vs video); and (5) reframe the 55.4/48.6 precision/recall in Table 2 to make the cross-taxonomy mismatch with REAL-COLON’s polyp-only labels explicit. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewer points out that EndoBench is suitable for VQA but inadequate for segmentation and detection due to the need for full-length procedure testing and unverified AI filtering, while also noting that the rebuttal failed to address evaluation bias towards Gemini models and that the paper requires major revisions to improve methodological clarity and explain low precision/recall results.

title: Computer-Assisted Intervention in Capsule Endoscopy: A Real-Time Edge-AI Auditing System
reviewer_1_strengths: 1- Clinical and Practical Utility: Video Capsule Endoscopy is the primary non-invasive modality for visualizing the entire small bowel, and the authors tackle it with a temporal model designed specifically for efficiency. By focusing on edge deployment, they move beyond simple analysis and provide a framework that can be used in real-time to monitor the procedure. 2- Temporal and Multi-Task model: The pipeline is well-engineered, featuring a comprehensive ablation study on temporal window sizes (ranging from 5 to 195 frames) and a comparison between single-task and multi-task learning. The small size of both spatial and temporal decoders allow for temporal modelling with a high inference speed. 3- Hardware validation: The deployment on a Jetson Nano provides empirical evidence of the system’s efficiency. Providing concrete latency numbers on constrained hardware supports the “Edge-AI” claim.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1- Incremental Methodological Novelty: From a deep-learning perspective, the architecture is relatively standard. The novelty of the work lies primarily in its application and hardware deployment insights rather than in a fundamental methodological innovation. 2- Lack of deployment ablation: While the edge deployment is one of the strengths of the paper, it would have been nice to have an ablation of the single frame models vs temporal models with different temporal windows. This would highlight the efficiency-performance trade-off.

author_feedback: The authors thank the reviewers for their insightful comments. [R2, R3, R4] Novelty, Temporal Modeling, and Contribution The contribution of this work is primarily a computer-assisted intervention system: the novelty lies in enabling real-time temporal VCE analysis under strict edge-computing constraints through a lightweight framework, a setting insufficiently explored by existing approaches. Under these constraints, the architecture integrates established backbones for causal online inference: (1) sliding windows contain only past and present frames, consistent with real-time deployment; each frame is encoded once by ResNet50 and reused across overlapping windows (stride = 1) through a ViT-Small temporal encoder for per-frame prediction; (2) temporal order is encoded via learnable positional embeddings, while frame predictions are aggregated through soft voting with entropy-based uncertainty; (3) homoscedastic MTL jointly optimizes anatomical localization and anomaly detection in a single edge-deployable model (30.5 ms/frame on NVIDIA Jetson Nano); and (4) the system is validated on a recent 2025 multi-center, multi-device dataset (~3.5M frames), including evaluation on an unseen dataset. We will clarify this framing in Section 1. [R4] SOTA Baselines and Pretrained Non-medical temporal baselines were not included because the primary scope of this study was real-time auditing of complete VCE procedures under edge-deployment constraints. A reviewer-suggested VLM contains >8B parameters, whereas our approach contains ~45M and runs fully online. VCE presents unique challenges, as the capsule moves through a continuously deforming organ without controlled navigation, while most temporal foundation models are trained in fixed-camera or operator-controlled settings. Benchmarking and fine-tuning such models for real-time VCE remains important future work. Selected temporal baselines previously applied to endoscopy video analysis included CNN+GRU and CNN+ViT models evaluated on VCE videos under the same protocol (Section 3.2). Regarding foundation-model pretraining, both CNN and ViT backbones were pretrained using self-supervised DINO on the GastroNet [15] dataset (>5M gastrointestinal images from 8 clinical centers). The proposed approach integrates these backbones for real-time VCE analysis under edge-deployment constraints, and results indicate improved performance (Table 1). The available GI-pretrained DINOv2 ViT-Base backbone (~86M parameters) [21] is not suitable for real-time deployment. [R3, R2] Results Clarity and Deployment Trade-offs The distinction between macro metrics (Table 2) and weighted metrics (text) reflects their complementary roles: macro metrics reflect performance across classes under severe imbalance, while weighted metrics account for class support. MTL-75 was selected to prioritize macro recall in the anomaly task. This configuration achieves 66.7% macro recall (Table 2), 77% weighted recall for the anomaly task (text), and 90.3% macro F1 for the anatomy task (Table 1) using a single model. We will better justify this selection in Subsection 3.2.Additionally, a systematic latency analysis across temporal window sizes and backbone architectures on edge devices is planned as future work. [R3] Clinical Relevance The anatomical classification task enables: (1) GI transit time and motility assessment; (2) detection of retrograde events associated with Barrett’s metaplasia [22]; and (3) early detection of capsule retention (0.7-1.4% of examinations). We will clarify the clinical utility in the final paragraph of the Results section. Additional Galar annotations (e.g., good/reduced-view) are only available for 6/80 studies. Since anatomical continuity is preserved across reduced-view frames, our temporal context supports inference under visual ambiguity, while entropy-based uncertainty identifies low-confidence predictions without explicit view-quality labels, a key advantage over frame-wise approaches.

title: Contrastive Learning under Noisy Temporal Self-Supervision for Colonoscopy Videos
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The observation that colonoscopy workflows are inherently sequential provides an intuitive and practically grounded source of self-supervision. This is particularly valuable in medical imaging where annotation costs are prohibitive. 2.The max-based contrastive loss (Eq. 1) is an elegant solution to the label noise problem inherent in temporal associations. By allowing the model to “ignore” noisy positives rather than forcing all bag members to align, the formulation better reflects the uncertainty of the self-supervision signal. This is more principled than heuristic re-weighting schemes. 3.The method achieves state-of-the-art performance across all four downstream tasks. 4.The analysis of exponential sampling, curriculum learning, and multi-level objectives provides clear evidence for each component’s contribution. 5.The lightweight architecture and minimal data requirements address deployment constraints in clinical settings, where computational resources and annotated data are often limited.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Novelty of temporal self-supervision requires clearer positioning: While applying temporal proximity as a supervisory signal to colonoscopy is novel, the broader concept is well-established in video representation learning. Works such as MoCo-v3 and temporal instance discrimination methods have long exploited temporal continuity. The paper should more explicitly differentiate its contribution from these prior approaches, particularly regarding domain-specific adaptations for endoscopic imagery (e. g. , handling deformation, occlusion, instrument interference). 2.The max-based objective resembles strategies in Miech et al. [21] for learning from uncurated instructional videos, where not all temporally co-occurring pairs are reliable. 3.All experiments use tracklets constructed from ground-truth detections, completely decoupling representation learning from detection and tracking errors. In real colonoscopy pipelines, detection/tracking failures are frequent due to motion blur, occlusion, and instrument interference. 4.The condition “at least one tracklet in Bi should be more similar to ai than any tracklet in Bi is to any other anchor aj” is relaxed to the point that it may provide insufficient gradient signal, especially when bags are highly impure. The paper does not analyze the gradient dynamics or provide theoretical justification for why this objective leads to better representations than simpler alternatives (e. g. , label smoothing, robust aggregation). 5.The comparison with foundation models focuses on parameter count and FLOPs but does not account for differences in pretraining data scale, augmentation strategies, or task-specific fine-tuning protocols. Claiming superiority over DinoV2-giant based solely on downstream metrics while ignoring the massive pretraining gap is misleading.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The use of a noisy supervision signal (and the modification of the loss function to encode mismatches between anchors) is novel and particularly well-suited for this data. The method deals well with realistic colonoscopy video data, as shown through its performance on downstream evaluation tasks. In terms of broader impact, the main idea of the paper is likely to apply to other kinds of sequential data as well.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are several empirical choices in the paper which work well in the given setting but may not transfer to other contexts, for example, for the bag construction, the use of the exponential distribution and the choice of the temperature parameter. This is only a minor criticism. The comparison with other methods is good but not exhaustive (for example, no comparison with recent video SSL methods).
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The problem setting is highly practical: it avoids relying on costly and highly specialized polyp entity annotations, and instead directly exploits the inherent temporal order in colonoscopy procedures to construct a self-supervision signal. This substantially lowers the barrier to training data acquisition and makes the method more suitable for scaling to real clinical scenarios. The method design is well targeted: rather than naively treating temporally close tracklets as always-correct positive pairs, the authors explicitly recognize that such associations can be noisy, and therefore introduce a noise-aware contrastive loss. This allows the model to tolerate incorrect temporal associations and prevents the representation learning process from being misled. The training strategy is well designed: through temporal rank-based sampling and curriculum learning, the model starts from nearby samples that are safer but less diverse in the early stage, and gradually incorporates more distant samples that are more diverse but also noisier. This design effectively balances stability and diversity. The experimental results are convincing and efficient: the method performs well across four downstream tasks, including retrieval, re-identification, size estimation, and histology classification. It outperforms existing self-supervised and supervised baselines, and matches or exceeds foundation models on multiple tasks. At the same time, the model itself is lightweight and is trained on only 27 videos, indicating strong efficiency and a favorable performance-to-cost ratio.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The temporal assumption is relatively strong: the method relies on the premise that tracklets that are temporally close are more likely to belong to the same polyp, but this assumption may not remain stable in scenarios with multiple polyps appearing consecutively, repeated revisits, or more complex procedural operations. The experimental setting is somewhat idealized: the tracklets are constructed from ground-truth detections, and the paper does not yet sufficiently validate the end-to-end performance under realistic conditions such as detection errors, tracking drift, and missed detections. The generalization evidence is still limited: although the method achieves promising results when trained on only 27 videos, the training scale remains relatively small, and more empirical evidence is needed to support its robustness across centers, devices, and more complex clinical distributions. The mechanism analysis could be further strengthened: while the paper includes ablation studies, the stability of the noise-aware loss under different noise levels, bag purity conditions, and parameter settings is still not analyzed in sufficient depth.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for the time dedicated to review our work and for the valuable feedback they provided. We are pleased by the early acceptance to MICCAI 2026.We will take the reviewers’ suggestions into consideration in our future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a temporal contrastive framework for colonoscopy videos that uses temporal closeness as a cheap, noisy supervisory signal and reshapes the contrastive loss to handle realistic violations of this signal, such as multi-polyp scenes and revisits. The idea is that tracklets that are temporally close are likely to depict the same polyp, and the loss is modified to encode mismatches between anchors instead of treating positives as hard. The novelty over standard temporal contrastive learning is concrete. Two reviewers endorse the work. R2 (Accept) calls it “a very solid paper, with a clear methodological contribution backed up by good results.” R3 (Weak Accept) emphasizes the practical value of avoiding polyp-entity annotation and judges the framework technically sound. R1’s Weak Reject says novelty is “limited relative to existing literature in temporal contrastive learning and robust optimization”, but does not cite any specific prior work the authors should have positioned against. Without that, the negative review does not outweigh the two positive ones.

title: CoRe-DA: Contrastive Regression for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Surgical Skill Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: Open-sourced code and dataset. Thank you for making this available Interesting considerations of information and gradient flow through different modules to prevent model collapse with contrastive learning Thorough comparison with existing methods Good performance on unlabelled datasets
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Error is still high relative to the range of the scores Since all unlabeled data is used for training contrastive loss, unclear how the relative module will act on unseen data. Granted, this is not uncommon in unsupervised learning, but it’s not a great indicator of generalizability to unseen users
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel and important problem formulation. Existing SSA methods are domain-specific and generalize poorly, while unlabeled surgical video is increasingly abundant. Framing SSA-UDA as regression (rather than binary classification, as in prior work [11, 23]) preserves the granularity required for meaningful feedback to surgeons. 2.Solid benchmark contribution. The four datasets cover genuinely different domain shifts — open vs. robotic, dry-lab vs. clinical, different instruments and procedures. This will be a useful resource for the community. 3.Well-motivated methodology. Exploiting the observation that OSATS/M-GEARS criteria are domain-agnostic, and leveraging relative scores (rather than absolute ones) to learn domain-invariant representations, is a principled choice. The combination of dual-head consistency, stop-gradient, and pseudo-label self-training is coherent. 4.Strong empirical results. Improvements are substantial on both settings with low variance across seeds (±0.03, ±0.05). Fig. 4 is particularly compelling — competing methods collapse predictions toward the mean, whereas CoRe-DA preserves score ordering across the full range. 5.Thorough ablations. Table 3 systematically evaluates each loss term, the stop-gradient mechanism, and background mixing, which is appropriate for the MICCAI standard.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient differentiation from prior contrastive regression work Section 2.2 explicitly builds on CoRe+GART [29] and follows [5] for the relative regressor design (concatenated pooled features + MLP). The authors claim to be “the first to explore contrastive regression as an adaptation strategy,” but the novelty relative to a naive combination of CoRe/GART with target self-training is not clearly isolated. Is the contribution the triplet sampling (source–exemplar–target), the consistency loss between R_abs and R_rel, or both? 2.Fairness of test-time background mixing The test-time transformation mixes source-exemplar backgrounds into target videos (λ = 0.25). While using source information at test time is not formally forbidden in UDA, this raises two concerns: （1）Table 3 shows a non-trivial drop (SCC 0.47 → 0.43) when this component is removed. （2）Were the competing baselines (MDD, DARE-GRAM, RSD, CO2A) evaluated with any comparable test-time augmentation? 3.Exemplar count and inference cost Testing uses M = 10 exemplars per target video, requiring 10 forward passes averaged at inference. The paper reports monotonic improvement from M = 2 to 12 (plateauing at 12), but does not report inference time or FLOPs. This is a meaningful cost for clinical deployment. Please add an efficiency comparison against baselines.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem in surgical AI: adapting skill assessment models to new procedures and environments without labeled target data. The benchmark contribution is valuable, since prior work in this area is limited and often focuses on classification rather than regression. The proposed method is well motivated, technically coherent, and consistently outperforms strong baselines across both UDA settings. The paper is also generally well organized, with useful ablations and an additional semi-supervised experiment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The cross-dataset label harmonization deserves stronger justification. Although the source and target domains share overlapping OSATS/M-GEARS components, reducing them to a single summed score may obscure differences in rubric interpretation, score calibration, and component importance across datasets. A key part of CoRe-DA is exemplar-conditioned inference at test time, together with background mixing. This is an interesting design choice, but the paper does not fully analyze how sensitive performance is to exemplar selection, the mixing ratio, and the additional test-time computational cost. The proposed method combines several reasonable components, including relative-score supervision, target self-training, and background mixing, but the current analysis does not fully disentangle which component drives the largest gains. This is especially important because the main ablation is limited to a single adaptation setting and a single run. The empirical evaluation focuses on the summed final skill score, whereas the underlying rating systems (e.g., OSATS and M-GEARS) are multi-component. Reporting adaptation performance for individual skill dimensions would provide a more informative and clinically meaningful analysis. The statistical evidence could be strengthened. For example, the paired significance analysis appears to be based on predictions from a single run, whereas significance assessed across repeated runs or dataset splits would better support the robustness claims. The benchmark settings conflate multiple sources of domain shift, including task variation, operative environment, and surgical platform. A more fine-grained analysis of which shift factors are most challenging would improve the scientific insight of the study and clarify the method’s expected range of generalization.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1, R2, R3, MR. We are glad our work is “interesting-R1”, “valuable and timely-R2”, “well motivated, technically coherent-R3”, “addresses a novel, important, underexplored problem-all” with “strong, convincing results-all”. Answers follow and will be added in final paper. R1-High errors: CoRe-DA yields much lower errors/SD than all methods (Tab.1). MAE of 4.29 is reasonable for [6,30] JIGSAWS range, given no target labels for training. On RARP-skill it even beats fully supervised baselines (MAE 1.93 vs 2.10 [4],suppl.). R1-Generalizability: Using all unlabeled target data to train and test is standard in UDA [8, 30] given small datasets. Future work to study this with larger ones. R1-We will restructure Fig.1. R2-Differentiation from prior contrastive work: We are the first to propose contrastive regression as an UDA strategy, introducing novel components:(1) triplet sampling enabling cross-domain contrastive regression, (2) cons. loss between R_abs and R_rel, (3) self-training (L^T_cons with stop-grad). Each one is essential (per ablations,Tab. 3). [5,29] do not address domain adaptation (pure AQA models). R2-Fairness of test-time BG mix, non-trivial drop: Test-time BG mix is an integral design contribution of CoRe-DA, not applicable to competing methods as it requires exemplar anchoring (to extract the BG). Applying a global transform of the average source BG is of no value. Note, it’s not stochastic test-time augmentation (multiple random passes, often used to boost performance); it’s a deterministic, single-pass transformation to partially align low-level visual statistics across domains. From Tab.3 even without BG mix, CoRe-DA (SCC: 0.43,MAE: 4.57) outperforms all methods of Tab.1. R2,R3-Inference cost, exemplar selection, mix ratio: SSA is a post-op application, not real-time, so inference cost is not critical. GFLOPs are: Source-Only/MDD/DARE-G./RSD 670.638 (same model inference), Contra-S 2177.518, ViSA 912.435, CO2A 889.276, CoRe-DA (M=10) 1760.424. We empirically found random exemplar sampling to be slightly worse than uniform. Very small mix ratio values have minimal effect (mirroring ablation without BG mix), while values >0.25 distort target frames, degrading performance. R2,R3-CoRe-DA component gains, and disentanglement: Triplet sampling and self-training are inherently coupled and cannot be evaluated in isolation. Accurate Δy_T-E_hat predictions require R_rel to train on source-exemplar pairs, so they work jointly by design. Our ablations systematically remove one component at a time and evaluate the resulting performance drop to isolate each component’s contribution (incl. that of cons. losses). Single seed reporting is standard for ablations [3,9,16]. R3-Cross-dataset label harmonization: Our settings share identical label components (6 OSATS for AIxSuture-JIGSAWS, 6 M-GEARS for RAH-skill-RARP-skill); we do not transfer OSATS to M-GEARS as it violates UDA assumptions. We only use dry-lab-dry-lab or clinical-clinical pairs to reduce rubric/calibration mismatch. We assume marginal distribution shift with invariant label-conditional distribution (standard in UDA); relaxing this would require target labels (outside scope). OSATS and M-GEARS weight components equally, so summing introduces no bias. R3-Statistical evidence: We include paired t-test on all 4 runs for both UDA settings (p-value ranges: JIGSAWS/ RARP-skill). CoRe-DA’s improvements are statistically significant (or marginally) against nearly all cases: Source-Only (0.018-0.058/<0.05), Contra-S. (<0.05/0.000-0.070), ViSA (<0.05/<0.05), MDD (<0.05/<0.05), DARE-G. (0.024-0.056/<0.05), RSD (0.043-0.155/p<0.05), CO2A (0.043-0.084/<0.05). R3-Shift factors, individual skill components: All cases are suturing tasks. AIxSuture-JIGSAWS shifts platform (open vs robotic) and environment, RAH-skill-RARP-skill shifts environment/procedure. Fully isolating individual shifts and individual skill components scoring are important future directions

Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers recommend acceptance.
