title: ESRT: Endoscopic Stereo Reconstruction Transformer
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem, as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction in endoscopy are clinically useful but technically difficult due to specular reflection, weak texture, and unstable correspondence. The row-wise attention design is reasonable for stereo endoscopy, since disparity mainly occurs along the horizontal direction and this constraint can reduce unnecessary matching and computation. The reported efficiency is also a positive point, with fewer parameters, lower GFLOPs, and about 44 FPS compared with DUSt3R. The experiments cover several recent endoscopic reconstruction methods, and the visual examples look better than some baselines in selected cases.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper mainly combines a transformer reconstruction framework, epipolar/row-wise matching, and teacher-student distillation. These ideas have already appeared in related forms in stereo matching, transformer-based 3D reconstruction, and model distillation. DUSt3R already performs dense 3D reconstruction with cross-view matching, while Endo-FASt3r and EndoSfM3D have explored foundation-model-based endoscopic reconstruction. The paper does not make the difference from these works sufficiently clear. 2.The distillation strategy is also rather standard. Using DUSt3R as a teacher and training a smaller student model is useful, but the formulation itself does not seem very new. More analysis is needed to show why this distillation is specifically suited to endoscopic stereo reconstruction, rather than being a straightforward compression/adaptation of an existing teacher model. 3.The comparison is not fully convincing. Many baseline results are directly taken from previous papers, but the training and evaluation settings may not be exactly the same. It would be better to rerun key baselines under the same protocol, especially DUSt3R, Endo-FASt3r, and EndoSfM3D. 4.The clinical claim is overstated. The paper mentions real-time clinical applicability, but the experiments are only on SCARED, which is based on porcine cadaver data. There is no validation on real clinical gastroscopy cases, no lesion measurement task, and no user study with clinicians.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Strong results. Out of the comparisons provided by the authors, their approach (ESRT-Row) achieves best performance in depth estimation Effective ideas. student outperforms teacher despite the latter being frozen, demonstrating that the epipolar constraint and multiscale encoder are helpful Practicality. The authors demonstrate that their model is efficient compared to some baselines. Furthermore, their method seems like it does not require ground truth and is trained only with pseudolabels. Good writing. The method is clearly described and the paper flows well
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited method novelty. Row-wise (or epipolar constrained) transformer-based 3D reconstruction/depth estimation/stereo matching is fairly dated, and the first work of its kind also includes SCARED in their experiments (STTR Stereo Transformer, Li et al). The method is DUSt3R pointmap prediction + distillation + epipolar constraints, which has limited novelty Lack of ablation. For this type of study, the lack of thorough ablation is concerning, even though there are many components that raise several questions. How does distillation compare with train-from-scratch and full supervision from SCARED GT? How do the different loss term ideas contribute? How does DiNAT compare with other backbones like plain ViT (DINOv2-pretrained for instance) or Swin? Limited evaluation. Since this is stereo depth estimation, I am curious how the proposed model compares against methods like FoundationStereo, RAFT-Stereo, CREO-stereo, etc. Furthermore, DUSt3R is a originally a two-view reconstruction model. Would using FoundationStereo or another stereo model as a teacher be better since it’s more well-suited for this task? I am unsure if the entire training pipeline requires any ground truth data for training, or if the training only comes from pseudolabels from the teacher. Was any SCARED ground truth data used for training? Please clarify. Writing. I am unsure if the paper does indeed propose a “reconstruction transformer”. The proposed model seems to be more of a stereo depth estimator. Perhaps this claim can be made if other non-stereo datasets were also used to evaluate the model (e.g., C3VD). There are also other writing concerns, like the paper being motivated in the Introduction section with gastroscopy, but the method is only evaluated with ex-vivo porcine data.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) Precise problem formulation: The work accurately targets real-world clinical challenges in endoscopy. The three key objectives enforcing epipolar constraints, alleviating annotation scarcity, and achieving real-time performance are highly consistent with the clinical translation-oriented goals of MICCAI medical imaging research. 2) Effective core innovation: The proposed row-wise cross-attention is simple and physically meaningful, which directly conforms to the horizontal disparity property of stereo endoscopy. The motivation is solid and the design is reasonable. 3) Practical training strategy: The knowledge distillation scheme successfully addresses the shortage of endoscopic 3D annotations, aligns with the mainstream trend of self-supervised/weakly-supervised learning in medical imaging, and exhibits strong extensibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Over-reliance on the distillation strategy: The paper does not thoroughly discuss or analyze the quality of the “pseudo ground truth” provided by the teacher model under domain differences, nor the potential systematic biases. It remains unclear whether the method is overly dependent on the teacher model. 2) Insufficient ablation studies: The paper lacks complete and independent ablation studies for the three core components: row-wise cross-attention, knowledge distillation, and multi-scale fusion. As a result, the actual quantitative gains of each module cannot be verified.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and Reviewers (R1–R4) for their time and expertise, and address the primary concerns below. 1.Methodological Contribution and Novelty [MR, R1, R2] Novel Synergy: Unlike existing transformer-based reconstruction methods, our framework jointly integrates a multi-scale backbone and row-wise attention to explicitly enforce horizontal epipolar constraints across different feature scales. This design enables effective feature alignment and direct 3D reconstruction under strong specular reflections and visually similar textures in endoscopic images, without explicitly estimating camera intrinsic parameters or poses. By suppressing attention in geometrically invalid regions, the proposed architecture provides a physically meaningful solution for robust stereo matching in challenging endoscopic scenarios. Beyond Compression: Our distillation-based strategy uses sparse but reliable teacher correspondences, enabling the student model through multi-scale interaction and row-wise attention to effectively learn geometry-aware stereo matching. Thus, the student model surpasses the teacher model and achieves more robust performance under challenging endoscopic conditions. 2.Clinical Framing and Validation Domain [MR, R4] We appreciate R4 and the MR’s concern regarding the discrepancy between our clinical motivation (gastroscopy) and validation (SCARED porcine abdominal anatomy). Gold-Standard Validation: The SCARED dataset is the gold-standard MICCAI challenge benchmark for “stereo correspondence and reconstruction of endoscopic data”. Validating on SCARED is a necessary step to demonstrate technical merit within the surgical vision community. Refinement of Claims: We acknowledge that our “gastric mucosa-specific” phrasing may be overly focused. Following R4’s suggestion, we will reframe the final manuscript as a general endoscopic stereo reconstruction framework, positioning “gastric diagnosis” as a primary future clinical application. 3.Experimental Setup and Training Pipeline [R1, R2, R4] Experimental Settings: In Table 1, for experimental fairness, the results for Endo-FASt3R and EndoSfM3D were directly adopted from their original papers, as both methods are designed for monocular temporal reconstruction rather than stereo-pair matching. Therefore, their evaluation results were only based on the left-view split of the SCARED dataset, and our comparisons follow the same protocol. Their performance would further degrade with stereo-pair training, because they rely on temporal reprojection optimization rather than stereo correspondence learning. Training Strategy: For DUSt3R and ESRT, both methods use the rectified stereo pairs officially provided by SCARED under the same train/test split, making the row-wise cross-attention assumption valid. DUSt3R requires GT pointmap supervision, while ESRT does not use any SCARED GT pointmap for training. Instead, ESRT uses a DUSt3R teacher pretrained on large-scale stereo datasets without exposure to SCARED, and only utilizes sparse reliable pseudo correspondences for distillation. The proposed multi-scale and geometric-constrained design then learns robust stereo matching for challenging endoscopic features without dense annotations. 4.Ablations and Efficiency Evaluation [R2, R3, R4] Ablation Studies: Table 1 provides an explicit ablation: ESRT-Full vs. ESRT-Row. The improvement in AbsRel from 0.053 to 0.048 directly quantifies the “remarkable effectiveness” of our row-wise constraint. Hardware and FPS: The 44 FPS were measured on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with batch size 1 and input resolution 320x256, consistent with the SCARED dataset setting used by the SOTA methods. 5.Quantitative Completeness: $\delta$ Metrics [R4] Prior Studies: As shown in the experiments in EndoSfM3D, which is superior to other SOTA methods, $\delta$ is also omitted due to limited space. We appreciate reviewers’ understanding.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers commonly question the novelty and evidence behind the method, noting that it largely combines existing ideas—DUSt3R-style pointmap prediction, epipolar/row-wise matching, and standard teacher–student distillation—without clearly distinguishing itself from related stereo or endoscopic reconstruction methods, and without sufficient ablations to isolate the effects of distillation, row-wise attention, multi-scale fusion, losses, or backbone choices. They also raise concerns that the evaluation is incomplete and misaligned with the paper’s clinical claims, since experiments are limited to SCARED porcine cadaver data despite repeated gastroscopy/gastric-mucosa motivation, key baselines may not be evaluated under the same protocol, standard depth metrics are missing, and the dependence on teacher-generated pseudo labels is not adequately analyzed. | This paper has limitations on the experiments and evaluation: -Discrepancy between the clinical motivation (gastroscopy) and the validation (SCARED porcine abdominal anatomy). -Ablation study is limited. However, the methodology has good novelty, and it is effective for the applications: -Row-wise cross-attention -Multi-scale backbone This paper is expected to contribute to future advances in stereo reconstruction from endoscopic images, and I think it is acceptable. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors managed to provide convincing answers to the comments raised by the reviewers. The method is potentially impactful in the field of 3D reconstruction. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper addresses an important problem and reports promising efficiency and SCARED performance. The row-wise attention is reasonable, and the rebuttal clarifies the rectified-stereo setting and training without SCARED GT pointmaps. However, the main concerns remain. The novelty is limited, as the method combines DUSt3R-style pointmap prediction, epipolar/row-wise matching, multi-scale features, and standard distillation. The experiments lack key ablations, matched baseline comparisons, teacher-dependence analysis, and standard depth metrics. The original gastroscopy/gastric-mucosa framing is also not supported by the SCARED-only validation and would require substantial reframing. Overall, the work is promising but not sufficiently novel or validated for acceptance.

title: From Perception to Anticipation: Forecasting Vessel–Instrument Interactions in Endoscopic Surgery under Unreliable Observations
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant and well-motivated problem. Anticipating vessel–instrument interactions has clear implications for preventing complications such as vessel injury during ESD, making the shift from perception to anticipation highly meaningful. A major strength is the introduction of a new task and dataset, which provides a foundation for future research. The task is clearly defined and distinct from existing work on phase detection or segmentation. The work also stands out by explicitly modeling observation uncertainty, rather than relying on end-to-end learning to implicitly handle noise. The separation between reliability estimation and temporal modeling is conceptually clean and well motivated. Methodologically, the combination of cross-modal consistency and dual memory mechanisms is interesting and reasonably well aligned with the problem structure. The empirical results are convincing, with consistent improvements over baselines, particularly under unstable or noisy conditions. Finally, the demonstrated real-time performance strengthens the practical relevance of the approach.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A key limitation is the insufficient description of the annotation process, which is particularly critical given that a new task is introduced. Important details such as annotator expertise, annotation protocol, handling of temporal transitions, and inter-annotator agreement are missing. This raises concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of the dataset. Related to this, the paper lacks transparency and reproducibility in several aspects. Core components such as the CLR module, reliability score computation, and gating mechanisms are described at a high level but not specified in sufficient algorithmic detail. Additionally, the main methodological figure 2 is very hard to understand and visually overloaded. The temporal and/or logical path remains intransparent. Having this complexity in mind, it is a major weakness that there is no statement regarding code and/or data availability. Another concern is the reliance on automatically generated vessel segmentations (SAM2) as a core input to the proposed framework. While the paper explicitly aims to be robust to segmentation noise, no quantitative evaluation of segmentation quality is provided. Such a validation would provide an important reference for contextualizing the reliability of the input signal. Without this information, it is difficult to disentangle whether the reported robustness primarily arises from the proposed cross‑modal and memory mechanisms, or whether it benefits from already sufficiently accurate upstream segmentation. A quantitative assessment or at least a discussion of expected segmentation quality would strengthen the methodological clarity and interpretability of the results. Finally, the evaluation is restricted to a single, internally collected dataset, with no external validation. This makes it difficult to assess robustness across different clinical settings, devices, or institutions.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically relevant, Anticipating instrument–vessel interactions before contact is a meaningful step toward proactive surgical safety systems. 2.The emphasis on robustness to noisy inputs is well-motivated and practically relevant. 3.The combination of cross-modal learning and temporal modeling is logically structured.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is difficult to follow, with many concepts, variables, and modules introduced without sufficient explanation: 1.The core prediction task is not clearly specified early on. It is not immediately clear whether this is a standard classification problem, a sequence prediction task, or a forecasting problem. 2.Several terms, equations and components are introduced with insufficient intuition or justification, making it hard to understand how they contribute to the final prediction. For example, (a) the intermediate feature f(8) was selected for feature fusion, was other selections and impacts well studied? (b)The cosine similarity computation is inconsistent between the image and the text.(c) It is not clear how a_vis and a_align are derived. (d) Not all the components of the 10D geometry descriptor listed. (e), what is anticipation signal, and how it was computed (the classification results or computed on top of it?) (f) Hyperparameters such as memory sizes, thresholds, and fusion weights are not well analyzed. It is unclear how sensitive the method is to these choices. 2.The dataset is not well explained. what is the statistics of each class, how the dataset is split (randomly or clips from the same videos in the same set etc). 3.How noisy was the segmentation result, and how was cases with long periods lacking a reliable reference handled? 4.How was the instrument tip extracted? Overall, the lack of clarity significantly hinders understanding and weakens the paper’s impact.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The most significant strength of this paper is the formalization of the Vessel-Instrument Interaction Anticipation task. While existing research in surgical AI has largely focused on real-time segmentation and perception, this work proactively addresses surgical safety by forecasting potential risks before they occur. Shifting the focus from reactive detection to predictive anticipation is a highly meaningful contribution that directly addresses the need for early warning systems in complex procedures like Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD). The proposed hierarchical architecture is also technically impressive, particularly in its ability to handle noisy and unreliable surgical data. The Cross-modal Latent Recovery (CMLR) module effectively utilizes an information bottleneck to filter out noise from segmentation masks, ensuring that the temporal reasoning process is based on reliable features. Furthermore, the Dual Asynchronous Memory (DAM) module is a clever solution for modeling the heterogeneous nature of surgical interactions. By decoupling transient instrument dynamics from stable interaction prototypes, the framework maintains high predictive accuracy even when frame-level observations are limited or degraded.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: While the task of anticipation is novel, the reported Macro F1 score of 70.80% suggests that the system may still produce a significant number of false alarms or missed detections. In a high-stakes surgical environment like Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD), a 30% error margin could lead to alarm fatigue for surgeons or, more critically, a failure to prevent actual vessel damage. The authors should have provided a more detailed failure case analysis to discuss how these errors would be managed in a real clinical setting. The dataset composition also raises concerns regarding the generalizability of the proposed framework. The study utilizes a newly constructed multi-case ESD dataset, but the paper does not specify the diversity of the surgical equipment or the variations in anatomical conditions across different patients. Since the appearance of vessels and the handling of instruments can vary significantly between surgeons and hospital settings, the lack of cross-center validation or a more diverse testing set limits the proof of the model’s robustness. Another weakness lies in the definition of the anticipation window. The paper mentions predicting upcoming states from a short observation window, yet it does not clearly define the exact lead time or the prediction horizon. Without a rigorous analysis of the trade-off between the prediction horizon and accuracy, it is difficult to evaluate whether the system provides enough reaction time for a surgeon to actually alter their movement and avoid an accident. Finally, although the dual asynchronous memory module is designed to handle temporal reasoning, its superiority over simpler temporal models like Transformers or LSTMs with attention mechanisms is not sufficiently justified through extensive ablation studies. The authors should have compared their memory module against a wider range of state-of-the-art temporal architectures to clearly demonstrate that the added complexity of dual asynchronous processing is necessary for achieving the reported performance.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. R1 appreciated the “conceptually clean” decoupling and “convincing” results; R2 valued a “meaningful step” toward proactive surgical safety; R3 recognized the “highly meaningful contribution” and “technically impressive” architecture. Responses below: 1.Dataset construction & annotation (Meta, R1, R2, R3): (i) Dataset. The dataset contains 3330 clips from 30 cases across four sites (esophagus/stomach/colon/rectum: 310/400/2200/420 clips) and three classes (no_interaction/approaching/touching: 1650/960/720 clips). All cases were split at the case level into 22 training and 8 testing cases (2430/900 clips), avoiding within-video leakage while preserving label/site distributions. (ii) Annotation. Two trained annotators with 4+ years of endoscopic research experience independently labeled all clips, using the visible vessel–instrument relation at the target frame. For state-changing clips, the label follows the state at the 4th-s target frame. Initial agreement was 94.4% with Cohen’s kappa=0.90, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. 2.Task formulation & lead-time (R2, R3): The task is a forecasting problem formulated as 3-class classification of the future interaction state. The model takes 16 frames from a 3-s observation window and predicts the state at the 4th-s target frame, yielding Δt=1s lead time. The anticipation signal in Fig.4 is the class-wise softmax probability on f^m (Eq.1), and its touching curve rises 0.5–1s before contact, supporting timely preventive response. 3.Method clarifications (Meta, R1, R2): (i) CLR. f_t^(8) is an intermediate ViT-B layer preserving spatial detail before semantic abstraction. Layer ablation over {6, 8, 10, 12} confirms layer 8 is optimal, outperforming the second-best setting, f_t^(10), by 1.73 Macro-F1.- 10-D geometry descriptor encodes spatial proximity (tip-vessel distance), motion (1st-/2nd-order changes, moving average), position (tip x, y), visibility (vessel area ratio, tip and vessel visibility), and topology (tip-inside-vessel). (ii) Reliability terms. Two reliability signals are estimated before fusion: a_t^vis measures geometric observation stability and visibility from g_t, while a_t^align=[1+cos(h_t^f,h_t^g)]/2 measures consistency between the visual and geometric latent representations. (Fig.2 notation will be aligned with the text formula.) (iii) Gating. ψ_t weights transient-memory readout, r_t (Eq.3) controls prototypal admission/compensation, and λ_t (Eq.5) balances transient and prototypal fusion. (iv) Hyperparameters. Transient/prototypal memory sizes (8,20) perform best among 2–40, with nearby settings within 0.79 Macro-F1.Threshold τ=0.50 performs best over 0.3–0.7, and fusion weight λ_t (Eq.5) is learned end-to-end, with category-adaptive values shown in Fig.3(b). 4.Segmentation performance, impact & instrument tip (R1, R2): Segmentation noise has limited impact due to our reliability-aware mechanisms. Vessel segmentation achieves Dice/IoU=84.64/73.37, and the visible active-tip center is manually annotated to isolate vessel-mask noise from tip-localization errors. Fig.3(a) analyzes visually unstable clips with inconsistent masks: F1 drops by 8.17 for our model vs. 32.84 for the baseline, showing that robustness arises from the proposed mechanisms rather than clean input. For prolonged unreliable spans, r_t blocks prototypal admission, preserving accumulated prototypes. 5.Failure analysis & clinical interpretation (R3): Errors mainly arise in non-routine motion patterns and concentrate more on the ambiguous approaching class than on the safety-critical touching class, as shown in Tab.1 (F1=64.3 vs. 73.7). For clinical use, r_t filters low-reliability evidence, while sustained high-risk predictions support surgeon verification. 6.Code & data release (Meta, R1, R2): We will open-source code, weights, and annotation protocol. The dataset will be released under a data-use agreement.

More details on the dataset should be provided. | The authors managed to opportunely improve the methods and the dataset description. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The responses addressed the concerns about description of the annotation process and reproducibility, missing algorithmic detail. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper introduces a novel and clinically meaningful task: vessel–instrument interaction anticipation in endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), shifting from retrospective recognition to proactive forecasting, supported by a new annotated multi-case dataset and a reliability-aware framework combining cross-modal latent recovery and dual asynchronous memory. R3 regarded the task formulation as a highly meaningful contribution and the architecture as technically impressive. title: GES-Net: A Gesture, Error, and Smoothness Aware Network for Surgical Skill Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: Model represents an improvement over prior work on two distinct datasets for surgical skills assessment. Paper explores the interplay between skill, gestures, and errors.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Some of the comparisons in the results are biased by differing amounts of information used by each model. Justification on the interpretability of the feedback provided by the model is missing.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper targets an important weakness in current robotic surgical skill assessment methods: many output only a single score, with limited diagnostic value. The proposed decomposition into gesture, error, and smoothness is well motivated and closer to how human evaluators think about performance. 2.Rather than attaching auxiliary heads in a superficial way, the paper uses the auxiliary tasks in structurally meaningful places. This is a good example of using domain knowledge to shape the architecture, not just to add extra losses. 3.Among the proposed modules, SMG is interesting. It uses gesture labels for guidance early on, then partially masks them to encourage the model to infer semantics from visual cues rather than overfitting to dense labels. That is a thoughtful design choice for balancing supervision and autonomy. 4.The performance on RARP-skill is a notable strength. The paper reports SCC 0.76 and MAE 1.38, outperforming listed baselines by a meaningful margin. Since one of the paper’s messages is improved generalization to real clinical settings, this result matters.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper’s distinctive contribution is mainly the particular combination of gesture alignment, error weighting, and jitter modeling for skill assessment. That is valuable, but it is not a major methodological leap. This is especially relevant given prior work already cited by the authors on interpretable or gesture-aware skill assessment, such as Wang et al. 2020, ViSA 2022, Contra-Sformer 2023, and step-by-step prompting for error detection in robotic videos by Shao et al. 2024. 2.GES-Net is more interpretable than a plain regression network, but the paper occasionally suggests stronger transparency than it actually demonstrates. For example, gesture-feature similarity and error-weight profiles are useful diagnostics, but they do not yet amount to fully validated interpretability; there is no case study showing that surgeons or educators find these outputs actionable; the model still depends on learned latent features whose semantics are not fully disentangled. 3.A major practical limitation is that the method relies on gesture labels and binary error annotations during training. That is substantially more annotation than pure score-prediction methods require. The paper motivates this by saying single-score supervision is sparse, but it does not fully discuss the annotation burden or whether the accuracy gains justify that additional supervision. Since dense error labels are expensive in clinical videos, this matters for real-world scalability. 4.The paper evaluates only needle passing and suturing because these contain binary error annotations, excluding knot tying. That narrows comparability with broader JIGSAWS skill-assessment literature. It also means the method is demonstrated mainly on tasks where the extra supervision is available, rather than across the full benchmark. 5.The comparison table mixes methods with missing MAE values and methods that may not use the same supervision or auxiliary labels. The paper says some methods were reimplemented using official code for fairness, especially on RARP-skill, but the exact reproduction protocol is not described in enough details. It is therefore hard to know how directly comparable all reported gains are.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The manuscript has several major strengths. author_feedback: We thank the AC and reviewers for their feedback. We are encouraged that reviewers recognize the significance of the topic explored (R1, R2, R3), the soundness of the method design (R2, R3), strong empirical results (R1, R2, R3), and good writing quality (R1, R2, R3). We provide clarifications on the received comments: Fairness of comparisons (R1): Our method utilizes additional annotation types (gesture and error labels) beyond the skill score labels used by most baselines. This is indeed a design premise of our framework: the core contribution is to demonstrate how jointly leveraging multiple types of readily available surgical annotations can improve skill assessment performance and feedback. The comparison with single-task baselines is intended to quantify the benefit of this multi-task paradigm. Comparisons with other multi-task frameworks, which also leverage auxiliary annotations beyond skill scores, are included in Table 1. Scope of verification for interpretability (R1, R2, R3): A qualitative analysis of the jitter features and soft error weighting on the RARP-skill dataset is provided in Figure 3.The jitter curves capture operation smoothness differences across surgeons and reveal surgical steps with frequent pauses, offering targeted feedback for skill improvement. Similarly, the soft error weighting indicates which steps involve errors critical to skill improvement, providing insights beyond simple skill score prediction. In future work, we plan to include quantitative analysis and a user study based on surgeon feedback to further explore the impact of smoothness metrics and soft error distributions on surgical workflow optimization. Application scalability (R2): We appreciate the reviewer raising this point. Surgical gesture recognition and error detection are well-established tasks in the surgical AI community, and the gesture and error labels used in our framework are sourced from publicly available datasets, requiring no additional annotation effort beyond what is already available. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the reliance on auxiliary annotations may limit scalability in settings where such labels are unavailable. Future work will explore weakly supervised approaches for the auxiliary tasks to reduce this dependency. Deployment considerations (R3): The current framework is designed for offline skill assessment, where videos are processed post-procedure to provide structured feedback to trainees. This is standard in surgical training; thus, real-time inference is not required. We acknowledge that inference efficiency and robustness in real-world environments are important considerations for broader deployment, and we plan to include a dedicated discussion of these aspects in future extended versions of this work.

title: HadBalance: A Plug-and-Play Unified Global Geometric Prior Framework for Generalizable Biomedical Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The manuscript is generally well-structured and clearly written. It provides a detailed explanation of the Hadwiger prior and the underlying theorem, making the work accessible and understandable for readers The proposed method is well-formalized and presented in a way that is straightforward for the reader to follow The use of real-world datasets, although limited to three, is a positive aspect, as it allows readers to evaluate the applicability of the method in practical scenarios The authors have made the source code publicly available. While the training and inference scripts are not included, the provided code still enables readers to implement the method with minimal effort The figures are carefully curated and, when viewed on a PC with the ability to zoom, are clear and easy to interpret
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major weaknesses: The authors state that they “observe that most medical segmentation targets are globally near-convex”. I think this is a very strong claim which is not supported by any evidence in the paper. It is also informal, how is it measured or quantified in this context? It is also unclear which types of medical structures were considered when making this statement. Even if it was an assumption, this is quite strong and should be better justified, either through empirical analysis or references to prior work The authors said in the manuscript “Incorporating geometric cues [. . . ] is a common way to improve structural consistency; however geometric priors are largely task-specific [. . . ] and lack a unified foundation that generalizes across most organs and modalities and supports transferable geometric constraints”; the term “foundation” in this sentence feels somewhat vague and could be replaced with a more precise description of what is lacking. Also, the statement appears to frame task-specific geometric priors as a limitation due to their lack of generalizability, but, in medical imaging it is often both reasonable and expected for priors to be tailored to specific anatomical structures, as different organs exhibit distinct shapes and variability. The sentence needs to be rephrased for clarity and precision The AGB module, as much as it is well formalised and if I understood correctly, computes alpha(t) for each optimisation step, using the non-linear least-squares solver from scipy. This introduces a number of significant practical issues that are not discussed anywhere in the paper (except for a brief two word mention in the conclusion). First of all, the complexity of the scipy solver scales with the number of network parameters at least linearly, and more importantly it is embedded within another optimization process, so it adds a lot of computational overhead. Moreover, scipy does not support GPU computation; therefore, if the authors indeed used the scipy solver, it implies that either data must be transferred between GPU and CPU during each optimization step or the model training is being done on CPU, both of which are highly inefficient. The drawback of the training time is not discussed, and comparison of training costs are not reported in the experiment and result section The authors do not compare their method with other state-of-the-art approaches on each dataset. As a result, it is not possible to assess whether their work achieves comparable performance to existing methods on the datasets they use Standard deviations and COnfidence intervals are missing in every table of quantitative results. Given also the fact that train/validation/test set sizes are not reported, it is difficult to assess whether their method provide statistically significant results from the other methods, given that performance differences are very low for the most part (e. g. 86,19 vs 86,35) In the conclusions, the authors state: “In this paper, we observe that many medical segmentation targets exhibit globally near-convex geometry”. This claim is too strong and not supported by the evidence presented. The manuscript only includes a few examples from three medical targets, which is insufficient to generalize broadly. Additionally, the statement is informal and should be either supported with empirical analysis, clarified as an assumption, or softened to reflect the limited scope of the evidence Minor weaknesses: The images in the manuscript are quite small, making it difficult for readers, especially in printed format, to distinguish details such as text and formulas. In the introduction, where the authors outline their key contributions, colons are overused: “Our key contributions are as follows: 1: [. . . ]”. I recommend using a closing parenthesis after the item number instead, like “1) […]”, to improve readability The datasets used in the experiments are barely described, consisting of just a three-sentence paragraph with only citations. There is no discussion of what the datasets contain, the number of observations, or how the data were collected In the experimental setting, the authors train several backbones, they measure their performance, and perform a new training from scratch using the strongest backbone with their COAB module (for each dataset). While this comparison between backbone A + COAB versus backbone A alone is reasonable, it is unclear why only the strongest backbone was selected for this experiment. The manuscript does not provide any justification for this choice, why not add COAB to all the backbones for a more complete comparison? DRIONS-DB dataset is missing in the ablation study, with no justification in the text; also the Module / Loss columns are repeated in the table “HadBalance outperforms NASH and Fairgrad” is very strong, given the fact that only in few comparisons there is a clear separation between the methods (3 out of 9). The claim needs to be softened The authors perform a comparison of their method against two gradient-optimisation methods (NASH and FairGrad), however they do not explain in a few words what they are and how they operate, for more clarity they should be explained briefly

In introduction, page 2, paragraph 2 [ref needed], the authors claim that “most medical segmentation targets are globally near-convex” without any reference or experiment backing this claim. reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.This method uses area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic as a theoretically sound, interpretable, and transferable global shape prior for medical segmentation. Unlike task-specific geometric constraints, this prior generalizes to different organs and modalities, representing a significant conceptual advancement. 2.This method addresses a key practical problem: shape priors often over-regularize non-convex anatomy. CAOB automatically removes conflicting gradient components (PGPs) and adaptively balances the loss (AGB) without requiring manual weight adjustments, making it stable and easily integrated into existing models. 3.The framework was validated on three different datasets (carotid artery, polyp, optic disc) using six mainstream backbone networks. Its performance outperforms strong baselines including nnUNet, TransUNet, and state-of-the-art multi-task optimizers (Nash-MTL, FairGrad), particularly showing consistent gains in boundary accuracy. 4.HadBalance is model-agnostic and can be directly integrated into existing segmentation pipelines, demonstrating strong clinical and engineering potential.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.CAOB requires separate backpropagation for each loss term, which increases training time and GPU memory usage compared to standard single backpropagation methods. This paper does not provide efficiency analysis or optimization strategies. 2.Experiments were conducted only on three near-convex-dominated 2D datasets. Its performance on highly non-convex organs (e.g., liver, lung, heart) and 3D volume data has not been tested, limiting its generalization potential. 3.This paper does not compare with state-of-the-art learnable shape priors or topology-aware segmentation methods, making it difficult to determine the relative advantages of Hadwiger constraint-based methods. 4.Convergence of fixed-point iteration in AGB is not analyzed. Stability and sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., pooling size, ρ) have not been thoroughly discussed.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and ACs. Responses are as follows (R: Reviewer, Q: Question): The near-convex assumption: We agree that “most medical segmentation targets are globally near-convex” was too strong; our intent was to use near-convexity as a qualitative motivation, not to make a universal empirical claim over all medical structures. We will revise “most” to “many”, soften “we observe that”, and add convex/star-convex prior references (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., JMIV 2025; Royer et al., CVPR 2016; StarDist, MICCAI 2018) with examples such as optic disc, nuclei, and cardiac structures. HadBalance does not pre-classify samples as near-/non-convex; instead, it applies A/P/χ priors to all samples and uses CAOB to suppress conflicting prior-gradient components when these priors would over-regularize genuine non-convex structures [R1Q1Q5, R2Q3]. The missing benchmarks: Dataset-specific SOTA methods such as Polyp-PVT (Dong et al., 2023) and Meng et al. (MICCAI 2022) are useful per-dataset baselines, but our experiments test HadBalance as a plug-and-play global geometric-prior framework rather than a separately tuned SOTA pipeline for each dataset [R1Q4]. Shape-prior methods such as You et al. (TMI 2025) and Song et al. (IJCAI 2024) introduce architecture-level modules/statistical shape models, so a direct comparison would mix architectural and training effects with our Hadwiger-prior and CAOB contributions. Topology-aware methods such as Hu et al. (NeurIPS 2019) and Li et al. (TMI 2025) mainly target topology preservation for topology-critical structures, such as vessels, and address a different objective from our work [R4Q3]. For [R1Q9], we selected the strongest backbone on each dataset as a stricter setting to test whether HadBalance can further improve an already strong baseline. The efficiency analysis: CAOB follows the per-objective-gradient paradigm: separate gradients are needed to estimate conflicts and balance objectives. The A/P/χ regularizers are lightweight pooling/convolution/gradient-magnitude operations; the main overhead is multiple backward passes, which is shared by methods such as FairGrad and Nash-MTL. The SciPy solver is not applied to the full gradients or network parameters. After per-objective gradients, we compute pairwise inner products on GPU to form a small K×K Gram matrix (K=4), and SciPy only solves the resulting 4-dimensional α problem. Thus, the CPU transfer is limited to this small Gram matrix, not full gradients or parameters, and training remains GPU-based [R1Q3, R2Q4, R4Q1Q4]. Regarding convergence, AGB does not perform high-dimensional fixed-point iteration; it solves a low-dimensional constrained least-squares problem for K=4 weights, and stability is empirically supported by CAOB ablations and gradient-alignment analysis. Sensitivity was under-discussed: D = {7,15,31} was fixed across experiments for multi-scale A/P/χ maps, while ρ is a scale-control term whose absolute effect is mitigated by the subsequent α normalization rather than acting as a dataset-specific loss weight [R4Q4]. Generalization analysis: 3D extension is feasible, but not by directly reusing the 2D A/P/χ formulation; it would require 3D intrinsic volumes and a redesigned differentiable 3D χ computation [R2Q2, R4Q2]. Highly non-convex organs are outside the validated scope of this submission, since Hadwiger priors are primarily motivated by near-convex geometry, and we therefore do not claim generalization to such organs here [R4Q2]. Results Analysis: We agree that the CUBS DSC margin is small and should not be judged from a single Dice value alone. Full HadBalance improves the strongest CUBS backbone by +1.21 BFScore, and on the more shape-heterogeneous CVC-ClinicDB, it improves over LS by +1.04 DSC, +1.50 IoU, and +1.64 BFScore, indicating that CAOB more robustly integrates Hadwiger priors without manual loss-weight tuning [R1Q4]. We will add confidence intervals to better reflect statistical uncertainty [R1Q4, R2Q1].
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The idea is not completely obvious, and the theoretical foundation is interesting, but whether it will have real impact in medical AI is still unclear because the evidence is limited. The three reviewers gave recommendations of reject, accept, and weak accept; I’d like the authors to partake in rebuttal (issues: the near convex assumption, the missing benchmarks, the efficiency analysis, etc.). | Despite a split from reviewers, I recommend acceptance. I think the CAOB mechanism addresses the practical over-regularization problem in a mathematically sound way. The rebuttal adequately resolved the two sharpest concerns: the near-convex assumption was conceded and softened with prior-work support, and the SciPy efficiency objection was clarified. Missing benchmarks against architecture-level shape-prior methods and modest performance margins remain a limitation, but are defensible given the plug-and-play framing and the meaningful boundary-level predictions. I encourage authors to amend their camera-ready with proper discussions. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend rejection. The paper addresses an interesting direction—using global geometric priors for biomedical segmentation—but the current submission does not sufficiently support its claims of being unified, generalizable, and plug-and-play. The main concern is that the core assumption, namely that many biomedical targets are globally near-convex, is not rigorously justified. The connection between Hadwiger’s theorem and the proposed practical losses is also overstated: area, perimeter, and Euler characteristic do not uniquely encode near-convexity and may be inadequate for complex or highly non-convex anatomy. The methodological novelty is limited. The proposed regularizers resemble existing shape/topology losses, and the conflict-aware optimization component is not clearly distinguished from prior multi-objective gradient-balancing methods. The derivation and practical stability of the adaptive weighting strategy are also insufficiently analyzed. The experiments are too narrow for the paper’s broad claims. Evaluation is limited to three relatively small 2D datasets, with no strong evidence on more challenging non-convex, thin-structure, multi-component, 3D, or cross-domain settings. The reported gains are mostly modest, and statistical validation, runtime analysis, and stronger comparisons to recent shape/topology-aware segmentation methods are missing. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the authors’ rebuttal and the post-rebuttal recommendations from reviewers, I recommend Accept. The rebuttal effectively addresses the key concerns.

title: Hi-FL: Hierarchical Federated Learning Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Multi-Institutional Surgical Phase Recognition
reviewer_1_strengths: A key strength of this work is the adaptation of vision-language models not only to capture global variability across surgical procedures, but also to enable the development of center-specific models. Additionally, the paper presents an extensive experimental validation in different type of procedures.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The introduction is relatively long, limiting the space available for presenting experimental results or discuss. Regarding the datasets, the number of videos per dataset appears to be relatively limited. Probably, dataset with frame-wise temporal labels are scarce, but the authors didn’t mentioned it. Additionally, Figures 3 and 4 are difficult to interpret due to their small size and low resolution. Some elements of the legends also appear to be cropped, which further reduces their clarity. An example may be beneficial to illustrate the model’s performance with and without the proposed hierarchical adaptation and federated learning components. Despite the observed improvements over the baseline, the reported results exhibit noticeable variability. The manuscript does not provide sufficient analysis to explain this behavior. Finally, the paper lacks a dedicated discussion of its limitations.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper focuses on cross-institutional domain shift. The problem originates from real-world clinical scenarios, and the proposed solution has clear practical value. The main strengths of this work can be summaried from two aspects: a) Innovation of the hierarchical framework. Surgical phase understanding is decomposed into a three-level structure of “Procedure-Phase-Action”, which accurately distinguishes between universal surgical semantics and local institutional noise. This framework solves the limitation of flat categories in traditional methods. b) Solid experimental analysis. Comprehensive comparative experiments and ablation studies are conducted against state-of-the-art federated learning methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Although this work holds several major strengths as mentioned above, there also exist several concerns that need to be addressed in the revised version. a) The methodology part is insufficiently clear. The introduction to the core hierarchical mechanism is simply too brief, and specific details of the multi-level structure are not adequately shown in Fig. 1 and Section 3.2.Especially in Fig. 1, which requires careful explanation, as it corresponds to the components in the ablation experiments of Section 5.4.Currently, it is somewhat confusing. b) Insufficient quantitative validation of hierarchical disentanglement. Hierarchical disentanglement is only achieved through the indep loss, but there is no evaluation to confirm whether the three-level features well capture semantics of different granularities. The effectiveness is questionable. c) Comparisons with state-of-the-art federated learning methods for surgical phase recognition are lacking. d) The figures and tables need to be improved. The description of qualitative results in Section 5.2, including the legends, lacks clarity. The paper should emphasize the presentation of its core components, and the writing style can be further adjusted.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper addresses an inherent problem during the decentralized federated learning framework to improve the consistency across hospitals without violating any data sharing constraints. Major strengths: The centroid component provides a class level alignment signal across centers without sharing raw videos. Class-wise centroids are simple proxies for each surgical phase at each hospital. Each site shares one average embedding per class instead of full features or raw data. This is a genuinely federated-specific mechanism. Unlike the hierarchical module, the centroid exchange is directly aimed at cross-center heterogeneity. The TAR loss is conceptually clean: it pulls a frame embedding toward its correct class centroid and pushes it away from other class centroids. This gives more structure than plain cross-entropy, because it encourages class-consistent geometry across institutions, not just correct local labels.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The contribution of the federated alignment component is not clearly isolated. Although the paper compares against prior federated methods, it does not include a direct ablation of TAR or centroid exchange within the proposed framework. Therefore, it remains unclear how much of the gain comes specifically from the federated semantic alignment term. The method description contains several tightly coupled components, and some formulations are not presented clearly enough for easy interpretation. In addition, parts of the notation appear ambiguous or insufficiently explained such as equation (4) in Methodology. Improving the clarity of the method section would strengthen the paper considerably. The paper focuses mainly on positive results, but provides little discussion of limitations, such as when the method may fail, how sensitive it is to hyperparameter choices in broader settings, or how well it may generalize beyond the evaluated datasets. A short discussion of limitations and future work would make the paper more balanced.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We will improve Figs. 3&4 for better readability and add FedAvg & non-FL examples (R1Q3,4). Fig.1 will be revised to map each equation/component from Sec. 3.2 & 5.4 (R2Qa,d). We will add a Discussion section (R1Q6, R3Q3) on: dataset scale limits from costly surgical annotation; sensitivity, noting the method assumes primarily phase-distributional heterogeneity; and reliance on expert labels with future directions toward weakly/self-supervised methods. We commit to releasing our codebase. Bypass is public; for the other datasets we will provide preprocessing scripts. R1 Q2: We will shorten Sec.1-2 to create space for Discussion. On dataset scarcity: dense frame-wise surgical annotation requires expert surgeons to label long procedures frame by frame (Maier-Hein et al., MedIA 2022). MultiCholec and Bypass represent the practical upper bound of surgical FL benchmarks, motivating our 5%-50% regime. Q5: Variability arises from multi-center heterogeneity (e.g., Bypass (Lavanchy et al., IJCARS 2024): omentum division routine in Strasbourg but not Bern) and the data-scarce regime (5% data, 16-shot), where small frame changes affect optimization. Federation is a stabilizer: removing it collapses ACC and inflates variance: MultiCholec: Local ~34.1±4.5; FedAvg 40.9±4.8; Hi-FL 51.9±3.6 Colorectal: Local ~25.0±10.2; FedAvg 33.2±2.4; Hi-FL 42.5±2.0 Bypass: Local ~32.1±5.3; FedAvg 43.7±5.2; Hi-FL 47.9±4.8 We will add this analysis. R2 Qa: We will expand Sec.3.2 and redesign Fig.1 linking each stream to its ablation. Four levels (L) operate on xt. (L1, ablated by A2) Global Procedural: causal running mean via bottleneck MLP produces bounded scale vector st. (L2, ablated by A1) Temporal Phase: parallel causal Conv1D capture phase transitions at increasing timescales, yielding additive shift vt. (L3) Action: at = Wact xt, identity-initialized; at fusion at is the operand L1 and L2 act upon (at st + vt), gradients flow through scale/shift jointly, driving Wact to amplify relevant dimensions and suppress irrelevant VLM features. (Ablated by A3) Dynamic Text: meta_net shifts CLIP prototypes conditioned on causal running mean on the classifier side. All levels are combined as zt (defined in Sec.3.2), with gate G controls how strongly the hierarchical correction overrides the frozen VLM. Qb: Disentanglement is quantified per-dataset. Pearson correlation (lower is better) between L1 and L2 (L3 being dependent on them) is lowest for Hi-FL (Colorectal 0.017, MultiCholec 0.025, Bypass 0.024) and rises when components are ablated (up to ~0.1 on average for the datasets), suggests reduced linear dependence between L1 and L2.Removing the independence loss also drops accuracy: 42.5→41.0 on Colorectal, 51.9→50.2 on MultiCholec, 47.9→46.8 on Bypass. Qc: Table 1 compares Hi-FL against five VLM-SOTA methods highlighting our contributions. Most other phase-based FL methods, like FedCy, use vision-only encoders without semantic grounding, unlike VLM-based methods. R3 Q1: TAR contribution is most clearly seen on Bypass, where removing it drops accuracy by 4.1pp (47.9→43.8) and raises Pearson from 0.024 to 0.043.On MultiCholec: Hi-FL 51.9 vs. No-TAR 49.2 (2.7pp drop, Pearson 0.025→0.041). On Colorectal: 42.5 vs. 42.0 (Pearson rises 0.017→0.064), showing TAR improves cross-center representation consistency beyond accuracy. Q2: We will revise the methodology presentation, see R2Qa. We will rewrite Eq.4 with all terms defined: the independence loss penalizes absolute cosine similarity between mean-centered L1 and L2 activations, minimizing this term forces the optimizer to find two solutions that are orthogonal. Q3: Hyperparameter sensitivity (S1-S3) confirms robustness, with <1pp accuracy variation on Colorectal and <2pp on MultiCholec/Bypass across a 10×knowledge-guard range (wkg = 0.01→0.1) and 0.1-0.7 repulsion margin. reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The problem is relevant and well motivated. 2.The method is fairly coherent, and the depth-adaptive attention design is reasonable. 3.The experiments are broader than average for this format, with multiple datasets and ablations. 4.The reported gains are consistent across the benchmarks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper combines several ingredients that are already present in the surrounding literature, including wavelet-based segmentation, hyperbolic representation learning, hyperbolic attention, and hyperbolic MLR. This matters because the paper’s central claim is about the value of geometry-aware modeling. 3.The experimental evidence is promising but still a bit incomplete for a method paper. The manuscript does not report variance across runs, confidence intervals, or statistical testing. Some improvements over the strongest related baseline are not very large, so it is hard to judge robustness. In addition, the brain MRI experiment is described using image counts, but the split is not stated clearly enough at the patient level, which is important for ruling out possible leakage in slice-based evaluation.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive comments. Below we address the major concerns. (@R1,R2,R4) Novelty and geometry contribution: Our contribution is not a direct replacement of Euclidean operators with existing hyperbolic modules, but a depth-adaptive geometry-aware segmentation strategy: pixel-wise HSA refines shallow spatial features, while channel-wise HSA recalibrates deep semantic features. We will revise the motivation to avoid over-interpreting anatomical hierarchy. Although many anatomical patterns are hierarchical or nested, our method does not rely on a strict tree-structured label assumption. Instead, hyperbolic geometry provides a geometric prior for organizing dense features across network depths, from boundary/texture cues to region-level semantic dependencies. To isolate the hyperbolic contribution, we conduct Euclidean-counterpart ablations under the same backbone and attention placement. Replacing the hyperbolic components with Euclidean counterparts reduces Dice/IoU from 0.844/0.759 to 0.822/0.735 on Brain Tumor, and from 0.832/0.759 to 0.820/0.736 on TN3K. Table 4 of the main paper consistent gains when HSA is incorporated into TransUNet and U-Mamba, indicting that the improvement mainly comes from geometry-aware modeling rather than only from the wavelet backbone or architecture changes. (@R1) nnU-Net comparison: We additionally evaluate nnU-Net using the same data split and preprocessing protocol. On Brain Tumor, our method achieves 0.844/0.759 Dice/IoU, compared with 0.8267/0.740 obtained by nnU-Net. (@R1,R2) Statistical significance and MRI split: We repeat the experiments with three random seeds (42, 1234, 3407) and now report mean±std. On Brain Tumor, our method achieves 0.8443±0.0042/ 0.7592±0.0054 Dice/IoU, while the Euclidean counterpart obtains 0.8224±0.0057/0.7351±0.0066.The improvement is statistically significant (p<0.05). The MRI split is patient-level: all slices from the same patient are assigned exclusively to either training or testing, avoiding leakage in slice-based evaluation. (@R1,R4) 3D extension: We agree that 3D validation is important. The current submission focuses on 2D benchmarks, and we will clarify this as a limitation. Methodologically, HSA is not restricted to 2D and can be extended to volumetric segmentation by replacing pixel-wise HSA with voxel-/window-wise HSA while retaining channel-wise recalibration. We will add this discussion as future work. (@R2,R4) Efficiency: The plain Euclidean baseline requires 61.34 GFLOPs and 46.846 ms inference latency. The Euclidean variant of our design requires 67.44 GFLOPs and 47.747 ms, while the full hyperbolic model requires 67.94 GFLOPs and 51.219 ms. Thus, compared with the Euclidean variant, hyperbolic modeling introduces only 0.50 GFLOPs and 3.472 ms extra latency, while bringing consistent gains. (@R4) Hyperbolic hierarchy for segmentation: We agree that hierarchical non-Euclidean modeling is more common in classification. However, prior segmentation works, such as Hyperbolic Image Segmentation (CVPR’22) and Hyperbolic CLIP-based Open-vocabulary Semantic Segmentation (CVPR’25) suggest that hyperbolic representations can also benefit dense prediction by modeling pixel-level decision boundaries and hierarchical semantic alignment. In our work, anatomical hierarchy is a motivation rather than a strict label-tree assumption. We use hyperbolic geometry to model the coarse-to-fine feature organization: shallow layers capture textures, edges, and boundaries, whereas deeper layers encode region-level semantic dependencies. Accordingly, stratified HSA uses pixel-wise attention for local spatial refinement and channel-wise attention for semantic recalibration. (@R4) Reproducibility: We will provide more details, including preprocessing, data augmentation, optimizer settings, training protocols, evaluation settings, and the patient-level split for Brain Tumor. The code and trained models will be released upon acceptance.

title: Induce to Empower: Improving Lightweight Baselines via Foundation Model Induction for Generalized Polyp Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors did not directly use the basic models such as SAM and DINOv2 as frozen backbones, nor did they simply distill the features of large models to small models. Instead, the lightweight model generates synthetic prototypes that correspond to foundation priors internally, and gradually absorbs various prior information through reconstruction alignment. Furthermore, these multi-source priors are not simply concatenated, but first transformed into lightweight models that can generate and control internal representations, and then selectively fused through Transformer and Mamba.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The experimental results are not sufficient enough, and there is a lack of evidence to prove why UFMI is superior to conventional distillation. This study emphasizes the suitability for clinical real-time deployment, but does not report metrics such as inference speed (FPS), latency, GPU memory usage, etc. Only parameters/FLOPs are not sufficient to prove real-time performance. In addition, lightweight and easy to deploy models such as U-Net, U-Net++, PraNet, etc. are used in this paper. Whether they can truly improve generalization ability without significantly increasing deployment burden needs to be verified with experimental data.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for the constructive feedback and encouraging comments. We are pleased that the primary objectives of Lite-π were recognized. We address the main concerns below. Novelty- Induction vs. Polyp-DiFoM / Distillation (R2, R3): We thank the reviewer for highlighting Polyp-DiFoM is the closest prior work. While both methods leverage foundation model (FM) priors for lightweight polyp segmentation, Polyp-DiFoM follows a distillation paradigm: it extracts FM features, decomposes them into low-/high-frequency components using FFT, and aligns student latent features with these teacher representations through MSE losses. In contrast, Lite-π follows an induction paradigm. Instead of forcing the lightweight model to imitate external FM features, Lite-π reconstructs polyp-relevant FM’s prototype features from the model’s own latent space and aligns them with frozen FM priors through reconstruction supervision. Key Differences: Since the FM prototypes are generated from task-trained lightweight representations, Lite-π learns to retain task-relevant semantic and boundary priors while suppressing irrelevant, redundant, or noisy FM responses. This is ensured by jointly optimizing the segmentation loss and feature reconstruction loss, where the reconstructed FM features directly influence the segmentation representation. Therefore, only FM-induced features that are useful for polyp segmentation are reinforced. This functionality is naturally not available in conventional distillation, where the student may inherit irrelevant, redundant, or noisy teacher responses, potentially degrading segmentation. Ablation Depth (R1, R2, R3): The current ablation study was designed to analyze the inductive effect of progressively incorporating multiple foundation models, since the proposed UFMI framework is designed as a unified induction module. The Transformer/MambaVision fusion, reconstruction alignment, and progressive weighting are tightly coupled within UFMI and jointly operate to perform semantic prototype induction and fusion. Therefore, the current ablation already validates the main mechanism: scalable multi-FM induction improves generalization without a significant computational burden. Nevertheless, we agree that additional component-level analysis could further improve clarity, and we will expand the ablation discussion in the revised manuscript to better explain the role and interaction of these tightly integrated components. Runtime, Latency, and Deployment Cost (R1, R2): Due to page constraints, we only reported parameters and FLOPs. Lite-π already shows modest Parameters-FLOPs overhead: U-Net increases from 16.7M-73.9G to 19.6M-74.3G, U-Net++ from 9.1M-65.9G to 10.1M-66.6G, and PraNet from 30.4M-13.1G to 34.9M-13.9G. Compared with SAM-Mamba/SAM-MaGuP (>100M parameters and >400G FLOPs) [Tables 1–2 ], Lite-π remains substantially lighter while achieving competitive accuracy. These results support the low deployment burden of Lite-π; we will include additional FPS, latency, and GPU memory reporting where space permits. Generalization with Low Deployment Burden (R1): Compared with the original baselines, Lite-π improves average mDice by +11.07% across all 15 dataset-backbone cases and by +13.32% on unseen datasets, demonstrating cross-dataset generalization with lightweight inference. Fair Comparison, Implementation Details and Reproducibility (R3): We will explicitly state that all reproduced methods use the same dataset split, input size (352×352), augmentation, training budget, and hyperparameters. Further, we will provide source code upon acceptance. Statistical Reporting (R3): Following standard practice in polyp segmentation, our manuscript provides a comprehensive evaluation across five benchmark datasets and six widely used metrics. The improvements shown are robust, reproducible, and not dataset-specific. We will clarify this strength in the revised manuscript.

title: Injecting a Low-Rank Background Prior: A Plugin for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The translation of the radiological “Figure-Ground Segregation” cognitive process into a computational low-rank modeling problem is highly intuitive and elegant. Moving away from computationally expensive online SVD (common in dynamic MRI/video processing) to a globally learned, dictionary-style memory bank is a smart adaptation for static image segmentation. 2.The LRBP is designed as a true “plugin. “ The authors successfully demonstrate its compatibility with distinct architectural paradigms (ResNet-34, MedNeXt, Swin-Unet). Furthermore, the computational overhead is remarkably low (+0.30% parameters, +0.01% GFLOPs), making it highly practical for clinical deployment.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The motivation of the paper is doubtful. Medical images (like ultrasound and endoscopy) feature highly heterogeneous and noisy backgrounds. Applying a linear PCA to deeply learned, highly non-linear bottleneck features to define a “subspace” is mathematically questionable. 2.The PCA basis B is updated gradient-free every 10 iterations. While computationally efficient, discrete subspace updates during continuous gradient-descent training can sometimes cause training instability or loss spikes. The authors should briefly clarify if any instability was observed and how the periodic update aligns with the momentum of the optimizer. 3.The so-called “Oracle Teacher” is not a neural network; it is simply a hard-coded heuristic formula (Equation 2) that calculates cosine similarity between GT foreground and background. Training a lightweight MLP (Student) to regress this scalar value via Smooth L1 loss is standard supervised regression, not “Knowledge Distillation. “ 4.Table 1 primarily shows improvements over the host backbones themselves. Comparing the method to only two other networks (CMUNeXt, EGE-UNet) is entirely insufficient. The authors must compare their method against state-of-the-art (SOTA) models specifically designed for Kvasir-SEG and BUSI. Since LRBP is proposed as a plugin, it must be compared against other widely used plug-and-play modules. The comparison with the SE block (Table 1b) is inadequate. How does LRBP compare to spatial attention (e. g. , CBAM), boundary-enhancing modules, or other explicit background suppression/feature recalibration techniques? Without this, the necessity of the complex PCA-memory-bank pipeline is not held.

reviewer_3_strengths: (1)The paper presents a novel perspective by focusing on background modeling rather than foreground discrimination. (2)The proposed LRBP is modular and lightweight, making it easy to integrate into existing architectures. (3)The method shows consistent improvements in ASD, which is clinically meaningful for boundary accuracy. (4)The framework is well-structured, combining subspace learning, residual modeling, and distillation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1)The entire framework is built upon the assumption that background features lie in a low-rank subspace, while lesions are sparse outliers. However, this assumption is not rigorously validated. The provided evidence (PCA cumulative explained variance) is insufficient. High explained variance in PCA is a well-known property of high-dimensional feature spaces and does not necessarily imply intrinsic low-rank structure. (2) The memory bank is constructed exclusively from ground-truth background features, which introduces several critical issues: 1)The model relies on GT-derived background statistics during training, but such information is unavailable at inference. 2)Any mislabeling in background regions directly contaminates the learned subspace. 3)The memory bank may encode dataset-specific background patterns, limiting generalization. (3) The method reduces the residual signal to a scalar energy value, discarding directional information. This is a significant simplification: Residual vectors may encode richer anomaly cues. The paper claims domain misalignment but does not empirically validate it. This design choice may limit the expressive power of the method. (4) The teacher signal is defined via cosine similarity between FG/BG features, which is heuristic: No theoretical grounding for this choice No comparison with alternative gating strategies Student input is overly simplistic (5) Inconsistent dataset usage in ablation studies. The ablation experiments are conducted on a different dataset (TN3K) than the main benchmarks (Kvasir-SEG and BUSI). This violates the principle of controlled experimentation, as both the model components and the data distribution are changed simultaneously. As a result, it is unclear whether the reported performance differences are attributable to the proposed modules or to dataset-specific characteristics. (6) Lack of statistical significance analysis. The reported improvements, particularly in Dice, are relatively small. However, the paper does not provide any statistical significance analysis (e.g., p-values or confidence intervals) to support that these gains are meaningful rather than due to random variation.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers (R1, R2, R3) and meta-reviewer (Meta) for the constructive feedback. We have grouped the major concerns regarding claim calibration, terminology, and experimental framing, and address them below. Low-rank background prior (R1, R3, Meta). Regarding concerns that applying PCA to non-linear deep features may be mathematically questionable or lacks rigorous validation: we do not claim a theorem that medical backgrounds are globally low-rank in raw image space, nor that lesions are universally sparse outliers. Motivated by search-by-subtraction, LRBP relies on the encoder to model nonlinearity and then uses an explicit linear PCA basis as an efficient, interpretable empirical feature-space prior; kernelized variants can add cost and reduce residual-map interpretability. The operational question is whether scalar residual energy, even without vector direction, is useful for FG/BG separation. The manuscript provides this evidence: a BG-learned basis captures most BG energy with small rank, residual energy separates FG/BG with AUCs of 0.971 (Kvasir-SEG) and 0.890 (BUSI), and median residuals show clear shifts. Thus, our intended claim is an empirical feature-space prior, not a proved intrinsic low-rank structure of medical images. Memory bank, PCA updates, and inference (R1, R3, Meta). Addressing concerns about reliance on ground-truth (GT) at inference and potential training instability: GT masks are used only during training, specifically for sampling background features, computing the background reconstruction loss, and constructing the GT-guided gate target. At inference, no GT information is used: the memory bank and PCA basis are frozen, and within LRBP, test images are processed by projection onto the learned basis. Furthermore, the PCA basis is a non-trainable buffer updated periodically from the memory bank, not an optimizer-updated parameter. Thus, PCA updates are gradient-free and decoupled from AdamW/backpropagation, mitigating the concern that the basis introduces optimizer-level training instability. Ablation baseline and TN3K dataset (R2, R3, Meta). Regarding the concern that ablations on TN3K may not be sufficiently controlled or lack a clear baseline: in Table 1(b), the baseline is explicitly the identical ResNet-34 U-Net used in the main study. All LRBP ablation variants use the same TN3K split, host, and training protocol; only the LRBP component changes. The SE block is included only as an additional architectural comparison. TN3K, our largest auxiliary dataset, was used for component analysis to provide a stable setting for rank sweeps and mechanism analysis, while Kvasir-SEG and BUSI were used for the main benchmark evaluation across three host architectures. Choice of K and empirical thresholds (R2, Meta). Addressing the lack of explanation for PCA K values and heuristics: K=16 was selected empirically and is consistent with Fig. 2(a), where the BG basis reaches 95% cumulative explained variance at around K=10–13 across Kvasir-SEG and BUSI; K=16 is therefore a conservative rank. We also reported a rank sweep in the TN3K ablation (K=4, 16, 64), confirming K=16 offers the best trade-off. The Dice<0.5 criterion is used only for hard-sample mining during training, not as an inference threshold. These are empirical settings, not universal constants. “Oracle Teacher” terminology and gating (R1, R3, Meta). We agree this is a heuristic, not classical KD. It is GT-guided gate supervision: FG/BG cosine similarity is a separability proxy for when residual injection is reliable. Table 1(b) compares static injection, no teacher guidance, and a heuristic gate. Our intent was privileged supervision, not a separate teacher model. Overall, these concerns mainly reflect framing issues rather than contradictions in the empirical findings. LRBP remains a decomposition-free inference-time plugin using a learned background basis and adaptive gating to improve boundary accuracy.
