author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. We appreciate the acknowledgement of our work’s clinical relevance. We especially thank R2 for recognizing our clinical reliability. We will gladly incorporate your suggestions in the camera-ready version. [R1 & R3] Dataset Concerns Our objective is fine-grained diagnosis (adenoma vs carcinoma). To the best of our knowledge, there is no public dataset that includes gastric images with adenoma/carcinoma labels along with pixel-level segmentation masks, so using a private dataset was inevitable. Although PICCOLO is a colonoscopy dataset, gastroscopy and colonoscopy share fundamental anatomical morphologies. Testing on PICCOLO serves as a rigorous test of our proposed method’s cross-domain generalization capabilities, as mentioned in our manuscript “We test whether our training methodology …. is transferable beyond the gastric domain.” [R1] Clarification on datasets used for training We clarify that the performance of GastroNet-5M reported in the paper (Table 1) is indeed the result after fine-tuning on our private dataset. Despite fine tuning a 5M dataset pre-trained model, the performance (AUC = 0.744) fell short of MAGE (AUC = 0.786). [R3] Augmentation Concerns MAGE provides a fundamental architectural advantage over aggressive augmentation. Standard photometric augmentations alter the global statistics of the image, but the trained network still processes the full global context. Due to this, it can still learn spurious correlations from background mucosa or glare. In contrast, our “Achromatic Expert” is trained on a strictly constrained input (locally cropped and grayscaled). It is forced to rely solely on the morphological and textural patterns of the lesion itself, decoupled from global signals. Distilling this localized knowledge to the main network actively suppresses the main network’s attention to non-lesion artifacts. During preliminary experiments, we observed that applying color/texture augmentations to the baselines did not improve performance and often degraded it, providing the motivation for an explicit architectural approach. We also clarify that all baselines and our proposed method were trained using the exact same simple data augmentations (random horizontal/vertical flip), ensuring a fair comparison. We will make this clear in the revised manuscript. [R3] Comparison with IRM/Domain Generalization IRM mathematically requires training data to have explicit labels regarding the “environment” of each sample. In endoscopy, confounding artifacts are entangled within single images. Thus, it was infeasible to apply IRM without exhaustive annotations of such artifacts as different environments. [R1, R3] Reproducibility & Hyperparameters We apologize for omitting these details. distillation temperature τ = 4.0, attention weight β = 300 , Input resolution: 224x224 (all experiments) Batch size = 32 Hardware: 1x RTX 3090 Optimizer for PICCOLO experiment: AdamW (default settings) Optimizer for all other experiments: Adam (default settings) Scheduler: Cosine Annealing with max LR = 1e-4, min LR = 1e-6 (all experiments) We commit to publicly releasing the complete source code, configuration files, and pre-trained weights upon acceptance. This slight gain from using a nonzero α stems from the additional supervision from the ground truth labels. Yet as seen from Figure 3(b), the difference between raw diagnostic performance of α = 0 and α = 0.5 at 0 degrees hue shift is minimal. We will address this trade-off in the revised manuscript.

title: Mask to Concept: Auto-Promptable SAM3 via Efficient Test-Time Concept Embedding Search for Few-Shot Annotation
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strengths of the paper are the strong and convincing experimental results, supported by excellent ablation studies and insightful analysis. The empirical evaluation is particularly thorough, with carefully designed experiments that clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed M2C framework. The annotation efficiency analysis is a highlight of the work: the results show that the hybrid uncertainty estimation not only improves active selection of hard samples but also enables a meaningful early exit strategy for easy samples, which are confidently segmented via concept aligned embeddings before further updates. This design leads to consistently better performance under fixed annotation budgets and clearly outperforms random sampling baselines, while the full system achieves the best annotation quality with minimal human effort. The ablation studies further strengthen the paper by showing that both uncertainty components contribute complementarily, and that combining them is essential for efficiently distinguishing easy and hard samples to reduce annotation cost. In addition, the paper is very well written with a clear and compelling storyline that guides the reader through motivation, method, and results in a coherent way. The qualitative and quantitative results are well aligned and reinforce each other, and the comparisons on annotation efficiency provide a strong practical argument for the system’s usefulness in real medical labeling workflows. Overall, the presentation is strong and contributes significantly to readability and impact.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper lies in the limited mathematical grounding and interpretability of the proposed uncertainty formulation. While entropy is a well established and theoretically sound uncertainty measure, the concept geometry prompting inconsistency term is less rigorously motivated, making the final hybrid uncertainty score feel somewhat heuristic despite strong empirical performance. Closely related to this, it remains unclear whether the resulting uncertainty estimates are well calibrated. The paper does not provide a thorough analysis of calibration quality or position the proposed uncertainty formulation within the broader landscape of uncertainty estimation methods in medical imaging. This makes it difficult to assess how the method relates to established probabilistic or Bayesian approaches. In addition, the overall algorithm resembles iterative refinement strategies similar in spirit to expectation maximization, but this connection is not explicitly discussed or formalized. A clearer theoretical framing could improve interpretability and strengthen the methodological contribution. Finally, the dataset selection is somewhat limited, relying on relatively standard and potentially dated benchmarks, with limited diversity in modalities and task settings. Broader evaluation would improve confidence in the generality of the findings. Overall, while the engineering design is strong and the empirical results are convincing, the main limitation is the lack of deeper mathematical rigor, calibration analysis, and broader validation.

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper constructs Mask to Concept, a framework designed to adapt SAM2/3 for few-shot medical image segmentation by optimizing concept embeddings to automate the prompting process. The strengths of the work lie in its high computational efficiency, strong empirical performance across multiple benchmarks, and a well-motivated hybrid uncertainty estimation module that effectively reduces manual annotation effort. However, reviewers have raised concerns regarding the “training-free” claim given the optimization of embeddings, the lack of rigorous mathematical grounding for the uncertainty formulation, and the need for fairer comparisons against optimized text prompts or stronger baselines like nnU-Net. Additionally, further clarification is required regarding the simulation of human corrections and the sensitivity of the chosen hyperparameters. With average scores (6, 3, 4) leaning toward a rebuttal to address these methodological clarifications and validation concerns. | Based on the outcome of the rebuttal process, two reviewers assigned an “Accept” score, while one reviewer assigned a “Reject.” Notably, although Reviewer 2 recommended rejection, he also emphasized that “the paper is extremely practical”. The authors should clearly clarify the “training-free” claim in the camera-ready version. Given that the overall sentiment is positive, the inclination is to “Accept” this paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper proposes to adapt SAM3 for few-shot medical annotation by optimizing a concept embedding from a few labeled masks and using a hybrid uncertainty score for human-in-the-loop sample selection. While the idea is potentially useful, the current evidence is not sufficient for acceptance. My main concern is that the claimed contribution is not convincingly isolated. The method is described as “training-free,” but it still performs gradient-based optimization of a learnable embedding using labeled masks, which is closer to test-time prompt/embedding tuning than a truly training-free method. The novelty over existing prompt tuning, textual inversion, and few-shot SAM personalization methods is not clearly established. The experimental comparison is also problematic. M2C uses SAM3, whereas the SAM-based baselines use SAM-H, so the reported gains may largely reflect the stronger backbone rather than the proposed concept-search mechanism. The paper lacks essential controls, such as direct SAM3 text prompting, SAM3 with box/point prompts, SAM3 with naive learned prompts, and variants that isolate the effect of concept embedding optimization from the effect of the backbone. The annotation-efficiency evaluation is not fully convincing. Human corrections are simulated with ground-truth masks, and the overall quality metric includes human-labeled samples, which can inflate the apparent efficiency. The uncertainty module uses heuristic components and a fixed threshold, but there is no calibration analysis or robust validation that HUE reliably identifies truly difficult or low-quality cases across datasets. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a framework for few-shot medical image annotation with SAM3 by optimizing concept embeddings and using hybrid uncertainty estimation to reduce manual annotation effort. Although concerns remain about the “training-free” wording and theoretical grounding of uncertainty, the rebuttal clarified these issues. Overall, the work is empirically strong and sufficiently valuable for acceptance.

title: MMIC-EndoDepth: Self-Supervised Endoscopic Depth Estimation with Multi-Mechanism Illumination Correction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The central contribution of the paper is the introduction of the IAPC module, which is integrated into the training pipeline between view synthesis and the photometric loss computation to correct illumination-induced appearance changes. 2.To further enhance robustness, the method extends IAPC into a multi-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) formulation applied across pyramid levels, where multiple complementary experts predict per-pixel affine photometric transformations such as scale and bias. 3.A pixel-wise gating mechanism is then used to adaptively fuse the outputs of these experts in the parameter space, enabling the model to handle diverse illumination distortions at different scales while performing spatially varying photometric correction.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The design of the depth binning strategy appears to be somewhat imperfect. The paper states that in colonoscopy scenarios, a simple observation is utilized: brightness varies with the distance between the camera and tissue (closer regions are generally brighter, while farther regions are darker). However, in the fourth row of the endoscopic images in Fig. 3, it can be observed that some distant regions still contain bright speckle-like patterns caused by specular reflections. Although the visualizations in Fig. 3 show that MMIC-EndoDepth performs better than other methods, the estimated depth maps still exhibit orange regions in distant areas. Therefore, I am concerned that the depth-based design in this component may potentially interfere with the effectiveness of the pixel-wise and patch-wise photometric correction mechanisms intended to handle illumination distortions. 2.Could the authors elaborate on why an affine photometric model (αI+β) is appropriate for handling complex illumination effects such as specular highlights and inter-reflections？ 3.The quantitative impact of the gating mechanism does not appear to be evaluated in the ablation studies. Could the authors clarify this? 4.The paper does not specify the shapes of the final fused α and β maps. My understanding is that both have the same spatial dimensions as the input image (i. e. , H×W), but this appears to be inconsistent with the cube-like illustration shown in Fig. 2. 5.The notation for βqs, βps and αqs, αps appears to be inconsistent between Fig. 2 and the Method section, where the order of the subscripts is reversed or not clearly aligned. 6.In the last line of the paragraph “Expert 3: …”, there is an extra space before the period.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: It is important to note that the widely known problem in depth estimation in endoscopy (breakdown of photometric assumptions due to illumination variations) is tackled head-on. The idea of decomposing illumination distortion into multiple mechanisms is reasonable and consistent with endoscope-specific phenomena. The design of the IAPC is clear, and in particular the design of gated fusion in parameter space rather than image space is reasonable from the perspective of study stability. The experiments are carefully conducted and include comparisons with strong baselines such as EndoDAC and AF-SfMLearner. As shown in Table 1, there is a significant improvement (Abs Rel 0.207 → 0.101), particularly in C3VD, with very high performance on the evaluation data. author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. R#1/#2 1.Motivation and novelty Our motivation is the clinically common setting where annotations of different granularities coexist, including precise masks, boxes, points, noisy masks, and multi-expert annotations. These annotations provide complementary supervision: masks offer boundary cues, boxes provide localization constraints, points indicate lesion presence, and noisy/inner/outer masks reflect uncertainty in lesion extent. Instead of treating weak labels as precise masks or training separate models for each annotation type, MALFOY uses label weights as a controllable interface between heterogeneous annotations and the segmentation model. Specifically, the weights jointly modulate the loss and condition the dynamic HyperConv layers, allowing the trained model to recommend different segmentation behaviors by searching for the optimal weight vector for a given objective. 2.Comparison and analysis The current experiments compare MALFOY with representative weakly supervised methods across single- and multiple-baseline settings. Table 2 shows consistent improvements in both segmentation and localization metrics on polyp and breast cancer datasets. Fig. 3 further analyzes different proportions of precise masks and bounding boxes, showing that MALFOY better benefits from additional weak annotations than the single-baseline setting. Fig. 4 visualizes searched label weights and shows that the best solution is generally not one-hot, indicating that different annotation types are complementary. Fig. 5 also demonstrates the extension to multi-expert uncertainty modeling. 3.Generalization MALFOY is evaluated on 2D colonoscopy, 3D breast DCE-MRI, and multi-expert prostate segmentation. These settings differ in modality, dimensionality, annotation type, and target anatomy. R#3 1.Role of ID ID is only the sample index for Searching-R, not an input to the segmentation model or used during inference. It is included because the mapping from λ to loss is one-to-many: different cases can have different losses under the same λ. Thus, ID helps the RF regress case-specific λ-loss relations during weight search. 2.RF details We will add these details in the revision. “For each case in a batch, we record {epoch, ID, λ, loss} during training, producing approximately n_epochs × n_cases records with no extra training overhead. We use a sklearn RF regressor with 100 trees and default parameters. Records are split 8:2 for training and validation. Training takes 3.9 min on the polyp dataset and 1.6 min on the breast dataset. The RF achieves MAEs of 0.0025/0.0031 on training sets and 0.0066/0.0074 on validation sets for the two datasets, respectively, suggesting sufficient accuracy for ranking different λ values.” 3.Visualization of annotations (a) In this work, we only focus on binary masks for two datasets. For future extension, multi-class scenarios where inner/outer masks would be defined per class (e.g., on tumor label only, not organs). (b) The noisy mask is generated by applying a random B-spline deformable transformation to the precise mask, which introduces random shape and boundary perturbations while keeping the lesion roughly localized. 4.Loss (a) L_seg is defined in Eq.1, which comprises DSC and CE. (b) Each weak annotation is converted into a dense mask with the same resolution as the input image; e.g., a bbox is converted to a rectangular mask, and a point is converted to a circular mask. This unified approach allows identical loss computation across all annotation types, enabling label weighting to control annotation-specific learning. 5.Searching speed Searching-V takes around 156/77 min (polyp/breast) for 100 steps, and searching-R takes around 34/14 min for 10000 steps. 6.Novelty of Searching-V Validation set-based selection is mainly used to select the best checkpoint, whereas our searching-V selects the best λ for the given checkpoint.

reviewer_1_strengths: 1)The paper is among the first to leverage mosaicing and frame matching to construct paired training data for CLE image restoration. 2)The data curation pipeline is carefully designed and provide a meaningful technical contribution. 3)The approach is well-motivated by the inherent trade-off in CLE systems between temporal resolution and image quality.

If frames are sampled from the same spatial regions or video sequences, there may be overlap, which could overestimate performance. reviewer_2_strengths: Dataset Contribution: The construction and public release of the MaLissa dataset provide a foundational resource for future research in the specialized field of Lissajous-scanning CLE. Algorithmic Design: The introduction of a phase-correlation module specifically tailored for extremely sparse pixel alignment effectively bypasses the limitations of traditional optical flow methods when dealing with substantial missing data. Efficiency Exploration: The use of feature caching and ResFFT modules demonstrates a meaningful attempt to balance restoration performance with computational latency for potential clinical applications.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Rationale for the Scanning Strategy and Task Setup: The introduction claims that conventional raster scanning is mechanically limited at high speeds. However, mature clinical CLE systems (e.g., Cellvizio by Mauna Kea Technologies) utilizing high-frequency resonant scanners (e.g., 4kHz or 8kHz CRS) already achieve high-quality, full-sampling imaging at frame rates of 12-15 fps. Clarification Required: What is the specific clinical advantage of the Lissajous scheme over these established raster-scanning solutions at the 10Hz scale? Why choose a scheme that results in 70% missing pixels at 10Hz only to necessitate complex algorithmic repair, rather than utilizing existing full-sampling hardware?. Lack of Quantitative Resolution Validation: The core clinical value of CLE is cellular-level resolution. Current evaluation relies solely on computer vision metrics like PSNR and SSIM, which do not confirm whether the algorithm authentically restores physical high-frequency structures or merely performs visual smoothing. Generalization to Higher Frame Rates: While the title emphasizes “High-rate,” experiments only validate performance at 10Hz. As frame rates increase to 30-60 fps, the sparsity of the Lissajous trajectory will increase further and the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) will drop precipitously. The robustness of the algorithm under such extreme undersampling remains unproven.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The dataset is a real contribution. author_feedback: We appreciate the thoughtful feedback from the reviewers and AC. Rationale for Lissajous CLE (R2): Cellvizio is not a “clean raster” but a post-processing dependent platform with a structural pixel ceiling. Cellvizio drives a 30k-fiber bundle with a MEMS raster scanner, and thus has HW-bound limits: (1) honeycomb blanks between fiber cores, which Cellvizio addresses with dedicated post-processing (Le Goualher’04, Bedard’12); (2) a ~30k pixel ceiling fixed by core count, with FOV shrinking to 240 μm at high-res. Single-fiber raster systems (e.g., Convivo) avoid bundle artifacts but are limited by low frame rate from single-axis resonance, causing severe clinical drawbacks (Xu’25). Lissajous CLE bypasses both ceilings: single fiber removes the bundle pixel ceiling, and dual-resonant scanning decouples frame rate from per-axis line count. Just as honeycomb removal is standard for Cellvizio, Lissajous reconstruction is intrinsic to this architecture. Our work tackles this challenge. 10Hz vs. High-rate (R2): We agree that this can be confusing. We’ll revise “high-rate” to “10Hz.” We target 10Hz due to its clinical relevance, as established in prior works [6,7]. Details on train/val split (R1, R3): MaLissa is splitted at the clip level, where each raw clip was acquired from a distinct non-overlapping spatial location on the tissue. Each clip exhibits significantly distinct visual characteristics (Figs 4,5). Through this split, we aim to assess generalization under a challenging setup, without leakage. Narrow data scope (R1, R3): This is why our dataset—MaLissa—is a meaningful contribution. We contribute the first open dataset for Lissajous CLE, and we could not evaluate on other datasets as there is none. Also, we use only one device, as there is only one Lissajous CLE system on the market. Comparison clarity (R1): To clarify, the comparison is in the last paragraph of sec.2.We’ll relocate them to the introduction, as suggested. Latency (R2, R3): We clarify that Tab.1 results correspond to the “end-to-end latency,” whereas matters for 10Hz deployment is the “throughput.” In fact, we can parallelize multiple frame-wise processing threads via pipelining—i.e., start processing the next frame whenever we’re done encoding (not full processing) the previous frame. This can reduce the per-frame gap to under 100ms. We’ll clarify this point in the revised manuscript. Questions on ablation (R3): We optimized for visual clarity over PSNR/SSIM, and the current configuration works clearly the best in this regard (Fig. 5). On MedSAM pseudolabels (R3): The key takeaway of segmentation results is that our method is effective in preserving structural consistency. Although not fully-clinical, we believe these results are still meaningful. Biased to low motion? (R3): It turns out that the ratio of large-motion frames (>100px) remains similar after matching (>15%). Thus, the bias does not look very severe. We’ll clarify this in the revised version. Too focused on PSNR/SSIM (R2): While we acknowledge the lack of physical resolution validation, we believe our downstream task evaluation can be a complementary evidence for functional resolution; indeed, several recent microscopy works (e.g., MiHATP, Joint EM) utilize similar PSNR/SSIM+Task evidence as main evaluation metrics. Retrieval and segmentation tasks can be a good proxy, as these tasks require recovering high-frequency details to achieve a high accuracy. Equation typo (R1): Thank you. Will fix! Potential interpolation artifact? (R1): Measured pixels in 2Hz images are quite dense with <10% pixels unmeasured, and thus do not introduce such artifacts. Template matching details (R1): We used OpenCV TM_SQDIFF_NORMED with 2048^2 window. Empirically, this is robust to large motion; the deformation is not significant in our data [10, 18]. Feature alignment stability in early stage (R1): It is stable even at early stages, as the displacement estimation relies on raw model input, not encoder features.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Surgical triplet recognition is highly relevant for surgical workflow understanding, and the paper clearly identifies three core difficulties: modeling long-range temporal context, preserving local temporal details, and capturing semantic dependencies among triplet components. The proposed architecture is well aligned with these motivations. In particular, combining an SSM/Mamba branch with a dilated convolution branch is a reasonable design to balance global and local temporal modeling, and the graph-based fusion module is a sensible attempt to explicitly encode interactions between instrument, verb, target, and triplet-level semantics. 2.In Tab. 1, the proposed method improves over prior methods across multiple settings, and the best model with SwinB(384) achieves the highest reported APIVT = 42.0, outperforming CurConMix-Ens at 40.7 and TERL-Ens at 38.5.The gains over CurConMix are also fairly consistent across backbone sizes, which supports the claim that the proposed temporal and semantic modeling modules contribute beyond the frozen spatial backbone. 3.The paper includes an ablation study isolating the impact of the temporal modeling block and the graph fusion module. Table 2 shows that replacing the baseline with MS-DCM improves APIVT from 38.8 to 40.3, and adding TGF further improves it to 41.2.This provides some evidence that both components contribute meaningfully to the final performance.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The method novelty is somewhat limited. The proposed method is largely a combination of several existing design ideas: a frozen Swin-based spatial backbone, a hybrid temporal module combining Mamba/SSM with dilated convolutions, and a GCN-based semantic fusion module. While the combination is sensible and appears effective, the overall contribution feels more like a strong architectural integration than a fundamentally new formulation for surgical triplet recognition. 2.All quantitative evaluation is performed on CholecT45 only. For a method whose main claims are about temporal modeling and semantic dependency modeling in surgical triplet recognition more broadly, validation on a single benchmark makes it difficult to judge generalization. This is especially relevant because the method is presented as a general triplet recognition approach, not as one tailored specifically to one dataset. 3.The paper also motivates itself partly through the limitations of Transformers in long-sequence modeling and the advantages of Mamba-style temporal modeling, but it doesn’t provide any efficiency or complexity analysis. There are no results on runtime, memory, FLOPs, or parameter overhead for the proposed temporal module. Since one of the main motivations for using Mamba is its linear complexity and long-range modeling capability, I would have expected at least some quantitative evidence that the proposed design is more efficient or scalable than relevant alternatives. At present, the benefit is only indirectly argued, not demonstrated. 4.The paper’s discussion of class imbalance and long-tail recognition is not fully backed up by the experiments. The introduction emphasizes severe long-tailed distributions and introduces a weighted multi-task loss to address this, but the experimental section does not include any tail-class analysis, per-class breakdown, or comparison showing that the proposed loss particularly helps rare but safety-critical classes. 5.The method relies heavily on a frozen CurConMix/Swin-based spatial backbone, and the main contribution is effectively in the temporal-semantic head on top of that backbone. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but it does mean the paper should be framed more explicitly as improving the temporal-semantic modeling stage rather than as a full end-to-end rethinking of triplet recognition.

author_feedback: Thanks for comments. To R1 1.DCM: The DCM block uses a general-purpose architecture, while it is specifically tailored to capture surgical-domain temporal patterns, from long procedural dependencies to short instrument-tissue interactions. 2.Comparison with TGF: We compare the TGF module against an MLP with a similar parameter count and a Transformer variant under the same setup. The MLP achieves 40.7% mAP, slightly behind our 41.2%. The Transformer variant yields 40.4% mAP but requires 11.86M parameters, more than double our 5.28M. These results demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency advantages of our module. To R2 1.DCM Layers: The asymmetric choice of N=6, M=5 stems from the complementary strengths of dilated convolution and Mamba. The six initial dilated layers provide a receptive field of 127, covering full action segments while complementing Mamba’s global semantics. The three subsequent five-layer refinement stages smoothly expand the receptive field from 127 to 313 for longer actions, without conflicting with Mamba’s global modeling. An ablation study reveals an inverted-U trend in mAP: 39.7% (3,2), 41.2% (6,5), 40.5% (9,8), and 40.2% (11,10), confirming (6,5) as the optimal setting. 2.Presentation of TGF: We will update texts in the final version.We construct the graph in three steps. First, from each of the three feature sequences (shallow, deep, fused), four 1×1 projectors extract four semantic nodes: Instrument, Verb, Target, and Triplet, resulting in twelve nodes. Second, nodes from the same sequence form a cluster with full intra-cluster connections, ensuring cross-component consistency per scale. Third, inter-cluster edges connect nodes of the same semantic type across clusters, forming chains (e.g., Instrument nodes across shallow, deep, and fused scales), where the fused nodes serve as anchors to absorb complementary information. After two graph convolution layers, the updated fused nodes go to separate residual-connected classification heads, and the Triplet node of the fused sequence is projected back for the next FPN stage. 3.Multi-scale features as a cluster: A fused node cluster is necessary-separate f_3 and f_4 clusters only exchange semantics without real fusion. We build a coarse f_fusion (f_3 + f_4) and let GCN refine it. Without it, raw clusters lack distinct triplet semantics. Adding the fusion improves mAP from 40.9% to 41.2%, confirming its anchor role. 4.Classification head: All GCN fusion outputs go to classification heads, but only the lowest-level (f1+P1) features are used for final prediction; the rest act as auxiliary supervision during training. Unlike prior methods that share undecoupled features across heads, our task-aware heads receive decoupled, semantically distinct features from the GCN module. 5.CholecTriplet2021: Our model obtains 37.2% mAP against CurConMix’s 36.0%, indicating the effectiveness on this dataset. To R3 1.Novelty: 1) We propose the DCM block, a Mamba-dilated convolution hybrid that balances global context and local features, to capture surgical temporal patterns, unlike existing CNN or Mamba models. 2) We propose a task-aware graph fusion module that explicitly models semantic correlations among triplet components while aligning cross-granularity features during fusion. This novel design enables the model to learn both intra-cluster correlations and inter-layer relationships between coarse and fine semantic representations. 3) Results validate its effectiveness. 2.CholecTriplet: Our model obtains 37.2% mAP on CholecTriplet 2021, surpassing CurConMix’s 36.0%. 3.Efficiency: The basic Transformer (full-attn) 37.86M params, 54.16 GFLOPs; window-attn Transformer (win=64) 37.87M, 39.04 GFLOPs; our DCM module 34.21M, 34.04 GFLOPs. DCM shows clear efficiency advantage, indicating the involved Mambda’s linear complexity. 4.Frequency-Weighted Loss: mAP improves from 40.5% to 41.2% with FWL, indicating its effectiveness to handle class imbalance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal should address four decision-affecting concerns. First, limited methodological novelty: the DCM block, GCN fusion, and task-aware classification head are recombinations of components already used in the literature; the rebuttal should make the specific contribution explicit. Second, the Task-aware Graph Fusion needs comparison against alternative fusion designs and a parameter-matched control, since the gain may stem from added capacity rather than the GCN itself. Third, the paper provides no efficiency analysis (runtime, FLOPs, parameters) and no per-class or tail-class evidence to support the long-tail motivation. Fourth, evaluation on the official CholecTriplet2021 challenge test split would substantiate the SOTA claim beyond CholecT45 cross-validation, and the rationale for the asymmetric stage depths in the DCM block should be provided. | The paper combines a dilated convolutional Mamba block with a task-aware graph fusion module for surgical action triplet recognition. The reviewers raised concerns about novelty, the need for a parameter-matched control to isolate the contribution of graph fusion, the lack of an efficiency analysis, and the lack of evaluation on the official CholecTriplet2021 split. Two reviewers endorsed acceptance after the rebuttal; one maintained Reject on novelty and surgical insights. The contribution is a careful architectural integration rather than a fundamentally new formulation, but the rebuttal makes the integration choices defensible. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After rebuttal, two reviewers are satified with the response but one reviewer thinks the novelty is limited. Although the methodological novelty remains moderate and the design is largely an effective integration of existing temporal and graph modules, the empirical performance and post-rebuttal reviewer balance support acceptance as a borderline/weak-accept paper.

title: Occlusion-aware Disparity Estimation via Depth Prior Embedded Cost Volume for Stereo Endoscopic Images
reviewer_1_strengths: The idea of converting a coarse depth map into a probability distribution (Eq. 2) and using this distribution to iteratively refine the cost volume (Algorithm 1) is both interesting and well-motivated.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Methodology: Parameter Settings: The procedure for defining or tuning $\sigma$ in Eq. 2 is currently unclear and requires further explanation. Unsubstantiated Claims: The authors state that refining the cost volume helps resolve occluded regions in stereo matching. However, the evaluation section lacks specific experiments or ablation studies designed to validate this claim. Writing & Presentation: Incomplete List: In the final paragraph of the Introduction, the authors state that their contributions are “fourfold,” but they only enumerate three points (“First. . . “, “Second. . . “, “Third. . . “).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinical and technical relevance: The paper studies stereo disparity estimation for endoscopic images, which is an important problem for 3D reconstruction and surgical navigation. The focus on occluded or unmatched regions is practically meaningful, since these areas are a common source of failure in laparoscopic stereo matching. 2.Reasonable methodological design: The proposed framework introduces monocular depth priors into stereo matching through a coarse disparity estimation module and a depth prior embedded cost volume. Encoding the depth prior as a disparity probability distribution and fusing it with the original cost volume via cross-attention is a sensible design, especially for improving robustness in occluded regions. 3.Solid empirical validation: The paper includes quantitative comparison against several recent baselines on the SCARED dataset, together with ablation studies on the main components such as DPCV, occlusion masking, auxiliary loss, and iterative refinement. These experiments help support that the proposed modules contribute to the final performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is of generally good quality, but several aspects would benefit from further clarification and discussion. 1.Novelty: The overall idea of incorporating monocular depth priors into stereo matching is reasonable, but the methodological novelty appears somewhat limited. The framework mainly combines a coarse depth-to-disparity prior, probability-based prior encoding, cross-attention fusion, and occlusion-aware refinement, all of which are built on top of an existing stereo backbone. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of what is fundamentally new relative to prior cost-volume refinement and fusion-based stereo methods. 2.Occlusion-specific evidence: The paper is motivated by improving disparity estimation in occluded or unmatched regions, but the experimental evidence for this claim is still somewhat indirect. Most results are reported on overall metrics, while more dedicated quantitative analysis specifically within occlusion regions would make the central claim better supported. 3.Clarity and technical details: Some parts of the presentation could be improved. For example, the naming of the proposed module is not fully consistent in the method section (DPCV vs DECV in section 2.2, maybe they are the same thing?), and several implementation choices, such as the design of the probability distribution prior and the effect of iteration number, could be explained more clearly. This would make the method easier to follow and assess.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Well-Structured Methodology: The integration of DECV, CDE loss, and iterative refinement forms a cohesive and logical pipeline. The architectural choices directly target the identified problem of occlusion in endoscopic scenes. Ablation Validation: The effectiveness of each proposed module (DECV, CDE loss, masking) is clearly demonstrated through a systematic ablation study, proving their individual contributions to the overall performance. Efficiency: The model appears to balance the trade-off between inference speed and accuracy effectively, which is vital for real-time surgical navigation. Clear Motivation: The use of monocular cues as a prior to “fill in” the gaps where stereo correspondence is physically impossible (occlusions) is a sound and intuitive approach for the surgical domain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Missing State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Baselines: The review of current stereo matching literature is incomplete. The paper lacks a performance comparison with modern high-performance architectures like RAFT-Stereo and IGEV-Stereo, which currently define the SOTA for iterative refinement and cost volume construction. Specific Impact on Occlusions: While the paper claims to solve occlusion-related issues, there is no isolated quantitative analysis for these regions. Can the authors provide error metrics (e.g., EPE or D1-all) specifically measured inside the occlusion masks? This would verify if the performance gain is truly coming from the proposed occlusion-handling mechanism. Monocular Uncertainty: Monocular depth estimation is generally less accurate than stereo matching in non-occluded areas. How does the system prevent the lower-fidelity monocular priors from degrading the high-precision stereo-matched regions? A discussion or experiment on the “noise” introduced by the monocular prior is needed. Domain Specificity: The proposed modules seem generally applicable to natural images. Does the design include specific considerations for the unique properties of endoscopic images (e.g., specular reflections, textureless tissue, or fluid presence) compared to standard outdoor/driving datasets? Discrepancy in Latency Reporting: In Table 1, the inference speed is reported as 25.65ms, yet Section 4.1 mentions 45.23ms. Does the 25.65ms figure only account for the proposed refinement modules, excluding the backbone? For a fair assessment of real-time viability, the total end-to-end processing time (45.23ms) should be the primary metric reported.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and all reviewers for the constructive comments. 1.SOTA Comparison Rationale (R#2, R#3): We agree with the reviewers that the selection of SOTA baselines in the current experiments is relatively limited,a comprehensive comparison with RAFT-Stereo, IGEV-Stereo, and other SOTA methods related to CV construction​is planned for the extension paper. Regarding the chosen baselines, HSM, DeepPruner, and MSDESIS represent the state-of-the-art for surgical scenarios, while ACVNet​represents the SOTA in CV construction, which is the primary focus of our improvement; further ablation studies will be conducted. GMStereo​is a multi-task framework that incorporates monocular depth estimation, but it does not explicitly use the monocular prior to guide the stereo matching process. 2.Occlusion Validation (R#1, R#2, R#3): We acknowledge the reviewers’ concern that the occlusion validation in the current manuscript is insufficient. A quantitative analysis (EPE, D1-all, Bad3)focused on occlusion will be presented in the extension paper. In the current version, qualitative analysis (Fig. 3n) demonstrates that our method yields lower error in the left-image occlusion regions (caused by camera baseline disparity) compared to the backbone (Fig. 3m). This visually proves the efficiency of our approach in occluded areas. 3.Novelty (R#2, R#3): Our fundamental novelty lies in addressing the precision degradation of CV-based methods at disparity discontinuities. Monocular depth estimation does not suffer from these specific failure modes. Thus, we probabilize the monocular depth prior​to enhance the CV, providing geometric guidance where traditional matching fails. This differs from prior hard features or directly connection concatenation based works. 4.Technical Details and Implementation (R#1, R#2): R#1:The standard deviation σ in Eq.2 controls the spread of the PDF; we empirically selected σ=0.2.Ablation study is planned for the extension paper. R#2: a) We have standardized the module naming to DPCV​throughout the manuscript. b)The normal distribution（σ=0.2） for the probability prior was empirically selected; we plan to explore adaptive parameter selection in future work. c)Regarding the iteration number, our ablation study tested various values, and the results indicate that 1 iteration​ currently offers the most balanced trade-off between performance and efficiency. 5.Reproducibility and Resources (R#1, R#2, R#3): We confirm our commitment to releasing all code upon acceptance. 6.Monocular Uncertainty(R#3):​We acknowledge that monocular depth estimation is generally less accurate than stereo matching in non-occluded areas. Thus, we restrict CV updates only to masked regions to safely leverage the monocular prior（Alg.1）. Regarding noise, the CDE implicitly suppresses noise by leveraging the intrinsic geometric relationship between stereo pairs to output robust coarse inverse depth. Notably, although LeRes-ResNet50（applied in this work） and LeRes-ResNeXt101​exhibit different noise characteristics, we observed similar disparity estimation results during training. This result empirically demonstrates that our method is robust to noise in the depth prior. 7.Domain Specificity(R#3): The proposed modules demonstrate effectiveness on the FlyingThings3D dataset during pre-training. This confirms that our method generalizes beyond surgical scenarios to other domains. DPCV targets stereo-occluded regions​where the monocular depth prior is assumed to be more accurate than stereo matching. Consequently, the network’s performance in specular highlight regions depends on whether the underlying monocular depth estimator can effectively handle such artifacts. 8.Latency(R#3):​ The 25.65ms refers to the added overhead of our modules. In the revised manuscript, we report the end-to-end time (45.23ms) as the speed metric . 9.Typo Corrections (R#1): R#1:We have corrected the “fourfold” to “threefold”.

title: On the Robustness of Temporal Vision-Language Models for Surgical Endoscopy Videos
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The motivation on surgical endoscopy is noisy and investigate the robustness motivation is clear and sound, especially the paper emphasizes worst case failure rather than only average performance. 2.The paper benchmarks three recent surgical TVLMs across three datasets, seven conditions (clean + six corruptions), and two corruption-coverage settings, for 294 dataset-level evaluations and 593,488 clip-level evaluations. These contribute to a large-scale study.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Although I appreciate the benchmark setting, the methodology novelty is limited if author presented this paper as method paper. The underlying common-corruption benchmark paradigm was established by ImageNet-C (Hendrycks & Dietterich, 2019), which already evaluates multiple corruption types across five severity levels. In medical VLMs, Imam et al. (2025) already introduced MediMeta-C and RobustMedCLIP, combining a corruption benchmark with few-shot adaptation for robustness. In endoscopy specifically, Wang et al. (2024) already benchmarked robustness under synthetic corruptions for depth estimation, and VeRA itself is an existing PEFT method from Kopiczko et al. (2024). So the real novelty here is narrower: applying these ideas to temporal surgical TVLMs with an endoscopy-specific corruption set and analysis. That is still useful, but it is not a fundamentally new robustness formulation. 2.The introduction motivates prompt-based, open-vocabulary recognition, but RobustEndoCLIP is trained with cross-entropy on a fixed in-dataset label set and is evaluated only on those same seen vocabularies. So what is shown is stronger closed-set robustness with text prompts, not robustness of unseen-label transfer or open-vocabulary generalization after adaptation. A held-out-label, cross-dataset prompt-transfer, or retrieval evaluation after tuning would be needed to support that stronger claim.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and underexplored problem: the robustness of surgical TVLMs under realistic endoscopic corruptions. It introduces a well-motivated corruption benchmark spanning six clinically relevant perturbations. The proposed RobustEndoCLIP is practically interesting because it shows that lightweight few-shot parameter-efficient tuning can substantially improve robustness without changing the prompt-based deployment interface.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The technical novelty of the proposed method appears limited. RobustEndoCLIP is essentially built on top of an existing temporal CLIP-style model and adapts it using VeRA, which is itself an existing parameter-efficient tuning method rather than a new methodological contribution of this paper. 2.The baseline comparison is somewhat narrow. Although the paper evaluates three recent TVLMs, these baselines all come from a closely related line of surgical video-language pretraining work, rather than representing a broader spectrum of temporal vision-language models. As a result, it is still unclear whether the observed conclusions would generalize to a wider set of architectures, including stronger general-domain video-language models or additional medical/surgical multimodal models. 3.The evaluation is still limited in scope, being centered on prompt-based classification with a fixed corruption setting, which makes the robustness claims less comprehensive than they could be. 4.Additional weaknesses are that the “few-shot” setting still uses 16% labeled training data, the corruptions are synthetic rather than real clinical degradation, and the paper provides limited analysis of why VeRA improves robustness beyond reporting the gains.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This study sought to assess the robustness of Temporal Vision-Language Models in the surgical endoscopic setting. The authors compiled three open-source endoscope datasets and conducted a taxonomic study on different types of endoscopic video corruptions. This work conducted empirical studies on three start-of-the-art TVLM models and two PEFT fine-tuning methods.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main concern is the lack of methodological innovation. The corruption taxonomy is more like common sense rather than the author’s insight/contribution. The dataset is from other open-source works without any re-annotation. Meanwhile, I am not confident that the benchmark experiment is comprehensive or solid. There is no innovation regarding parameter-efficient fine-tuning. In addition, this paper does not specify what task these TVLMs are intended for.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We appreciate the reviewers’ effort and constructive comments. We are glad that R1 recognized the clear motivation, worst-case focus, and large-scale evaluation; R2 highlighted the clinically meaningful Endo-C6 setting and practical robustness gains; and R3 noted the empirical study of TVLM robustness, taxonomy, datasets, and TVLM/PEFT evaluation. Below, we address the concerns point-by-point and will incorporate clarifications in the revision. R1.1/R2.1 Contribution scope relative to prior work. We appreciate R1/R2’s framing and will emphasize the paper’s central contribution: a clinically driven Endo-C6 robustness study for temporal surgical TVLMs, with RobustEndoCLIP as the limited-supervision adaptation setting. Prior work addresses natural corruptions, medical VLM robustness, or endoscopic depth estimation, but not prompt-based surgical TVLMs under GI/laparoscopic acquision artifacts. To our knowledge, Endo-C6 is the first benchmark for this setting, combining paired label-preserving corruptions on real clips, domain/temporal artifact structure, limited-supervision analysis, and mean/worst-case reporting. It reveals artifact-specific failures: smoke dominates laparoscopy, GI sensitivity is model-dependent, and clean accuracy poorly predicts corrupted robustness. R1.2 Prompt-based vs. open-vocabulary scope. We agree experiments use fixed dataset vocabularies, not held-out-label transfer. Here, “prompt-based” means CLIP-style class-name prompts matched with video embeddings. Claims concern label-preserving corruptions under this interface, not unseen-label adaptation after tuning. We will clarify the task as CholecT50 phase, Kvasir GI landmark/pathology, and TEMSET-24K action classification. R2.2 Baseline selection. SurgVLP, HecVLP, and PeskaVLP are recent public surgical TVLMs with comparable CLIP-style interfaces and no Endo-C6 exposure. Identical prompts, sampling, splits, corruptions, and temporal coverage enable controlled comparison; broader VLMs/surgical multimodal models are valuable future works. R2.3/R3.3 Task scope and benchmark strength. Endo-C6 evaluates prompt-based temporal clip classification: CholecT50 phases, Kvasir GI landmark/pathology classes, and TEMSET-24K actions. Within this scope, it is comprehensive and solid: full public GI/laparoscopic test splits, 3 datasets, 3untuned TVLM baselines plus RobustEndoCLIP configurations, clean+6 corruptions, 2 temporal coverages, and 294 dataset-level/593,488 clip-level evaluations under identical prompts, sampling, splits, severity, and aggregation. This controlled design isolates video-text alignment failures under label-preserving shifts and avoids broader claims. We will further clarify the task/scope and make it explicit in the final, and extend the scope in future work. R2.4 Few-shot, corruptions, and VeRA. The 16% setting is the largest limited clean-label budget; Fig. 4 reports 0/4/8/16%. Synthetic corruptions are deliberate: applied to real test clips, they keep labels/test composition fixed while varying only artifact type/severity, simulating routine endoscopic acquisition artifacts for reproducible paired stress tests. Table 2 shows LoRA can improve clean accuracy, but VeRA gives stronger corrupted performance with far fewer params (1,024 vs. 720,896; 29.13 vs. 16.92 average Mean-C), suggesting better regularization under corruption. R3.1 Methodological scope and taxonomy. The core contribution is a clinically motivated robustness benchmark and analysis for temporal surgical VLMs, not a new adaptation algorithm. Endo-C6 is not a generic corruption list: organizing clinically familiar artifacts by domain salience and temporal behavior enables interpretable smoke/laparoscopy and motion/defocus/GI findings. R3.2 Public datasets and re-annotation. We use public datasets to ensure reproducibility and isolate artifact-driven robustness failures. Since Endo-C6 applies label-preserving corruptions to existing test clips, re-annotation is not required.

title: OpenRC: An Open-Source Robotic Colonoscopy Framework for Multimodal Data Acquisition and Autonomy Research
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper provides a thorough and well-structured literature review, particularly regarding existing datasets in the field. 2.The work addresses a significant void in the community, as there is currently no unified, open-source hardware and software platform that enables reproducible closed-loop experimentation in colonoscopy. 3.The platform is designed to be low-cost, which increases its accessibility for research, and highly versatile, supporting the integration of several commercial colonoscopes and utilizing a modular actuation system. 4.A key technical advantage is that all data streams are timestamped using a shared system clock. Achieving precise synchronization is a highly significant and difficult task in multimodal applications, and this framework provides a robust solution to that challenge.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The authors state the system aims “to balance reliable advancement with safe force application”, yet no force quantification is provided to support this. To ensure safety, the shape of the endoscope and its contact points with the colon walls should be tracked, and the actual forces should be measured to ensure they remain within a safe physiological range. 2.The feeding module relies on friction for endoscope insertion and retraction. However, the authors do not report any friction coefficients or explain how they ensure that no slippage occurs during various manipulations. 3.It would be beneficial to report the material properties of the custom silicone phantom and provide a comparison to real tissue to justify its use as a valid model. 4.Figs. 3b and c appear much earlier in the text than they are discussed, which disrupts the flow of the paper. I suggest placing them after Figure 5.In addition, the term NDI in Fig. 3 is not defined. 5.Phantoms are not ex vivo setups, they are in vitro. 6.In the segment regarding “a low-frequency sinusoidal command (0.2 Hz) along the X axis (see Fig. 2(b)) for bending”, the reference to Fig. 2(b) appears to be incorrect.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Figures are well defined with clear illustration of information: Figure 1 and Figure 2 on system components; Figure 3, 4 on dataset stats and examples. Robotic colonoscopy with low cost and reliability/accuracy is a solid need. The multimodal dataset has reasonable amount of data collected and with cross-modal data collected could be a good resource for this field.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Dataset is all collected from phantoms and from structured tasks, which makes a large gap to real clinical translation and limits the usefulness of the dataset. The contribution of this hardware system and control software, may lack novelty in algorithmic aspect or methodological aspect. It may be more of an incremental work with all existing components.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.OpenRC is an open-source closed-loop platform that jointly covers observation, action, state, and pose, and it helps address a gap in the colonoscopy domain to some extent. 2.The overall system design of OpenRC is relatively well developed, covering the hardware setup, software system, and data format, with a reasonable level of completeness. 3.The constructed dataset contains diverse types of information and may offer certain value for research in this area.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper reads more like a description of the platform and dataset, with relatively limited system-level innovation and methodological contribution. 2.The current validation mainly focuses on motion consistency and latency, and there is still a lack of more direct evidence showing that the platform can effectively support downstream research. For example, it would be helpful to train a baseline policy or VLA on the collected data and report the corresponding performance. 3.The dataset is still limited in scale and collection diversity. If the intended use is to support large-scale VLA training, its value may be relatively limited.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing that OpenRC fills a gap in unified open-source platforms for reproducible closed-loop colonoscopy [R1, R2, R3], and that our dataset offers a valuable resource for the field [R1, R2, R3]. Major concerns: Novelty and Contribution [R2.2, R3.1]: R2 and R3 viewed the work primarily as an integration of existing components with limited methodological novelty. However, to the best of our knowledge, no similar open-source, low-cost, and extensible platform exists for reproducible closed-loop colonoscopy research using existing commercial colonoscopes. The novelty of OpenRC lies in the design of the integration and actuation framework and the overall workflow specifically developed to interface with existing clinical systems rather than rebuilding an entirely new robotic platform from scratch, which we believe has not previously been demonstrated in an open-source and reproducible form for closed-loop colonoscopy research. Unlike existing systems that are often expensive and proprietary, OpenRC integrates with commercial colonoscopes for under $5,000 while preserving the clinical workflow. Besides contributing a unique multimodal dataset, another major contribution is the unified hardware-software ecosystem enabling synchronized acquisition of commands, pose, proprioception, and video streams for future research in robotics, autonomy, and AI-assisted endoscopy. We will update the text to better reflect this. Phantom Realism [R1.3, R2.1]: R1 and R2 raised concerns regarding the phantom-only setting. As clarified in Sec. 2.4, the phantom setup was selected to enable precise 6-DoF ground-truth acquisition via EM tracking, consistent with prior colonoscopy datasets (e.g. C3VDv2 [11], SimCol3D [22]). Importantly, the phantom is fully decoupled from the proposed platform and serves as an example to demonstrate multimodal data acquisition. Our modular hardware-software framework can operate with different phantoms, colonoscopes, and image processors without modifying the overall system, enabling the community to integrate more anatomically realistic environments, sensors, and tasks as needed. Our custom phantom follows reported human colon dimensions and Paris-classified polyp morphology using silicone casting and modular 3D-printed molds, while the commercial phantom was included to increase appearance diversity. We will clarify this better in the text. Dataset Scale and Validation Depth [R3.2, R3.3]: R3 raised concerns regarding dataset scale and the absence of trained baseline policies. While modest in scale (~19 hours, 1894 episodes), the dataset is comparable to existing colonoscopy resources [11,22], uniquely providing synchronized action-state-pose-video streams. More importantly, OpenRC is designed as a community-driven open-source platform, enabling other groups to collect compatible multimodal data using their own scopes and phantoms and continuously expand the dataset over time. We agree that training VLAs/policies is an important future research direction (Sec. 5). However, this first requires a unified, reproducible, and accessible platform that the community can broadly adopt, which is the primary objective of this work. Our validation demonstrates the reliability of this foundation through repeatable actuation (Fig. 3a) and frame-level temporal coherence across all modalities (Fig. 3b-c). We will emphasize this framing in the discussion. Safety/Friction [R1.1, R1.2]: OpenRC preserves the colonoscope’s native compliance through adjustable preload control (Sec. 2.1). Slippage is visible during teleoperation and corrected in real time. Comprehensive shape, contact, and force tracking is planned as future work. Minor Concerns [R1]: (R1.4) We will revisit Fig. 3 as space permits and define NDI (Northern Digital Inc.). (R1.5) We will use “in vitro” in Sec. 5.(R1.6) Fig. 2(b) shows the frame in which the X axis is defined. We will clarify in the text.

title: Ordinal Priors for Colonoscopy Temporal Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: clinical motivation is reasonable; anatomical ordering is indeed a natural and sensable prior for temporal segmentation combination of ordinal regression objective and transistion constrianed decoding is clean this task-speicfic integration is suitable for MICCAI short paper
reviewer_1_weaknesses: both ORH and OCD are well-established and authors should not claim contribution on these two Test sets of 12 (REAL-Colon) and 20 (CAS-Colon) videos are small. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, making it difficult to judge whether the improvements are robust or within noise. ASFormer (BMVC 2021) and TeCNO (MICCAI 2020) are no longer state-of-the-art for temporal action segmentation. Comparisons with more recent methods would be substantially more convincing, e. g. DiffAct++ (Liu et al. , TPAMI 2025), sequence-to-sequence translation approaches (Behrmann et al. , ECCV 2022), multi-scale transformer models for surgical phase recognition (Zhang et al. , EMBC 2024), or action-aware segment modelling (He et al. , CVPR 2022). The wF1 and WMAPE values reported here for ColonTCN on REAL-Colon differ noticeably from those in the original ColonTCN paper on the same dataset. Not sure why? Also, the OCD enforces near-monotonic transitions, but endoscope movement does go back and forth during withdrawal; particularly around the cecum and ascending colon, as visible in the ground truth of Fig. 3(A). Will there be a over-smooth risk?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents a methodological advance by explicitly modeling colon anatomy as an ordered sequence rather than as independent classes, addressing a key limitation of prior approaches. It introduces (i) a distance-weighted ordinal regression loss that incorporates anatomical relationships into learning (as clearly illustrated in Fig. 2); (ii) an ordinal-constrained decoding scheme that enforces anatomically plausible transitions; and (iii) a post-processing strategy that improves temporal consistency by reducing flickering and unrealistic label changes, as supported by the ablation study. The method is validated on the challenging REAL-Colon dataset and further evaluated on the CAS-Colon dataset to assess robustness without additional fine-tuning.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major concerns: (i) The primary limitation is the restricted clinical scope, as the method focuses only on the seven withdrawal-phase anatomical segments and does not extend to full-procedure analysis, thereby limiting its applicability for assessing key clinical indicators such as cecal intubation. Moderate concerns: (i) The ordinal-constrained decoding may suppress valid retrograde events that can naturally occur during colonoscopy (e.g., as illustrated in Fig. 3(A), showing the first appearance of the ascending colon segment). This limitation is not discussed; (ii) The framework is designed for offline, post-procedure analysis, with limited discussion of real-time applicability or deployment in clinical settings; (iii) The evaluation is limited to the withdrawal phase.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper studies a meaningful clinical problem, namely the temporal segmentation of colonoscopy withdrawal videos into anatomical regions. Its most interesting conceptual contribution is the way it reformulates the task: instead of treating the anatomical segments of the colon as independent, unordered categories, the authors model them as an ordinal label space with a natural proximal-to-distal ordering. This formulation is highly consistent with the anatomical structure of the colon and the actual withdrawal process, and it also provides a clear explanation for why conventional classification-based temporal segmentation methods often produce anatomically implausible jumps. Another strength of the paper is that the method is simple, targeted, and reasonably interpretable. Rather than introducing an overly complicated new architecture, the authors inject the ordinal prior into an existing temporal segmentation framework through three focused components: an auxiliary ordinal regression head, a boundary-aware smoothness loss, and an order-constrained decoder. As a result, the method is easy to follow and potentially easier to reproduce, adapt, and extend. In this sense, the work is a good example of improving a standard pipeline by explicitly leveraging domain structure. Importantly, the paper does not stop at merely modifying the loss function. Instead, it incorporates the ordinal prior at both the training and inference stages: during training, prediction errors are penalized according to anatomical distance, while during inference, the decoder suppresses implausible backward transitions and segment-skipping behavior. This makes the overall approach more than a simple auxiliary-loss trick, and turns it into a relatively complete ordinal modeling framework.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper is that the methodological contribution appears more incremental than fundamentally novel. In essence, the work adapts existing ideas on ordinal learning and constrained decoding to the task of colonoscopy temporal segmentation, rather than introducing a genuinely new learning framework. This does not mean the work lacks value, since the task is clinically meaningful and the adaptation is sensible, but it does weaken the originality of the paper. Another important weakness is the lack of clarity regarding several key implementation details. The method introduces multiple important hyperparameters, including the loss weights, the boundary dilation radius, the temporal pooling window, and the backward used in the decoder. However, in the current manuscript, these quantities are mostly introduced only symbolically, while their concrete values and model-selection strategy are not clearly described. Since the final performance may be sensitive to these design choices, the omission weakens the reproducibility of the work. It also makes it difficult to assess whether the reported gains reflect a robust modeling improvement or depend substantially on careful hyperparameter tuning. For a methods paper, these details are important for both fair evaluation and practical reuse by others. A further weakness is that the overall framework depends on a strong structural assumption: namely, that the withdrawal process follows a near-monotonic anatomical progression, such that backward transitions are rare and segment skipping is anatomically implausible. This prior is clinically reasonable on average, and it is exactly what motivates the proposed constrained decoding. However, in real procedures, this assumption may not always hold strictly. Local revisits, unstable camera views, transient ambiguity, or uncertain segment boundaries may all produce short-term reversals or irregular transitions that are not purely errors. In such cases, the constrained decoder may potentially suppress predictions that are locally valid but globally disfavored by the prior. The paper would therefore be more convincing if it provided a more detailed failure-case analysis, especially clarifying when the constrained decoding helps and when it may incorrectly suppress true local backward motion or uncertain transitions.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the clinical motivation (R1, R2, R3) and the consistent integration of ordinal priors across training and inference (R2, R3). Our novelty is not in introducing new standalone components, but in a task-specific formulation of withdrawal-phase anatomical segmentation as an ordinal label space, implemented via ordinal supervision and ordinal-constrained decoding. We address the major concerns below. (A) ColonTCN discrepancy (R1). We thank the reviewer for flagging this point. The discrepancy with the original ColonTCN paper stems from different task definitions and evaluation targets. The original benchmark addresses full-procedure segmentation with a 9-class label space (including outside/insertion), uses ResNet50 features, and reports WMAPE as withdrawal-time estimation error. Our submission evaluates 7-class withdrawal-phase anatomical segmentation: non-withdrawal frames are excluded, GastroNet embeddings are used, and WMAPE measures anatomical segment-duration error. All baselines in Table 1 are retrained under the same split/feature/exclusion protocol for a fair comparison. (B) Requests for newer baselines (R1). We acknowledge the requests for comparisons to newer temporal segmentation methods. However, rebuttal rules do not allow new experiments, so we cannot add new baselines here. We instead clarify the existing protocol and note that robustness is already assessed via CAS-Colon evaluation and ablations in the manuscript. (C) Monotonicity and oversmoothing risk (R1, R2, R3). We agree that withdrawal is not strictly monotonic and that short local revisits can occur, particularly near cecum–ascending (Fig. 3(A) GT). Both components of our framework are designed as soft priors rather than hard constraints: the training-time ordinal objective penalizes anatomically distant errors without preventing local deviations, and ordinal-constrained decoding (OCD) applies tunable backward/skip penalties (Eq. (4)–(5)) so that strong evidence can override the prior. As shown in Fig. 3, OCD suppresses unsupported flickering and non-`adjacent jumps relative to both the ColonTCN baseline and our raw predictions. In the cecum and ascending, we consistently observe improved F1 over the ColonTCN baseline on both datasets (REAL-Colon: cecum +4.3pp, ascending +2.4pp; CAS-Colon: cecum +12.4pp, ascending +4.2pp). Nevertheless, we acknowledge a trade-off: overly aggressive decoding penalties could smooth brief valid retrograde events. We will discuss this risk and its mitigation in the final version. (D) Clinical scope and deployment (R2). We thank the reviewer for raising this important question regarding clinical applicability. Our framework targets withdrawal-phase region tracking for post-procedure reporting (documenting examined regions and lesion locations from the completed video), matched by the withdrawal-only CAS-Colon benchmark used for external validation. We acknowledge that this scope does not cover full-procedure endpoints such as cecal intubation assessment or real-time deployment during the procedure. We will clarify these scope limitations and discuss potential extensions as future work. (E) Reproducibility and implementation details (R1, R3). We agree that hyperparameters should be stated concretely. The submitted experiments used: CE (0.5), TMSE (0.15; threshold 4.0), boundary-smooth loss (0.5; radius r=5; KL), and ORH (λ_reg=0.3); OCD used α=10, β=5, free start, and pooling window w=3.Model selection used early stopping on validation wJacc with no test-set tuning. We will consolidate these into a concise table and, upon acceptance, release the code (links omitted per policy). For statistical robustness, paired, video-level bootstrap resampling (B=2,000) on the existing test outputs confirmed statistically significant improvements over ColonTCN in wF1, wJacc, and transitions (p<0.001). (F) Figure clarity (R2). We will add anatomical-segment labels to Fig. 3 in the final version.
