reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Demonstrates that careful memory curation and lightweight design can push a general-purpose model (SAM3) to strong, application-specific performance, potentially reducing annotation and domain-adaptation needs. 2.Evaluations span three widely used surgical benchmarks (EndoVis17, EndoVis18, CholecSeg8k) with consistent improvements over SAM3 in a zero-shot setting.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Comparison baselines for CholecSeg8k are missing. Only SAM3 is compared in Table 5.2.Missing implementation details. E.g. what are prompts for SAM-based baselines? Did you train the specialist models on your datasets? If so, what are the implementation details for these baselines? 3.The proposed model achieves SOTA performance in only a single category of EndoVis17 and two categories of EndoVis18.The authors should provide a more in-depth discussion to explain these specific results. 4.No statistical significance or variability reporting (e.g., per-sequence variance, confidence intervals) is provided.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for constructive feedback. Below, we address main recurring concerns and provide additional clarifications. 1.Efficiency/scalability (R2-W2, R3-W2/W3, R4-Q3/Q4): SAM3 already maintains per-object memory by fusing per-object masks with image features; ReMeDI differs in using a larger memory bank and a different frame-selection strategy. On EndoVis18 with a single RTX 4090, ReMeDI incurs modest overhead compared to SAM3: 6,299 vs 6,010 MB peak GPU memory (+4.8%), 4,820 vs 4,767 MB average GPU memory (+1.1%), and 351.1 vs 329.7 ms/frame latency (+6.5%). The expanded memory bank (M=15 vs 7) adds only ~5% to memory-attention cost since compute is dominated by image encoder. To ensure scalability: unconditional buffer is a per-object FIFO with max_size=15 storing recent frames with reliability above τ_occ (only 7 recent frames needed for occlusion-aware memory) while ReID bank is capped at 15 entries/object. ReID is lightweight, triggered only during occlusion recovery, and reuses already-computed image features. 2.Per-sequence variability/per-class analysis on EndoVis17 (R2-W1, R4-W3/W4): Across 8 sequences, ReMeDI achieves 74.50 ± 14.13 mcIoU versus 69.04 ± 17.75 for SAM3, corresponding to a 20% reduction in standard deviation across surgeries. These sequence-level means differ slightly from the frame-pooled paper-table mcIoU values since sequences are weighted equally. The improvement is statistically significant (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, ReMeDI wins 7/8 sequences), with a 95% cluster-bootstrap CI of [+0.64, +8.13] for paired ΔmcIoU. Per-class analysis shows improvements on 5/7 classes (vs SAM3), while the remaining two are statistically tied. On EndoVis17, SAM3 performs slightly better on UP class whereas ReMeDI performs substantially better on challenging EndoVis18 UP sequences. Overall, ReMeDI ranks among the top two methods in 4/7 classes; remaining gaps mainly against supervised methods. Our ReID module prioritizes precision in difficult re-appearance cases, occasionally over-rejecting recoveries and lowering performance on some classes (GR). 3.Pre-occlusion reliability/objectness (R2-W3/W4): ReMeDI uses lower-visibility pre-occlusion frames to aid recovery since they often contain critical identity cues. However, they can have unreliable predictions, and to avoid propagating them, the ReID module rejects ambiguous recoveries. SAM3 objectness is used only as a recovery trigger; final identity assignment is determined by ReID, making recovery robust to false-positive triggers. Performance might be affected if SAM3 fails to re-detect after reappearance, which is relatively rare in practice. 4.Similar instruments (R3 optional, R4-Q1/Q2): ReMeDI performs class-level rather than instance-level segmentation. Both SAM3 and ReMeDI-SAM3 use ground-truth first-appearance masks as initialization prompts so the model already knows instrument classes present. If a newly appearing instrument belongs to an already-tracked class, it inherits the same class identity; otherwise, an extra prompt would be required. 5.Baselines, prompts, CholecSeg8k (R4-W1/W2): All zero-shot SAM-family rows use the same first-appearance GT-mask prompt. Specialist baselines in Table 1 are reported from their published supervised settings without modification. For CholecSeg8k, Table 5 compares ReMeDI against SAM3 under zero-shot setting on the full dataset; existing supervised methods train/evaluate on subsets and are therefore not directly comparable. We additionally evaluated PerSAM, TrackAnything as zero-shot baselines (full MA-SAM2 code unavailable) and found ReMeDI-SAM3 to perform better, consistent with EndoVis17/18 results. These comparisons can be included in the final version (as new results are not allowed in rebuttal). Overall, ReMeDI is a training-free refinement of SAM3 that provides statistically supported gains under surgical occlusion with moderate overhead. For reproducibility, we will release the code upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal should address three decision-affecting concerns. First, the missing computational and efficiency analysis—runtime, latency, and memory overhead relative to vanilla SAM3—raised by all three reviewers, since this is central to the claimed practical advantage. Second, the missing baselines on CholecSeg8k, the incomplete implementation details for SAM-based and specialist baselines including prompt setup and training, the limited per-category SOTA on EndoVis17/18, and the absence of statistical significance or variability reporting. Third, the robustness of the re-identification scheme: same-class instance disambiguation, distinction between re-entry and new objects, and the apparent contradiction between low pre-occlusion reliability scores and their use as identity cues. | The paper proposes a training-free extension of SAM3 for surgical instrument segmentation, featuring relevance-aware memory filtering, an occlusion-aware memory, piecewise interpolation, and a feature-based re-identification module. The reviewers raised three decision-affecting concerns: missing computational and efficiency analysis relative to SAM3, missing baselines on one dataset, the absence of statistical significance reporting, and the robustness of the re-identification scheme. The rebuttal demonstrates modest overhead relative to SAM3, provides per-sequence statistics with a paired non-parametric significance test on the main benchmark, clarifies that the re-identification module rejects ambiguous recoveries to avoid propagating unreliable identity cues, and explicitly states that the module’s scope is class-level rather than instance-level. Two reviewers endorsed acceptance after the rebuttal; one maintained a Reject, arguing that the gains are marginal and limited to a subset of categories, which is a legitimate but secondary critique. The framework is clean, and the rebuttal addresses the most consequential concerns. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After the rebuttal, two reviewers R2 and R3 accpet and one reviewer R4 reject. After reading all the reviews，I agree with R4 that the performance gain is limited and unconvincing. Besides, there are other concerns about the computational efficiency and insufficient experimental validation. So the recommendation is Reject. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a practically valuable training-free extension of SAM3 for surgical video segmentation, and reviewers recognized its dual-memory design, occlusion-aware recovery, and feature-based re-identification as useful for improving temporal consistency under long occlusions. Although there are concerns about computational overhead, robustness in visually similar instruments, and incomplete benchmarking details, the rebuttal provided additional efficiency analysis, variability/statistical evidence, and clarification of the class-level formulation and memory design. Overall, the method shows meaningful zero-shot gains with moderate overhead and sufficient practical value to support acceptance.

title: Retrieval-Guided Semi-supervised Federated Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The labels-for-public SSFL setting is practical and relevant, and the paper addresses it with a clearly motivated retrieval-based perspective. 2.Using public labeled data as query-specific references, rather than only as a source of global model supervision, is the most novel and interesting part of the paper. 3.The gains on the heterogeneous polyp setting are substantial, which suggests that the retrieval-guided formulation may indeed be particularly useful under domain shift. 4.The paper includes qualitative examples and some ablation analysis, which is appreciated for a method that aims to exploit sample-level semantics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Regarding the dynamic head formulation in Section 2.2: The authors state that the cross-attention output omega in R^{2 x C} directly defines the parameters, with the ‘background channel’ serving as the bias. However, for a standard 1x1 convolution layer mapping from C input channels to 1 or 2 output channels (binary segmentation), the Bias should be a scalar or a vector of size 1 or 2, not a vector of size C. This is important because it is central to the proposed method. 2.Table 2b is incomplete or at least very hard to interpret. The ‘retrieval on train and test’ ablation appears to show only three configurations instead of a full 2 x 2 design, which makes it difficult to disentangle the contribution of retrieval during training versus inference. 3.The training pipeline is somewhat inconsistent with the paper’s main narrative. After federated aggregation, the server performs additional training on the public dataset using randomly selected references rather than retrieval-based references. This makes it harder to isolate how much of the gain comes from the proposed QAR mechanism itself. 4.There are several notation and presentation issues that reduce precision, such as the mixed use of R and S in the reference-supervision equation and the brief explanation of randomly reversed masks.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The idea of using a public dataset as a reference for queries (unlabeled client images) is novel in the context of semi-supervised FL for medical image segmentation. Good performance, as seen in Table 1, and includes appropriate baselines required in labels for public settings. Ablation Studies are particularly informative. It shows that even when the retrieved sample size is small, the model still performs well [Table 2(a)].
reviewer_2_weaknesses: One major weakness of the approach is the need for a reference dataset at test time. In an ablation study (Table 2(b)), when retrieval is omitted, random references are assigned instead of zero-filling or random noise filling. Which means during test-time inferences, we still need a reference to make a prediction, which is impractical in an offline scenario. Section 2.2 training strategy, last para, mentions random selection of references rather than semantic selection for diversity? What’s the justification for needing diversity here (assuming this is for server training)? There is no evidence (cited work or experiments) to support this claim. The number of clients in the non-IID setup is very low compared to the prior study[1]. It utilizes 4 clients in non-IID instead of 3 clients. [1] Ma, Y., Wang, J., Yang, J., Wang, L.: Model-heterogeneous semi-supervised federated learning for medical image segmentation. IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging 43(5), 1804–1815 (2024)
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Solid empirical gains in the heterogeneous setting. On the non-IID polyp benchmark, the reported improvements are substantial: R2S2Fed achieves 67.15 Dice / 57.43 IoU on average, compared with 59.66 / 47.83 for the strongest baseline LSSL. 2.Useful ablation on retrieval. The paper does include ablations on the number of retrieved references and on whether retrieval is used during training and/or inference. These studies provide some evidence that retrieval during training is more important than retrieval only at test time. 3.Qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative trend. The visual comparisons in Fig. 2 and the retrieval visualization in Fig. 3 help illustrate the authors’ intuition that semantically relevant public references may be more beneficial under heterogeneity.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty. The main concern is that the paper does not appear to introduce a sufficiently new algorithmic contribution. The proposed framework combines several familiar components: public-sample retrieval, cross-attention-based reference conditioning, dynamic/query-specific segmentation parameters, FixMatch-style semi-supervised training, and standard FedAvg aggregation. The paper itself states that the framework is inspired by prior hypernetwork/context-dependent segmentation approaches, which further weakens the novelty claim. As a result, the contribution feels more like an application-specific integration than a distinctly new method. 2.The federated learning component is fairly standard. On the FL side, the method relies on conventional FedAvg, and the server additionally trains on the public dataset after aggregation, as commonly done in prior SSFL works. There is no new federated optimization strategy, no communication-efficient mechanism, no privacy analysis, and no explicit treatment of client heterogeneity beyond reference retrieval. This makes the “federated” contribution less compelling. 3.Experimental scope is too narrow for the claimed generality. The experimental validation is limited to two 2D segmentation tasks: skin lesion segmentation on ISIC2018 and polyp segmentation across four datasets. The backbone is a relatively standard ResNet34 encoder-decoder. There is no validation on more diverse medical segmentation settings, no 3D benchmark, no stronger modern backbone, and no comparison to more recent segmentation paradigms. For a MICCAI paper claiming a generally useful framework, this scope feels insufficient. 4.The improvement in the IID setting is modest. On ISIC, the average Dice improves only from 84.71 ((FL)2) to 85.26, which is a rather small margin. This weakens the claim that the proposed mechanism provides broad and consistent gains beyond a more specialized heterogeneous setting. 5.Ablations do not fully support the strongest paper narrative. The paper emphasizes query-adaptive retrieval and query-specific adaptation at inference time, but Table 2b indicates that retrieval during training is the main source of gain, while retrieval at inference provides only marginal improvement. This suggests that the true benefit may come more from retrieval-enhanced training than from the claimed adaptive inference behavior. The paper should reconcile this observation more carefully.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for constructive feedback. We address the major concerns as below. 1 (R3.1, R3.2) Limited methodological novelty and FL contribution We propose a fundamentally new SSFL paradigm that reframes public labeled data from a generalized supervisory source into a sample-level semantic resource. Prior methods compress public labeled data into model parameters or pseudo-labels, inevitably losing sample-level semantics. We are the first to repurpose public data as a per-query reference. For each unlabeled client image, QAR dynamically retrieves the reference set as the encoder evolves, and a dynamic head transforms the retrieved references via cross-attention into query-adaptive parameters. These coupled mechanisms preserve sample-level semantics throughout federated training, enabling sample-level adaptation that differs from aggregation-based approaches. To demonstrate our framework, we intentionally use the simplest baselines. Our method still achieves the highest performance in both IID and Non-IID, maintaining strong results with FedAvg alone even under severe heterogeneity. Furthermore, our framework is compatible with optimization-based FL methods, expecting further gains when combined with them. 2 (R3.3) Narrow experimental scope We follow the experimental setting of Ma et al. (IEEE TMI 2024) for fair comparison. Our framework is backbone-agnostic and can be extended to 3D segmentation. 3 (R3.4) Small ISIC gain weakens the consistent-gains claim We achieve the best performance in both IID and non-IID settings. IID is a relatively easier benchmark where most methods are already saturated. Despite this, our method maintains stable performance across all clients, whereas competing methods exhibit drops on certain clients. 4 (R1.3, R2.2) Random selection for server-side training contradict QAR Random server selection and client QAR play complementary roles: random ensures global model stability, while QAR enables query-specific adaptation. With query and reference from the same public dataset, server retrieval selects near-identical samples, hindering generalization to the client-public gap. Replacing random with retrieval drops polyp dice to 18.45.5 (R1.2, R3.5) Incomplete Table 2b and weak inference-time gain undermine the adaptive inference claim. Completing the 2x2 ablation, the (training retrieval, no test retrieval) configuration shows only a 0.02 difference from the full setting, consistent with the trend when training retrieval is omitted. Regarding R3’s concern, QAR improves training by providing the dynamic head with better supervision through semantically relevant references, as evidenced by the ~5% drop shown in Table 2b. when training retrieval is removed. Consequently, the marginal inference-time gain is expected. We will revise Contribution 1 to “retrieval-guided training enabling reference-aligned inference” and update Table 2b. 6 (R2.1) Test-time reference dependency limits offline applicability Our framework achieves comparable performance with random references at inference (cf. Q5), showing representations are robust to the reference choice. A small reference set shipped with the model suffices for offline deployment. 7 (R2.3) Fewer clients in non-IID setup than prior work Although we follow Ma et al., CVC-ClinicDB and CVC-300 are derived from the same source data (EndoScene, CVC Barcelona), making them a single split rather than independent federated clients. We therefore conduct our experiments under a stronger heterogeneous setting with three datasets from truly distinct institutions. 8 (R1.1) Background channel as bias inconsistent with scalar bias of 1x1 conv The background channel of w is averaged across the channel dimension to yield a scalar bias. We will clarify Section 2.2.9 (R1.4, R2 Optional): Minor presentation and clarity issues. We thank the reviewers and will address these in the final version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I invite a rebuttal despite one “Reject” and two “Weak Accept” scores. The method is promising, but key concerns must be clarified: (1) the dynamic head formulation and bias dimension (R1), (2) the incomplete ablation in Table 2b and the need for a reference at test time (R1,R2), (3) the limited novelty and narrow experimental scope (R3). The rebuttal should focus on these technical clarifications and provide additional ablations or analysis to strengthen the claimed contributions. | After carefully considering the initial reviews, the authors’ rebuttal, and the final post-rebuttal opinions of reviewers, I recommend Accept. While Reviewer #3 raised valid concerns about novelty and experimental breadth, the rebuttal convincingly clarified the key technical issues (e.g., bias formulation, test-time reference dependency, and the role of random server-side selection). Reviewers #1 and #2, who initially rated the paper as Weak Accept, both upgraded to Accept after the rebuttal, acknowledging that the major concerns were adequately addressed. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Despite the authors’ efforts, several critical technical and empirical concerns raised by the reviewers and the AC panel remain insufficiently addressed: 1.Incomplete Ablation Studies and Over-simplification (Table 2b): The reviewers pointed out that the ablation experiment was incomplete. Though the authors provided the missing configuration, the justification for the experimental setup remains overly brief and over-simplified. The authors primarily stated that they followed existing literature without providing the specific, explicit details of the experimental settings required to make the ablation self-contained and convincing. 2.Test-time Reference Dependency and Practical Constraints: A major concern is that the framework requires reference samples during the inference/testing phase. Although the authors argued that the model can achieve comparable performance with random references or a small shipped reference set, this dependency inherently restricts the model’s flexibility, offline applicability, and deployment capability. Overall, while the core idea is noted, the combination of a constrained inference paradigm and insufficient depth in the ablation/experimental verification prevents the paper from meeting the acceptance threshold of the conference. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes R2S2Fed, a retrieval-guided semi-supervised federated learning method for medical image segmentation in the labels-for-public setting, where clients have unlabeled private data and a labeled public dataset is available. After considering the reviews and rebuttal, my recommendation is accept. While some concerns remain regarding the methodology novelty and test-time inference, the retrieval-conditioned use of public labeled data is a useful and timely direction for semi-supervised federated medical segmentation. Reviewers generally agree that the retrieval-based use of public samples is interesting, and two reviewers support acceptance after rebuttal.

title: Robust Colonoscopy Video Polyp Segmentation via Quality-Aware Memory and Prototype Alignment
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well motivated by realistic failure modes in colonoscopy videos, such as motion blur, specular reflections, occlusions, and large inter-frame displacement. The overall method is coherent: QA stabilizes short-term memory updates using reliability and consistency signals, while PA introduces long-term prototype anchors to counter appearance drift. This decomposition is intuitive and well matched to the task. Another strength is that the empirical gains are concentrated on the hardest evaluation setting: the method improves the best baseline by 2.9% Dice and 4.2% Sensitivity on SUN-SEG Unseen-Hard, and the ablation study shows that QA and PA provide complementary gains.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness is limited evaluation breadth. All experiments are conducted on SUN-SEG, so it is difficult to judge how well the method generalizes beyond this benchmark. A second weakness is that the technical novelty, while solid, is moderate: the paper combines ideas related to memory gating, dynamic memory, and prototype/feature-bank style retrieval that are related to prior works such as quality-aware dynamic memory, adaptive feature bank methods, space-time memory networks, and SALI. The contribution lies more in the task-specific integration than in a fundamentally new temporal modeling formulation. Finally, some implementation details that matter for reproducibility and robustness are not fully analyzed, such as initialization of the prototype bank and sensitivity to design choices like prototype-bank size, top-K retrieval, and update interval.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The paper addresses the degradation of single-frame queries and the subsequent noise propagation in colonoscopy video analysis. (2) The Quality-Guided Network presents a well-structured design. (3) The proposed method demonstrates quantitative improvements.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) Real-time performance is crucial for clinical deployment. However, the manuscript does not report inference speed (FPS), computational cost (FLOPs), or model parameters. Given the cascaded architecture with multiple attention modules, the practical feasibility remains unclear. (2) In Section 2.2, Eq. (4) extracts candidate prototypes using the current predicted mask. Unlike the QA module, this step does not apply a quality gate. As a result, high-confidence false positives may be added to the prototype bank. Under the LFU replacement strategy, frequently queried errors could persist in memory and potentially worsen the appearance drift the module aims to address. (3) The paper does not provide a code repository or dataset availability statement, which makes it difficult to verify implementation details or computational cost.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Effectively targets prevalent colonoscopy degradations (motion blur, occlusions), ensuring high practical value. 2.Logically separates short-term noise filtering (QA) from long-term drift tracking (PA) using a mathematically sound gating mechanism.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited Endoscopic-Specific Novelty: The QA module resembles generic CV techniques. Authors must clarify specific algorithmic differences from existing works or unique adaptations made for endoscopic scenes. 2.The “reference frame alignment” in the PA stage bypasses the QA gating, directly fusing unfiltered adjacent frames. This contradicts the introduction’s critique of traditional alignment methods and weakens the architecture’s overall consistency. Ablations or justifications are needed. 3.Dataset Limitation: Validation is restricted solely to the SUN-SEG dataset (proposed in 2022). Testing on broader, newer datasets (or cross-modalities like ultrasound) may be necessary to prove true generalizability.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their positive evaluation and constructive suggestions. We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of the clinical relevance and empirical performance of our work. We would like to clarify that prototype-bank related hyperparameters, including bank size, top-K retrieval, and update interval, were considered during method development, and the reported results use the selected configuration. Due to the space limit, detailed sensitivity analyses for all these factors were not included in the submitted manuscript. Regarding the concern on novelty, we note that the contribution of our method lies in the degradation-aware coupling between query stabilization and long-term prototype retrieval, rather than in using a memory or prototype bank in isolation. In colonoscopy videos, degraded frames caused by blur, reflection, occlusion, and large camera motion can corrupt the query features, which then propagate errors through temporal memory. This cascaded dependency makes QA and PA mutually connected: QA improves the quality of the query, while PA uses the improved query to recover stable long-term appearance information. We believe this degradation-aware formulation is different from generic memory gating or feature-bank retrieval methods, and we will revise the related-work and method sections to better clarify these algorithmic differences and their motivation in endoscopic scenes. We also agree that validation on additional datasets and clinical scenarios would further strengthen the evidence of generalization. Our current study follows the standard SUN-SEG protocol adopted by recent representative video polyp segmentation works, such as SALI, including the seen/unseen and easy/hard splits. This benchmark is well aligned with the degradation and robustness issues targeted in our work, enabling meaningful comparison within the established VPS setting. Broader cross-dataset and cross-scenario validation remains an important direction for future work. We thank the reviewers again for their time and constructive feedback.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a query-enhanced cascaded memory framework for robust video polyp segmentation under degraded conditions. All the three reviewers are positive and appreciate the paper’s contribution and good performance. However, there are also some concerns such as the limited experiments and writing issues. Overall this is a good paper and the recommendation is Provisional Accept.

title: RPG-SAM: Reliability-Weighted Prototypes and Geometric Adaptive Threshold Selection for Training-Free One-Shot Polyp Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The presentation of the paper is sufficient and the figures and visual examples further improve the readability of the paper. Overall I enjoyed reading the paper. The motivation for developing 1-shot segmentation for lesions is an important problem in medical imaging and contribution in this direction is valuable for the community The ablations performed in the paper are extensive and highlight reasonable design choices for each part of the pipeline
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The method is limited in scope to polyp segmentation by design, unlike previous methods (E. g. ProtoSAM[3] ) which are designed and evaluated to works on multiple modalities including polyps and CT scans, etc. The proposed method design by itself is refined to match the polyp morphology ( “we perform connected component analysis and retain only those components whose area is at least 20% of the largest component in that mask. To ensure morphological completeness, internal holes within these valid regions are filled”). This is a hand crafted feature to explicitly work well on polyp which contradicts the one-shot assumption of the task. It would be valuable to show another domain where this pipeline works as well besides polyps. The main results in Table 1 show marginal improvement to the most basic baseline ProtoSAM[3]. No statistics about the variability of the results are given, despite the seemingly sensitive design of hyperparameters and the delicate affect of template choice on the pipeline performance. Basically are the results of Table 1 are a consequence of just overengineering the problem and trying to get the best “numbers”, or a reflection of a profound methodological discovery that facilitates 1-shot segmentation? Also the baselines are much similar in design and hence showing the compute cost of this results improvement is needed for comprehensive reporting.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The authors present a training-free way to achieve better polyp segmentation, and demonstrate strong results across the board by better managing specularity and priors we know about polyps.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper could be improved for readability; I had to read it over multiple times to understand some concepts. Long-term viability: The paper is addressing binary mask generation for use as input to SAM2.This causes ‘information loss’ in a way since we are only able to feed in binary mask pixels. This adaptation is necessary since the mask input is an ‘API’ SAM2 provides, rather than addressing the problem in a clean way (ie. learning a prototype feature embedder, and feeding that into SAM). The new SAMv3 seems to address this issue directly, by enabling exemplar prompting, so I am wary of the long-term applicability of bespoke designs like the prompt mask estimation in this paper if the piece they depend on (SAM2->SAM3) could solve the underlying problem. This method does not carry to other non-polyp segmentation, since it uses multiple known priors about polyps (ie. roundness). This point does not affect my review, since the authors note this is a method for polyp segmentation, but it would be interesting to think about how these filters would work for other types of segmentation. Minor changes: “To enhance spatial consistency and reduce noise, we apply N iterations of a self-diffusion mechanism[11], updating Hinit by Hinit = Hinit · (fq · fq⊤)k.” This is not diffusion, and diffusion is not mentioned in [11]. This is iterative refinement. Please clarify, and provide more details here. Clean up and simplify the math wherever possible, at points the paper can be hard to read when reading it for the first time. Some ways to do so: list dimensions of each variable; remove terms if only used once; provide human-readable definitions for all important variables when using them. Fig.1: Letters (a,b) used for multiple purposes: both for left/right and for sub-images of pixel regions. Please use letters and numbers or some other mix to disambiguate. Fig 2.I recommend to emphasize the SLIC superpixels as their boundaries in the inset (after SLIC) are hard to see. R_k estimates cycle consistency of sorts. I would select a more clear term here than reverse purity factor. Please refer to work in point matching, since this is a common concept there. ReLUs (Why are ReLus being used?) C_k still has contrast even if the difference is negative. Please explain this selection, and why a non-linearity is chosen. “Intrinsic Reliability (Contrast Factor) and Query-specific Relevance (Reverse Purity Factor)” Please select a single term, and remove the parentheticals terms for your Contrast Factor (a) and Reverse Purity Factor (ie. cycle-consistency) (b); otherwise it requires the reader to juggle too many terms at once. Alternatively, rather than using parenthetical terms, define each of (a,b) in clear, easy-to-understand language.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive comments. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the importance of training-free one-shot medical segmentation, the clarity of our motivation, and the effectiveness of our ablation studies. We address the major concerns below. 1)@R1 @R2: Generalization beyond polyp segmentation. Although motivated by polyp segmentation, RPG-SAM’s core modules (reliability-weighted prototype mining, background suppression, adaptive thresholding, and iterative SAM refinement) are not limited to colonoscopy. On non-polyp CHAOS-CT, using 20 slices sequentially as one-shot supports with unchanged hyperparameters, RPG-SAM achieves Dice 77.63±5.74 and IoU 71.41±6.14, outperforming ProtoSAM (71.33±4.45 / 65.41±5.82; both p<0.001). This supports cross-domain generalization beyond polyp-specific morphology. 2)@R1: Marginal improvement, statistical significance, overengineering, and computational cost. We respectfully argue the gain is not marginal. Across Table 1 datasets, RPG-SAM averages 74.61±8.14 Dice and 67.87±7.77 IoU, compared with ProtoSAM’s 70.07±8.65 and 62.44±8.42 (+4.54 Dice and +5.43 IoU). Under a 30-support-slice Kvasir setting, RPG-SAM obtains 75.84±11.33 Dice and 68.90±11.08 IoU, versus ProtoSAM’s 59.21±13.37 and 50.59±13.64 (both p<0.001), showing robustness to support choice. RPG-SAM is also more efficient: 3.5 GB and 0.18 s per prediction versus 6.9 GB and 0.89 s for ProtoSAM. 3)@R2: Long-term viability in the context of SAMv3.Training-free methods remain valuable in medical imaging because they avoid task-specific optimization, large annotations, and retraining across datasets. Although learning a dedicated prototype embedder may be cleaner, it requires training and thus falls outside our training-free one-shot setting. We agree SAMv3 exemplar prompting is relevant; on Kvasir, SAMv3 reaches Dice 75.26 and IoU 69.77, still below RPG-SAM (85.65 and 78.65), suggesting that medical-specific reliability modeling and query-adaptive priors remain useful. 4)@R2: Clarification of “self-diffusion” We agree the term is misleading. This step is not generative diffusion but affinity-based iterative heatmap refinement. After Hinit is obtained, a query-query affinity matrix is computed from DINOv2 features, and Hinit is propagated over this graph so feature-similar pixels reinforce each other while isolated activations are suppressed. We will revise “self-diffusion mechanism” to “affinity-based iterative heatmap refinement”. 5) @R2: Why ReLU is used in the contrast and reverse-purity terms. ReLU acts as a reliability gate. For C_k, a negative value means the foreground prototype is closer to support background than foreground; keeping it would introduce unstable negative weights. For R_k, a negative value means reverse matches fall inside the support foreground less often than expected by the foreground area ratio, i.e., no better than chance. ReLU thus suppresses unreliable/non-consistent prototypes. 5)@R1 @R2: Readability, variables, figures, and minor changes. We will simplify notation, reduce variables, list key tensor dimensions, clarify Fig. 1 and Fig. 2, and use clearer terminology. 6)@R3: Detection and classification under clinical uncertainty. Our work focuses on training-free one-shot binary segmentation to reduce annotation dependence. It’s an important task, as also pursued by recent works such as OPSAM [11] . The reviewer’s suggestion on image quality, bowel preparation, polyp type, morphology, and size is highly valuable, and we will consider these factors in future stratified analyses and joint detection-segmentation-classification workflows.

title: S2DLight: Single Step Diffusion Network via Degradation-Aware Adaptation for Surgical Endoscopic Image Low-Light Enhancement
reviewer_1_strengths: The core strength of S2DLight lies in its systematic adaptation of large-scale pre-trained T2I diffusion models (Stable Diffusion) for surgical endoscopic enhancement. It ingeniously addresses the clinical bottleneck of slow inference through single-step reformulation, while integrating degradation-aware adaptation and semantic alignment to bridge the domain gap between medical and natural imagery. This framework provides a practical and efficient solution for deploying diffusion models within real-time surgical workflows.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The manuscript does not explicitly explain the rationale for why using a trained degradation estimation network is more effective at capturing low-light characteristics. 2.Regarding the training of the Degradation Estimation Network, the paper utilizes two patches from the same low-light image as positive pairs and patches from other images as negative samples for contrastive training. However, there is no explanation justifying this specific approach. What is the underlying rationale for this contrastive learning method? What specific problem is it intended to address, and how or why does this training enable the model to resolve such issues? 3.The single-step diffusion mentioned in the paper appears to resemble the DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) algorithm. Could the authors clarify the distinctions between the proposed method and DDIM, as well as its specific advantages?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is very well written, featuring a clearly explained methodology, excellent visualizations of the processing pipeline, and thorough qualitative evaluations and comparisons. The method addresses a real-world problem with well-posed motivation, the ablation study effectively justifies the pipeline’s design choices, and the authors commendably retrain a non-surgical LLIE method to ensure a fair comparison.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the quantitative results show a significant improvement over SOTA, the qualitative evaluation doesn’t really show differences or improvements over existing methods, such as LighTDiff or DiffLL, raising the question whether the additional computational costs and longer inference time are justified for the visual quality improvements. Reusing a pre-trained diffusion model but adapting it for single-pass inference raises the question of why a simpler, inherently non-diffusion-based approach was not used instead. Additionally, while the ablation study shows that Latent Structural Augmentation successfully bypasses the need for iterative refinement and improves performance, the paper does not demonstrate the performance difference between using standard diffusion refinement versus relying solely on this augmentation.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper addresses surgical endoscopic low-light image enhancement, a task with clear clinical relevance, by proposing S2DLight, a single-step diffusion framework. The overall framework is well designed and clearly problem-driven, and it effectively tackles several key challenges in adapting pretrained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models to the medical domain, including domain discrepancy, inference efficiency, and semantic-conditioning inconsistency. The comparative experiments and ablation studies on public datasets are sufficiently thorough and provide solid evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed method. Particularly commendable is the Single-Step Reformulation, which significantly reduces inference cost while largely preserving enhancement quality, making the method not only technically interesting but also promising for practical applications.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Although the paper reports strong quantitative results on the relevant datasets, it still has several limitations. First, the method is evaluated only on EndoVis17/18 and has not been validated in real clinical low-light scenarios. Second, no downstream tasks are included, which makes the clinical applicability of the method less convincing.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and insightful comments. We appreciate their recognition of the relevance, motivation, and experimental quality of S2DLight. The comments are valuable for improving the clarity of our manuscript. For clarity, W denotes weakness items and C denotes optional comments. [Common questions] [R1-W3, R2-W2/C1] Motivation for diffusion and difference from DDIM R: Our goal is not iterative sampling, but transferring pretrained Stable Diffusion priors to surgical LLIE, where medical data are limited. S2DLight differs from DDIM. DDIM follows a scheduled reverse trajectory. In contrast, S2DLight treats the encoded low-light latent as a degraded state at a fixed timestep and restores it in one forward pass. It neither starts from Gaussian noise nor recursively denoises the latent. Thus, S2DLight is a single-step latent restoration framework using SD priors, not a DDIM sampler. [R1-W1/W2, R2-C3] DENet and contrastive degradation learning R: DENet provides image-specific degradation guidance. Low-light degradation varies across frames due to illumination, exposure, noise, and tissue appearance; thus a fixed embedding cannot adapt to different degradation severity. In contrastive learning, patches from the same low-light image are positives because they share similar degradation, while patches from different images are negatives because their degradation statistics usually differ. This encourages degradation-related cues and suppresses local anatomy-specific information. Removing DENet or using fixed embedding would reduce the model to a generic prompt-conditioned enhancer. [R2-C2, R3-W1/W2] Synthetic degradation, clinical validation, and downstream tasks R: We agree that real clinical low-light data and downstream evaluation would further strengthen the evidence. However, paired real low-light/normal-light surgical data are difficult to obtain, since collecting well-aligned pairs under different illumination settings in real procedures is challenging. Thus, synthetic paired protocols are commonly used in surgical LLIE for training and fair comparison. We will state this limitation, avoid over-claiming clinical deployment, and discuss real-data collection, unpaired/semi-supervised adaptation, and downstream tasks as future work. [Reviewer-specific questions] [R1] Modules insufficiently explained R: We appreciate this comment and will better explain the modules: DENet provides image-specific degradation conditioning; contrastive learning separates degradation cues from anatomy; Single-Step Reformulation transfers SD priors without iterative sampling; and Latent Structural Augmentation compensates for reduced progressive refinement. [R2-W3] Standard diffusion refinement vs proposed single-step design R: The submitted manuscript includes 1/4/50-step comparisons, directly evaluating iterative refinement against our single-step design. Results show that S2DLight achieves better overall accuracy with much lower inference cost. This suggests that directly restoring the encoded low-light latent is more effective for surgical LLIE than repeated diffusion refinement, which may cause over-refinement or distribution drift. [R2-W1] Limited qualitative improvement R: We understand this concern. Differences between strong LLIE methods can be hard to observe due to limited figure size and fine endoscopic structures. We will add enlarged local regions. The consistent gains in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS further support improved fidelity, structure preservation, and perceptual quality. [R3-W2] Lack of downstream task evaluation R: We agree that downstream tasks such as segmentation or instrument recognition would provide additional clinical evidence. This work focuses on surgical LLIE, and our experiments evaluate paired enhancement quality, efficiency, and component effectiveness. We will avoid over-claiming clinical deployment and include downstream validation as future work.

The reviewers noted the promising performance but raised several important limitations. First, the methodological motivation remains unclear, particularly the rationale for the degradation estimation network, the contrastive learning design, and the distinction between the proposed single step formulation and existing DDIM style diffusion methods. Second, there is a disconnect between the strong quantitative gains and the qualitative examples, making it unclear whether the improvements translate into visibly meaningful enhancement or justify the computational complexity of a large diffusion backbone. Third, the experimental validation is limited to synthetic low light degradation on EndoVis17 and EndoVis18, without evaluation on real clinical low light scenarios or downstream surgical tasks, which weakens the practical and clinical claims. Decision is rebuttal. | After rebuttal, I recommend accept decision. The reviewers agree that the paper addresses a relevant surgical image enhancement problem with strong quantitative results, fair comparisons, and useful ablation studies. The main concerns relate to novelty, interpretability of individual modules, qualitative improvement over existing LLIE methods, and limited clinical/downstream validation. The rebuttal provides reasonable clarification of the distinction from DDIM, the motivation for transferring Stable Diffusion priors rather than using iterative sampling, and the role of DENet and contrastive degradation learning. While the lack of real clinical low-light validation and downstream task evaluation remains as limitations, these issues are adequately acknowledged and do not outweigh the methodological contribution and experimental evidence. As a result, the decision is accept. Having carefully looked at the reviews, the rebuttal and the paper, I feel that this is the most borderline case I have seen so far. Reviewers rightfully point out the lack of thorough clinical evaluation, but also see the technical merit. I would give this paper the benefit of the doubt. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): After the rebuttal, R1 maintained a Reject recommendation, R3 maintained an Accept recommendation, while R2, who initially provided a Weak Accept recommendation, did not provide an updated review. As stated in the rebuttal, the proposed framework neither starts from Gaussian noise nor recursively denoises latent representations, but instead operates as a single-step latent restoration framework using Stable Diffusion priors. This raises the question of whether a simpler denoising autoencoder, initialized with pretrained Stable Diffusion components, could achieve similar performance with a more straightforward design and justification. Considering these concerns, the paper is not recommended for acceptance. The authors are encouraged to address the reviewers’ comments when revising the paper for submission elsewhere.

title: S3H-Net: Injecting Hybrid Semantic-Spatial Guidance via Superpixel Hypergraphs for Medical Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors effectively integrate multiple concepts and improvements to address several key challenges: (1) the complex geometry of target structures and their blurred boundaries, (2) the limitation of fixed patch-based nodes, which inherently ignore object boundaries, and (3) the restriction of global reasoning to bottlenecks or skip connections. To tackle these issues, they propose a set of complementary enhancements. Specifically, the architecture employs a dual-encoder design, where a CNN captures local features while a hypergraph encoder models global, high-order relationships. For node construction, the method leverages a boundary-aware and differentiable superpixel algorithm, enabling better alignment with object boundaries. Furthermore, the authors introduce an injection module to effectively fuse features from the two encoders. The authors also provide a link to the code.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors do not report the model complexity in terms of the number of parameters or FLOPs. This is particularly important given that the architecture employs two encoders, one of which is a hypergraph module that is typically computationally expensive.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The boundary-aware SLIC is the most original contribution of the paper. Formulating the edge probability as a barrier integral (Eq. 1–2) yields an elegant and fully differentiable design that enforces strict boundary adherence at the node construction stage. (2) The hybrid hypergraph construction, which combines FCM-based semantic hyperedges with dilated spatial hyperedges, is well-motivated and reasonable, albeit somewhat incremental relative to prior hypergraph designs. (3) Comprehensive experiments across five medical imaging modalities demonstrate that S³H-Net consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with statistical significance testing further supporting the reliability of the improvements.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1)While the proposed framework demonstrates a certain degree of novelty as a whole, each of its major components is either an existing method or a straightforward extension thereof. In the superpixel module, although the introduction of boundary constraints via a composite-trapezoidal approximation of an edge-aware line-integral barrier shows some innovation, the overall architecture still follows the SSN framework. In the hypergraph reasoning module, the construction strategy is essentially a combination of two existing approaches (FCM-based semantic edges and dilated-window spatial edges). Similarly, the CCSI module closely resembles channel-wise co-attention, which has already been explored in existing works such as DuSFE[1], MA-Neck[2]. [1] “DuSFE: Dual-channel squeeze-fusion-excitation co-attention for cross-modality registration of cardiac SPECT and CT.” Medical image analysis 88 (2023): 102840.[2] “MA-Neck: Mutual attention-based feature enhancement for lightweight object detection.” Pattern Recognition (2025): 112254. 2) The choice of hyperparameters in the implementation section warrants further justification. In particular, the values λ_xy = 0.17 (SLIC compactness) and λ_b=0.5 (boundary sensitivity) are stated to be “set empirically” but without supporting evidence. It is unclear whether these values were determined through grid search, ablation studies, or simply adopted from prior work. A sensitivity analysis would strengthen the reproducibility of the method and help readers understand the robustness of performance to these settings. Relatedly, the number of sampled points K used in the trapezoidal approximation of the barrier integral (Eq. 2) is never specified. 3) The experiments section lacks a sensitivity analysis for the scale factor λ in the hybrid incidence matrix H=[H_sem||λ*H_spa]. Although the authors report λ=5 as an empirical choice, no evidence is provided to justify this value, and it is unclear how sensitive the model is to this balance between semantic and spatial hyperedges. 4) The paper would benefit from visualizations of the generated superpixels and the constructed hypergraphs overlayed on medical images. Such qualitative evidence is needed to substantiate the motivation presented in Fig. 1 that superpixels of anatomical boundaries are more faithfully than grid patches, and that the learned hyperedges capture meaningful high-order semantic correlations. 5) The overall presentation of the manuscript requires significant refinement. The writing style feels somewhat non-standard and repetitive, characterized by an over-reliance on “We”-led sentences. The authors are encouraged to revise the manuscript to achieve more varied sentence structures and to adopt more precise academic terminology. On the of Page 5 “Hypergraph Construction” reads: “…we employ the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm inspired by [9]…”. References should not be used as grammatical components of the sentence. Phrasings such as “…in [1]…” or “Reference [1] states…” are not acceptable. The authors should rephrase such sentences and ensure proper reference formatting throughout the manuscript. A careful pass for English constructions, grammatical errors, and formatting inconsistencies is strongly recommended to improve overall presentation quality.

author_feedback: We sincerely appreciate the constructive suggestions from reviewers. 1.Novelty (meta-reviewer, R2, R3) We agree that patch representations are effective, and we did not intend to claim that patches are generally problematic. Our concern is specific to graph/hypergraph reasoning: fixed patches crossing lesion/background boundaries may become mixed atomic vertices and affect high-order aggregation. We also agree that superpixels are not semantic labels, and will replace overstatements such as “semantic purity”, “strict alignment”, and “eliminate semantic ambiguity” with more precise claims: boundary-aware superpixels encourage locally homogeneous, boundary-adaptive primitives and reduce, rather than eliminate, boundary-crossing feature mixing. S3H-Net is not a simple aggregation of independent modules, but a task-driven formulation of superpixel-based hypergraph reasoning: boundary-aware differentiable SLIC provides adaptive vertices, HSSH models semantic-spatial high-order relations, and CCSI injects the reasoned topology back into pixel-level CNN features. The submitted ablation already includes a patch-node vs. superpixel-node comparison: without superpixels, HSSH uses fixed 8×8 grid patches as basic units. Replacing these patch nodes with superpixel nodes improves ETIS/USG DSC from 93.6/85.9 to 94.8/87.0 before CCSI is introduced, and the full model further improves to 95.4/87.5.DuSFE and MA-Neck are related in channel-wise recalibration, but CCSI targets a different problem: hypergraph-to-pixel semantic injection for medical segmentation. 2.Complexity (R1, R3) Under the submitted setting (256×256 input, NVIDIA 2080Ti), S3H-Net has 54.09M parameters and 10.33G FLOPs, with 1106.0 MB peak GPU memory and 91.17 ms/item inference time. The differentiable SLIC module itself contributes only 0.02G FLOPs and 2.91 ms/item, indicating that superpixel construction is not the main computational bottleneck. 3.Hyperparameter clarification (R2) We acknowledge that λxy, λb, and λ were insufficiently justified. λxy and λb control compactness and boundary sensitivity in differentiable SLIC and were selected from a reasonable grid based on validation behavior and qualitative superpixel stability. The scale λ in H=[Hsem||λHspa] balances semantic hyperedges and spatial priors: too small λ weakens local continuity, while too large λ makes the hypergraph overly local. We used λ=5 as a moderate balancing value. K in Eq. (2) is a numerical integration setting rather than a model hyperparameter; we set K=8, corresponding to 9 sampled locations including endpoints. 4.Practical significance and robustness (R3) Although the DSC gain is modest on saturated datasets such as DSB2018, the improvement is not merely numerical: S3H-Net consistently improves boundary-sensitive HD95 across modalities and achieves best or competitive overall performance. The submitted ablations show progressive gains from each component, and the DiffSLIC overhead is small (0.02G FLOPs, 2.91 ms/item), suggesting a practical accuracy/boundary benefit with limited extra cost. 5.Qualitative evidence for superpixels (R2) We clarify that the superpixel visualization in Fig. 1 Right bottom is an actual DiffSLIC output with 64 superpixels, not a manual illustration, and thus qualitatively supports boundary-adaptive node construction. We agree that hyperedge overlays would improve interpretability, but they would introduce new visual evidence beyond the submitted manuscript; therefore, we focus on clarifying submitted results. 6.Statistical reporting (R3) Table 1 already reports t-test p-values, and we will clarify the test protocol, paired unit, and sample size. 7.Writing (R2) We will also revise repetitive “We”-led constructions, improve terminology precision, and correct citation style; e.g., “we employ FCM inspired by [9]” will be revised to “Following prior hypergraph construction using fuzzy clustering [9], semantic hyperedges are formed by FCM.”
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The main weakness is limited novelty. The method is largely a combination of existing components: SLIC/superpixel node construction, hypergraph reasoning, semantic/spatial hyperedge construction, and channel-wise attention-like feature fusion. This concern is also raised by Reviewer #2 and Reviewer #3. The paper makes superpixels the central design choice, but this is not sufficiently convincing. Superpixels are an old and extensively studied representation. In 2026, using SLIC-style superpixels as a core DL/AI pipeline component requires much stronger justification than currently provided. There is generally nothing wrong with patch-based representations in modern vision systems. Patches are simple, stable, learnable, and widely successful. The paper’s argument that patches inherently cause semantic contamination is overstated. Superpixels may introduce additional instability. They rely on a grouping stage before the main learning system, and this stage can introduce errors, noise, and artifacts. If superpixels incorrectly merge lesion/background regions or fragment meaningful structures, the downstream hypergraph reasoning is built on corrupted nodes. The claims of “semantic purity,” “strict boundary adherence,” and elimination of semantic ambiguity are too strong. Superpixels are low-level perceptual regions, not semantic units. A Sobel-based edge/barrier term cannot guarantee anatomical boundary alignment, especially in noisy, low-contrast, or artifact-heavy medical images. The experiments do not adequately isolate the effect of superpixels. A controlled patch-node vs. superpixel-node comparison is necessary, with the hypergraph module and model capacity kept comparable. The paper compares only one superpixel construction choice. Since many superpixel algorithms exist and have different properties, the authors should compare SLIC with other superpixel methods or learned/differentiable superpixel approaches. Without this, it is unclear whether the gain comes from the proposed architecture, the chosen SLIC variant, or parameter tuning. Reviewer #2 points out that important hyperparameters are not justified, including SLIC compactness, boundary sensitivity, the balance factor between semantic and spatial hyperedges, and the sampled points used in the barrier integral. Sensitivity analysis is needed. Reviewer #1 and Reviewer #3 both raise the missing complexity analysis. This is a serious issue because the method adds a dual-encoder design, hypergraph computation, superpixel construction, and injection modules. Parameters, FLOPs, memory usage, inference time, and superpixel construction overhead should be reported. Reviewer #3 also notes that the gains over strong baselines are not always large. Given the extra complexity, the authors need to show that the improvement is practically meaningful, not just numerically higher. The statistical evidence is incomplete. The paper should report repeated runs or cross-validation results with mean ± standard deviation, and clearly explain the statistical test, paired unit, sample size, and correction for multiple comparisons. The related work is incomplete. The authors should discuss prior work on SLIC, differentiable superpixels/SSN, superpixel-based CNN/GCN/Transformer models, Vision GNN, Vision HGNN, AHGNN, G-CASCADE, and existing co-attention/channel-fusion modules such as those mentioned by Reviewer #2. The presentation should remove overclaiming. Terms such as “semantic purity,” “strict alignment,” and “eliminate semantic ambiguity” are not supported by the current evidence. The manuscript should use more precise and less absolute wording. Overall, the paper has major issues in novelty, methodological justification, and experimental completeness. The rebuttal should specifically address whether superpixels are truly necessary, whether they are more reliable than patches, whether the added complexity is justified, and whether the reported gains are robust under stronger ablations and fair complexity-aware comparisons. | The paper presents a coherent and empirically strong medical image segmentation framework that integrates boundary-aware superpixel node construction, semantic-spatial hypergraph reasoning, and semantic injection. While the methodological novelty is moderate and several claims are overstated, the method is relevant, technically reasonable, and shows consistent improvements across multiple datasets and baselines. The rebuttal addresses key concerns regarding patch-vs-superpixel comparison, computational overhead, hyperparameter clarification, and overclaiming. Remaining issues should be handled in camera-ready revision, including toned-down claims, clearer statistical reporting, complexity analysis, limitations, and better explanation of the superpixel design. The authors should address the following points in the camera-ready version: 1.Remove or soften “semantic purity,” “strict alignment,” and “eliminate semantic ambiguity.” 2.Add a complexity table: params, FLOPs, memory, inference time, and SLIC overhead. 3.Clearly label the patch-node vs. superpixel-node ablation in Table 2.4.Specify missing hyperparameters, especially barrier integral sampling K. 5.Add a limitation paragraph about superpixel failure cases and limited novelty. 6.Improve related work on SSN/differentiable superpixels, superpixel-based deep models, Vision GNN/HGNN, AHGNN/G-CASCADE, and channel/co-attention fusion. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies several concerns, including the patch-node versus superpixel-node comparison and computational overhead, but the core novelty remains limited because the method largely combines superpixels, hypergraph reasoning, and channel-style feature injection. Given the extra complexity and remaining concerns about superpixel reliability, hyperparameter sensitivity, and modest gains over strong baselines, the current evidence is not sufficient to establish a clear methodological advantage. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed reviews, mainly due to concerns about novelty, superpixel justification, and added complexity. After considering the rebuttal and updated reviews, I recommend acceptance. The paper presents a coherent superpixel-hypergraph segmentation framework, and its main strength lies in using boundary-aware superpixel nodes to support high-order semantic-spatial reasoning. The experiments cover five medical imaging modalities, and the ablation results, including the patch-node versus superpixel-node comparison, provide reasonable evidence that the proposed design is effective. The rebuttal addresses several important concerns by clarifying the role of superpixels, reporting complexity and inference cost, explaining key hyperparameters, and softening several over-strong claims. For the camera-ready version, the authors should incorporate these clarifications, avoid absolute wording such as “semantic purity” or “strict alignment,” report the complexity metrics, clarify the statistical testing protocol, and improve the related work and writing quality.

title: SCISSR: Scribble-Conditioned Interactive Surgical Segmentation and Refinement
reviewer_1_strengths: The idea of using scribble prompts for interactive segmentation is intuitive and practically relevant, especially for surgical scenarios with complex structures. The proposed framework is well designed and modular, easy to implement and extend to other prompt-based segmentation models. The method interacts with the backbone only through standard embedding interfaces, which improves generalizability and potential reuse across models such as SAM 3. The experimental results are strong and consistent across both in-distribution (EndoVis 2018) and out-of-distribution (CholecSeg8k) datasets, demonstrating good generalization. The paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The level of novelty is somewhat limited. While the use of scribble-based interaction is well motivated, similar ideas have been explored in prior work such as ScribblePrompt. The paper could benefit from more analysis of limitations and challenging scenarios, such as performance under sparse or imperfect scribbles.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents a solid idea that is motivated by the limitation of existing prompting types in SAM models, especially in surgical data where objects are small and occluded. The paper writing was clear and compelling and the flow of ideas was smooth. SCISSR is clean and easy to reproduce, making it a potential add-on to SAM-like architectures rather than a complete redesign. The experiments section is strong and comprehensive. The paper includes multiple baselines and prompt types. The gains are consistent in later refinement rounds and for challenging object classes. The inclusion of out-of-distribution evaluation further strengthens the claims regarding generalization. Overall, the empirical results show that scribble prompts provide richer spatial information than clicks.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the paper claims that SCISSR is general for all segment anything models (SAM1-3), this claim was not empirically validated. The current evaluation is limited to SAM 2, even a minimal experiment or partial validation would be enough to show that. The reliance on synthetic scribbles generated from ground-truth masks. Although the generation strategy attempts to mimic human annotations, it may introduce bias and may not fully capture the variability of real user interactions. This raises concerns about how well the method would perform in real annotation cases. Validation with human-generated scribbles especially from clinical experts would significantly strengthen the paper. The evaluation is only focused on endoscopic surgical datasets. reviewer_3_strengths: S1.Well-motivated problem and prompt modality. The motivation for using scribble prompts in surgical scene segmentation is clearly articulated and convincing. The authors make a compelling argument that points are too sparse and bounding boxes too coarse for targets with irregular morphology (thin instruments, curved vessels), while scribbles offer a natural middle ground with dense spatial coverage. Figure 1 effectively illustrates this point. S2.Clean and principled architectural design. The dual-track scribble pathway is an elegant design choice. Track 1 preserves the full interaction history via accumulated scribbles as dense prompt embeddings, while Track 2 focuses the model’s attention on newly corrected regions through SGF. The zero-initialization of both the LoRA adapters and the SGF scaling factor α ensures that the pretrained SAM 2 capabilities are preserved at the start of training, which is a thoughtful design decision. S3.Strong quantitative results and OOD generalization. The results are compelling: 95.41% Dice on EndoVis 2018 (R4) and 96.30% Dice on CholecSeg8k (R2) without any CholecSeg8k training data. The OOD generalization is particularly noteworthy—exceeding bounding box baselines by over 14 percentage points on CholecSeg8k demonstrates robustness. S4.Thorough convergence efficiency analysis. Table 2 provides a valuable analysis of convergence behavior across different Dice thresholds, showing that SCISSR reaches acceptable quality faster and with higher success rates than point-based baselines. The cumulative percentage breakdown per round is informative. S5.Informative ablation study. The component ablation (Table 3) clearly demonstrates the individual contributions of SGF and Memory. The scribble generation strategy comparison across four types (contour, centerline, wave, adaptive) provides useful practical guidance. The qualitative visualization in Figure 4 showing SGF-induced query modifications and memory-induced updates is helpful for understanding the mechanism. S6.Practical and lightweight design. Building on SAM 2 Tiny with only lightweight additions (Scribble Encoder, SGF, LoRA adapters) while keeping the image encoder frozen is practical. Training on a single RTX 4090 in 10 epochs demonstrates accessibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1.No validation of claimed architecture transferability to SAM 3.The paper repeatedly claims that the framework is “architecture-agnostic” and transferable to SAM 3 (Abstract, Section 1, Section 4). However, this claim is never experimentally validated. SAM 3 is only used as a point/box baseline, not as a backbone for SCISSR. Since this is listed as a core contribution (“architecture-agnostic design… making the approach transferable to architectures such as SAM 3”), the lack of experimental evidence significantly weakens this claim. Either the authors should demonstrate SCISSR on SAM 3 or substantially tone down this contribution claim. W2.Lack of real user study with human-drawn scribbles. All experiments rely on synthetically generated scribbles from ground-truth masks. While the authors add “mild spatial perturbations to mimic freehand variability,” synthetic scribbles may not faithfully represent the noise, inconsistency, and variability of real human annotations. This is particularly relevant for a method whose core selling point is the naturalness and practicality of scribble interaction. A user study, even a small-scale one, would significantly strengthen the practical claims. The authors acknowledge this in the future work section but it remains a notable gap. W3.Potentially unfair comparison with point-based baselines. The automated evaluation protocol generates corrective scribbles from ground-truth error regions, which inherently provides dense spatial information along boundaries and shapes. Point-click baselines, by contrast, receive only centroids of error-region connected components. While the authors partially address this by noting that even 10pt/ch degrades with more rounds, the information asymmetry between scribble and point prompts is substantial. A fairer comparison might normalize by annotation effort (e.g., time or number of annotated pixels) rather than by interaction rounds.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the Area Chair for their constructive feedback and address the major concerns below. Response to R1.W1: The novelty may be limited given prior work such as ScribblePrompt. SCISSR differs from ScribblePrompt in two key aspects. First, our Scribble Encoder treats scribbles as dense spatial embeddings rather than converting each scribbled pixel into a click as in ScribblePrompt-SAM. This preserves the continuous shape and boundary information of the scribble as a whole. Second, SCISSR introduces a dual-track pathway with Spatial Gated Fusion and memory-driven iterative refinement, repurposing SAM 2’s temporal memory for multi-round correction. ScribblePrompt does not incorporate such a memory mechanism. As shown in Table 3, adding SGF improves mDice from 88.16 to 90.53 at R2, and adding Memory further improves it to 93.49, supporting the effectiveness of these SCISSR-specific components. Response to R2.W1, R3.W1: Claims of transferability to other SAM variants are unsupported. We agree that our current wording overstates the empirical scope of this claim. To clarify our intended claim: SCISSR’s added modules (Scribble Encoder, SGF, and LoRA adapters) communicate with the backbone exclusively through standard embedding interfaces. This design is interface-compatible with SAM-like architectures. However, interface compatibility alone does not guarantee empirical transferability. In particular, SGF and memory injection operate on spatial image tokens, and backbones with different token geometry or spatial resolution may require further adaptation. We will revise the manuscript to replace the broad “transferable to SAM 3” wording with a more precise statement reflecting interface-level portability as a design principle, not an empirically validated property. Empirical validation on SAM 3 is outside the scope of the submitted manuscript. Response to R1.W2, R2.W2, R3.W2: Real human-drawn scribbles and imperfect scribble tests are absent. We agree that real human-drawn scribbles would be valuable for fully assessing clinical usability. Since large-scale real annotations are unavailable, synthetic scribbles enable controlled, reproducible evaluation across prompt types and baselines. Sec. 2.7 reduces idealization by using four geometry-aware scribble types with mild spatial perturbations to mimic imperfect freehand input. Preliminary feedback from domain experts during internal deployment preparation suggests that the scribble interaction is intuitive. However, this feedback is not used as formal evidence in the submitted evaluation; the current evidence remains the controlled synthetic-scribble benchmark. Response to R3.W3: The comparison with point-based baselines may be unfair. We acknowledge that scribbles and clicks carry different spatial information. Our comparison targets practical interaction paradigms under the same fixed-round correction protocol, not equal information per prompt. To avoid underestimating click prompts, we include both 1pt/CC and 10pt/ch baselines. Table 1 and Sec. 3.4 show that increasing click density does not consistently improve multi-round refinement. This is consistent with our interpretation that isolated clicks provide less structured shape/boundary information than scribbles. Preliminary expert feedback from ongoing deployment testing suggests that scribble-based correction is convenient in practice, but no expert feedback or time-based measurement is used as evidence for the submitted comparison. Rigorous time-effort evaluation remains future work. Response to R2.W3: Generalization beyond endoscopic datasets is not validated. SCISSR targets interactive surgical scene segmentation. Our submitted evaluation uses EndoVis 2018 and CholecSeg8k, which support cross-dataset and cross-procedure generalization within endoscopic/laparoscopic surgical scenes. Broader OOD validation is ongoing, and we will clarify this scope.
