author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We address each concern below. Reviewer 1: Q1&3: Domain Gap and Sim-to-Real Feasibility R1&3: We acknowledge the visual gap between simulation and clinical settings. However: 1)Prior work[1] has demonstrated successful sim-to-real transfer for this setup, confirming the practical relevance of our findings. Due to the difficulty of obtaining consistent real-world surgical data, simulation platforms such as SurRoL are increasingly serving as a key infrastructure for benchmarking surgical models. 2) Our simulation replicates real-world 7-DOF robotic kinematics and task success criteria, which are the decisive factors for task performance. 3) The visual gap can be effectively mitigated via style transfer. [1] Long Y, et al. Surgical embodied intelligence for generalized task autonomy in laparoscopic robot-assisted surgery. Science Robotics, 2025.Q2: Framework Flexibility and Data Diversity R2: SurgVLA-Bench covers atomic operations (grasp, place, reach) that form the basis of most surgical procedures. The framework’s modular design allows researchers to easily integrate new tasks by replacing anatomical models or adjusting trajectories. This capability to efficiently generate diverse datasets addresses the dual evaluation needs of assessing both task-specific proficiency and cross-scenario generalization. Q4: Realism of Deformable Tissue R4: We acknowledge certain surgical tasks, such as retraction and dissection, inherently require realistic tissue deformation. However, our current tasks can be completed without tissue deformation, so the evaluation remains valid. Realistic modeling of tissue deformation for complex maneuvers is a key focus of our future work. Reviewer 2: Q1: Platform Innovation and Future Work R1: Our work focuses on benchmarking rather than VLA architectural innovation. Our core contributions are: 1) We provide the first open-source (after acceptance), reproducible, multi-level evaluation platform for surgical VLA models, establishing a standardized pipeline that the community currently lacks. 2) The multi-layered task design systematically uncovers capability bottlenecks that single-task setups cannot reveal, providing clear directions for future surgical VLA research. Based on these contributions, we will expand the framework with more diverse tasks and multi-dimensional metrics to offer a comprehensive baseline for comparison. Reviewer 4: Q1: Lack of Zero-shot Baseline R1: Initial zero-shot tests yielded 0% success across all tasks, so we did not report them as a separate baseline. The reasons are: 1)General VLAs lack exposure to surgical instruments and anatomy. 2)Surgical kinematics differ from industrial settings. Therefore, zero-shot evaluation is not necessary, and we performed domain-specific fine-tuning and then conducted comparison. A full explanation and analysis will be included in the final version. Q2: Inconsistency in SmolVLA Performance Reporting R2: The 0% success rate in Table 2 comes from a multi-task training setup where task interference occurs. The 82% success rate mentioned in the text is from a single-task training setup. This stark gap shows that lightweight models like SmolVLA suffer from severe interference during multi-task learning, highlighting the need for more robust multi-task architectures in surgical scenarios. Q3: Insufficient Explanation for Generalization Results R3: T2-1 is not a distractor-free environment; it is a multi-object scene where instruments such as needles act as deliberate distractors. The performance drop compared to distractor-free T1-1 is therefore expected. Architecturally, unlike models such as π0.5 that employ explicit vision-language alignment, OpenVLA fuses image and language embeddings directly within the LLM. This leads to biases in understanding similar language tokens and a tendency to overfit to the scene, impairing the model’s ability to handle multi-object scenarios.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): SurgVLA-Bench is a benchmark framework for surgical VLA models. While timely, this work is limited to simulation, with associated issues of sim-to-real transfer, tissue deformation, etc. Further lack of a zero-shot baseline, inconsistency in reporting, and the lack of clarity around generalization prevent acceptance. | The rebuttal clarifies many of the reviewers’ concerns (data diversity, tissue realism, zero-shot baselines, etc.) While R1 raises valid concerns about sim-to-real transfer not being validated within this work, the rebuttal points out that Surrol has been shown to have good sim-to-real transfer in prior work. Moreover, with the potential for future work to separate surgical perception from surgical decision control, as in self-driving, this work provides a valuable benchmark for surgical decision control, which is arguably the more critical component for surgical autonomy. R1 also characterizes the work as a limited extension from Surrol. Unfortunately, the authors have no opportunity to respond to this point, which was not raised in the initial review, but I believe they would argue for the value of hierarchical task decomposition specifically suited for VLA evaluation, whereas Surrol focuses on atomic tasks. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend acceptance. The paper presents SurgVLA-Bench, a timely benchmark for evaluating vision-language-action models in surgical robotics. Although the work is primarily a benchmark rather than a new VLA architecture, it addresses a clear gap in the surgical robotics community by providing hierarchical tasks, standardized datasets, and evaluation of representative VLA models. The rebuttal addressed the main technical concerns raised by the reviewers. In particular, the authors clarified the scope of the simulator-based benchmark, the relevance and limitations of sim-to-real transfer, the current exclusion of deformable tissue tasks, the zero-shot baseline behavior, and inconsistencies in the reported SmolVLA results. Reviewers #2 and #4 support acceptance after rebuttal. Reviewer #1 remains concerned about simulation realism and clinical transfer, which is a valid limitation, but I view this as acceptable for an early benchmark contribution rather than a fatal weakness. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend the paper for acceptance. Even though the technical novelty is limited, the proposed benchmark and evaluated baselines are suitable contributions.

title: SurgZSD: Zero-Shot Surgical Action Triplet Detection via Attribute Composition and Clinical Feasibility Inference
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.This paper addresses a significant and practical challenge in surgical scene understanding—the ability to generalize to unseen instruments, targets, and actions—which is of great importance for real-world applications in various surgical procedures. 2.Rather than performing direct classification, the method utilizes VLMs to extract structured attribute representations, thereby enabling compositional generalization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.To my knowledge, both the ITG-Trip and MCIT-IG methods pre-trained the object detection model Deformable DETR on Cholec80.In contrast, this paper fine-tunes Grounding DINO on the CholecTrack20 dataset. The authors did not conduct ablation experiments for Stage A, which raises doubts as to whether the model’s performance gains are primarily attributable to Stage A. 2.This method does not perform training or inference at the frame level, thereby neglecting the temporal dependencies that are crucial for understanding surgical actions—a factor that is critical for contextual inference in surgical procedures. 3.The proposed framework consists of decoupled components across multiple stages, which limits end-to-end optimization and hinders clinical deployment. 4.As shown in Figure 2, after Stage 2, the instrument has already obtained a unique predicted probability. Why is it necessary to perform a Top-K operation on the instrument in Stage 3?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) This paper formulates a novel and challenging problem by introducing a strict zero-shot paradigm to surgical scene understanding, where training and testing classes are completely disjoint. （2）The framework innovatively synergizes an open-set object detector with a VLM and an LLM to bridge the domain gap without requiring fully annotated fine-grained surgical data for novel classes.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The topic shares conceptual similarities with a recent ICLR submission, “Cognitive-Awakening Chain-of-Surgery for Compositional Zero-Shot Surgical Triplet Recognition.” Although that work focuses on triplet recognition rather than detection, the underlying compositional zero-shot motivation is highly related. The authors should cite and explicitly discuss the differences and relative advantages of their proposed framework compared to this work. (2) The framework currently infers actions based purely on spatial interactions within isolated frames. Since surgical actions are inherently continuous and dynamic, have the authors considered incorporating temporal information in VLMs to further enhance triplet detection accuracy? (3) To ensure strict reproducibility, the promised code release must guarantee that all dependencies, the exact structured prompt templates used for the VLM, and the fully generated Knowledge Base are open-sourced alongside clear, step-by-step documentation.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper is well presented and structured, stating clearly the focus on each component of the method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The VLM questionnaire for action and anatomy are not clearly stated in the paper. Fig 2 could be modified to show the questions for each of I,V,T. 2.A curious question is does 3 questions with 4 options each sufficient to represent all laparoscopic surgical tools? Any reference / proof to support this i.e., some kind of graph or visual representation showing the known surgical tools to mapping to the questions and options in one-on-one manner. This kind of representation would strengthen the completeness of the proposed method. 3.What data is the VLM pretrained on? Is it a general purpose VLM or surgically trained VLM? If it is general purpose VLM then, in the extended version of this work it would be better to show an ablation with different off the shelf VLMs such that the effectiveness of the framework is portrayed. 4.Does the knowledge base contain information generic to all surgeries and triplets? If it contains information related to the triplets in evaluation then the zero-shot concept applies only to detecting the instruments and the title need modifications accordingly. 5.Since Dino is one method, if and when an extended version of this work is taken up different zero-shot detection methods need to be considered for ablation.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for constructive comments and recognition of novelty and clinical relevance. Our responses are provided below. 1.Fairness and Stage A (R1, R3, AC). We understand the reviewer’s concern about fairness. The comparison with ITG-Trip and MCIT-IG is intended to show that a zero-shot-oriented framework can still retain reasonable capability under the closed-set setting. CholecTrack20 is derived from Cholec80 and provides instrument localization, making it a reasonable source for detector fine-tuning. Deformable DETR is a closed-set detector, whereas the zero-shot setting may contain unseen instruments, thus Grounding DINO is used as an open-vocabulary model. SurgZSD is detector-agnostic: any reliable open-set instrument detector can serve as Stage A. We agree that detector-level ablations would strengthen the analysis and will include them as future work. Stage A provides localization proposals, while the main methodological contribution lies in the MKAC and CFCJI modules. The ablation studies in the manuscript demonstrate the effectiveness of these two modules. 2.VLM attribute-query scheme (R3, AC). We apologize that Fig. 2 simplified the query design and caused misunderstanding. “3 questions with 4 options” is only a compact illustrative example, not the full attribute vocabulary. In our work, the attribute dimensions are fixed for interpretability, but the candidate options are expandable. Thus, the method does not assume that four options can cover all instruments. A new entity can be added by defining its attribute prototype in the attribute space, without additional visual samples. We will revise Fig. 2 and provide the prompts and attribute vocabularies. 3.Temporal information, optimization, and deployment (R1, R2). We agree temporal context is important, especially for verb recognition. This work focuses on frame-level zero-shot triplet detection, temporal information is complementary to the framework. A natural extension is to replace the frame-level VLM parser with a video-aware parser that can incorporate motion and temporal context. This will be considered as future work. SurgZSD is intentionally modular: the detector, VLM attribute parser, and feasibility inference layer can each be independently inspected and optimized. Although this sacrifices part of the end-to-end optimization capability, it improves the transparency required for clinical review. 4.Top-K operation in Stage C (R1). Although Stage B scores instrument candidates, the top-1 prediction is only used for the instrument detection comparison experiment. For complete triplet prediction, relying solely on the top-1 prediction may be unreliable, because unseen instruments can share similar attributes. Stage C is designed to avoid locally confident but clinically implausible combinations. Therefore, Top-K serves global triplet optimization, rather than redundant prediction. We will clarify this in the revision. 5.Knowledge base and VLM usage (R3). The knowledge base contains no triplet-level information, such as triplet labels or frequency statistics, avoiding data leakage. It is built separately for instruments, targets, and verbs using general medical prior knowledge and semantic attribute prototypes generated with GPT-5.2.The VLM reasoning module in Stage B and Stage C is Qwen3VL-Plus, a general purpose VLM without surgical-domain training or fine-tuning. Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We will evaluate different off-the-shelf VLMs and further explore fine-tuning domain-specific surgical VLMs in the extended version. 6.CoCoS Comparison (R2). First, CoCoS recognizes unseen combinations of seen components, whereas SurgZSD detects unseen instruments, targets, and verbs. Next, SurgZSD relies on medical attributes and clinical feasibility constraints, while CoCoS leverages temporal Glance-Gaze-Think reasoning. Thus, they are complementary. 7.Reproducibility (R2). Upon acceptance, we will immediately release the code.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): SurgZSD presents an approach to zero-shot surgical triplet detection combining open-set Grounding DINO with a Medical-Knowledge-Guided Attribute Composition module and a Clinical Feasibility Constraint. Two key issues require response before a final decision: (1) Fair-comparison concern - prior triplet-detection baselines (ITG-Trip, MCIT-IG) pretrain Deformable DETR on Cholec80 training data, while this work fine-tunes Grounding DINO on CholecTrack20 (2) Scope of the VLM attribute-query scheme — the 3-question/4-option protocol has not been validated to cover the full instrument space. The authors should address these issues thoroughly in the rebuttal. | After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarifies key points such as the detector setup, attribute-query scheme, and design choices, but does not fully resolve concerns about fair comparison, coverage of the attribute space, and lack of temporal modelling. Overall, the reviewers in general lean toward acceptance due to the novelty of the problem and approach, but evaluation limitations remain.

title: TEDi: Temporal Memory-Enhanced and Denoising Transformer for Surgical Instrument Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The results appear to be decently better than existing methods and the current state-of-the-art. 2.The memory bank and encoder are a good contribution. Exploring the different queries for the memory bank was very interesting. 3.Good comprehensive evaluation on both the EndoVis datasets, identifying key recent papers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The acronym TEDi for Temporal memory-Enhanced and Denoising transformer for surgical instrument segmentation is pushing it a little. I would suggest using a better acronym. 2.The video provided in the supplementary materials shows random switching for the tool classes multiple times, predicting it incorrectly. This should have been mentioned in the paper, as it is a severe limitation: the model should not change the tool class between frames when the tool is still clearly visible.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1.Well-motivated problem formulation. The paper clearly identifies and articulates a practical and important problem in surgical instrument segmentation: while query-based models achieve good localization, they suffer from severe category prediction errors and temporal inconsistency. The empirical analysis (Fig. 3) convincingly demonstrates the two failure modes — high-confidence misclassified queries and low-confidence correct queries — which directly motivate the proposed modules. S2.Efficient query-level memory design. Unlike prior video segmentation methods that store dense pixel-level features, the proposed query-level memory bank is compact (storing N×d embeddings per frame) and avoids redundancy. The mask-aware gating mechanism (Eq. 1–2) that fuses spatial mask information into the query embedding space is a reasonable design that preserves spatial context in a compact representation. S3.Principled temporal consistency denoising. The TCD module provides a principled mechanism for enforcing cross-frame semantic coherence. The use of Hungarian matching to establish identity-aligned correspondences between the temporal reference and current-frame queries, followed by residual denoising cross-attention, is methodologically sound. The periodic reset every T frames to prevent error accumulation is a practical design choice. S4.Comprehensive experimental evaluation. The paper provides evaluation on two standard benchmarks (EV17 and EV18) with three metrics and per-category IoU breakdowns. The ablation study (Table 2) systematically evaluates the contribution of each component and the sensitivity to hyperparameters K and T. The query visualization analysis (Fig. 3) offers an insightful and convincing way to validate the effectiveness of the proposed modules at the query level.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.Limited novelty of individual components. While the overall framework is reasonable, the individual components draw heavily from established techniques. Query-level memory banks have been explored in video object segmentation (XMem [7], RMem [29]). The Hungarian matching for temporal alignment is standard in tracking literature (e.g., TraSeTR [28]). The denoising cross-attention mechanism resembles DN-DETR (Li et al., “DN-DETR: Accelerate DETR Training by Introducing Query DeNoising,” CVPR 2022) and related denoising strategies for detection transformers. The paper does not sufficiently discuss or differentiate from these closely related works, particularly DN-DETR and its extensions, which should be cited and compared. W2.Missing detailed computational cost analysis. The paper reports parameter counts in Table 2 but does not report inference time, FLOPs, or memory consumption. Given that TEDi introduces a memory bank, Hungarian matching at each frame, and a multi-block denoising decoder, the computational overhead relative to the baseline is a critical concern for real-time surgical applications. The claim of being “efficient” (Section 4) is not substantiated. W3.Lack of temporal consistency metrics. The paper claims to improve “temporal stability” and “semantic coherence across frames,” yet only reports standard per-frame IoU metrics. No explicit temporal consistency metric (e.g., temporal consistency score, class flip rate, mismatch rate across adjacent frames) is reported. This is a significant gap between the claimed contribution and the evaluation protocol.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a relevant problem in surgical vision, namely improving temporal stability for query-based surgical instrument segmentation rather than treating frames independently. 2.The method is clearly structured, with two intuitive modules—memory search enhancement and temporal consistency denoising—that directly target category confusion and temporal inconsistency. 3.The experiments are reasonably comprehensive, including comparisons on two EndoVis benchmarks, ablations, and qualitative analyses of query behavior.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not sufficiently clarify what is fundamentally new beyond prior temporal surgical segmentation methods. The claimed gains seem to come from better temporal use of historical queries and denoising, but closely related motivations—using temporal context, improving consistency, and leveraging cross-frame information—have already been explored in the cited surgical literature. The paper would be stronger if it more explicitly distinguished its contribution from MATIS and LACOSTE at the formulation level, rather than mainly through performance improvements. 2.The paper also does not adequately discuss its trade-off relative to recent SAM2-style methods. SAM2-related approaches typically rely on prompts, which makes them less directly comparable as fully automatic category-level segmenters, but they offer stronger generalization beyond a fixed closed set of instrument classes. In contrast, TEDi is designed for predefined instrument categories on EndoVis, so its improvements are demonstrated only in a label-fixed setting, and its ability to generalize to unseen instruments or broader surgical scenes remains unclear. A stronger paper should explicitly discuss this limitation and clarify the scope in which TEDi should be preferred over promptable segmentation frameworks such as SAM2 or Surgical SAM2.3.The paper lacks an efficiency analysis, making the reported gains harder to interpret. Although TEDi reports better accuracy, the paper does not provide a clear comparison of parameter count, computational cost, inference speed, or memory overhead relative to the baseline and prior methods. Since TEDi introduces extra memory retrieval and temporal denoising components, it remains unclear whether the improvement comes from a better design or simply from a larger and more computationally expensive model. This is an important omission for surgical video applications, where efficiency is often highly relevant. 4.There is also a presentation issue in the qualitative figures. Some visual results appear stretched or distorted, suggesting that the image aspect ratio may have been altered during figure resizing. This hurts readability and makes qualitative comparison less reliable, especially in a segmentation paper where boundary shape and instrument geometry matter.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Novelty: We appreciate the reviewers’ request to clarify our core contributions. Our method, TEDi, introduces a systematic “complement-and-denoise” paradigm that addresses limitations in existing work through three key distinctions. First, regarding temporal instrument segmentation methods, current methods like MATIS and LACOSTE fail to simultaneously manage information deficiency and feature-level semantic noise. MATIS operates at the backbone level without query enhancement, while LACOSTE propagates queries without feature-level semantic noise suppression, leading to accumulated errors. TEDi bridges these gaps: the MSE module retrieves historical context to compensate for occlusions, while the TCD module suppresses the categorical noise inherent in temporal propagation. Second, regarding Video Object Segmentation (VOS) methods like XMem or RMem, our approach is significantly more efficient. Unlike VOS frameworks that store dense, pixel-level features, our memory bank utilizes compact, instance-aware query representations specifically tailored for the requirements of surgical instrument tasks. Third, regarding DN-DETR, our TCD module is fundamentally different in function and application. While DN-DETR is a training-only strategy using random noise for convergence, TCD is a permanent architectural component. It uses prior denoised queries as stable cross-frame semantic anchors during both training and inference without introducing random noise. The synergy of this design is empirically validated in Figure 3: MSE increases the retrieval of correctly classified queries (Fig. 3b), while TCD prunes the misclassified ones (Fig. 3c). We will clarify these distinctions in the revised manuscript. 2.Efficiency analysis: An efficiency analysis have been conducted on one NVIDIA A100 GPU with 512×512 input resolution. TEDi has 60.58M parameters and 78.92 GFLOPs, compared to the Mask2Former baseline’s 56.91 GFLOPs. Notably, TEDi reuses query representations from previously encoded frames during temporal inference, so only the newly arriving frame requires backbone encoding. This yields an inference latency of 57.96 ms/clip, where the memory bank contributes only approximately 5.5 ms of additional overhead, with a peak GPU memory footprint of 666.1 MB. Among prior methods, TEDi has lower complexity than ISINet(264 GFLOPs) and comparable to QPD(71.38 GFLOP) and S3Net(88.04 GFLOP). 3.Temporal consistency metric: To further quantify the temporal stability illustrated in Fig. 3, we introduce the Class Flip Rate (CFR), defined as the proportion of matched instrument instances whose predicted category changes between consecutive frames. On EV18, TEDi reduces CFR from 11.4% (baseline) to 4.8%, validating that our MSE and TCD effectively suppress inter-frame category flickering through cross-frame memory retrieval and temporal-consistency denoising. 4.Limitations: Thank you for point these out and we agree that TEDi improves category prediction consistency over prior methods but does not completely eliminate temporal category flickering, as observed in the supplementary video. The main failure cases occur when prolonged occlusion, or when instruments remain visible but undergo significant appearance variation, causing our MSE to retrieve unreliable representations, and for rare instrument categories with limited training samples, which remain more susceptible to misclassification. 5.Compare with sam2: SAM2 acknowledges difficulty with nearby similar-looking objects(Ravi et al., 2024) and TEDi outperforms SurgicalSAM2(Liu et al., 2025) on the main EndoVis metrics under fully automatic evaluation. TEDi is preferable when automatic, closed-set category-level prediction is required, while SAM2 offers better open-set generalizability. We will clearly mention this in the conclusion of the revised paper. 6.Naming and figures: We appreciate these suggestions and will adjust all qualitative figures to correct aspect ratios in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal should clarify the technical novelty over prior temporal-memory and denoising approaches to surgical instrument segmentation, and provide the missing efficiency analysis (inference time, FLOPs, and memory overhead) since parameter counts alone are insufficient to substantiate the practical-deployment framing. The rebuttal should also report temporal-consistency metrics that align with the paper’s workflow motivation, and include a substantive discussion of failure modes and limitations. | The paper proposes a temporal memory-enhanced and denoising transformer for surgical instrument segmentation on the standard EndoVis benchmarks. The original concerns centered on technical novelty relative to memory-based VOS methods and query-denoising approaches, the absence of an efficiency analysis, and the lack of a temporal-consistency metric aligned with the workflow motivation. The rebuttal articulates clear distinctions: a compact query-level memory rather than dense pixel-level memory, and a permanent temporal-consistency denoising component that uses prior denoised queries as anchors, rather than a training-only random-noise denoising scheme. The reported efficiency profile substantiates the efficiency framing, and the newly reported class-flip-rate metric is consistent with the workflow motivation. Two reviewers explicitly endorsed acceptance after the rebuttal; the third did not update but raised mainly minor concerns. The contribution is coherent and well-validated. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend the paper for acceptance, as all the major concerns were addressed by the authors in the rebuttal period. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal effectively addressed the reviewers’ concerns, providing sufficient clarification and additional evidence where requested. Following the rebuttal, all reviewers expressed support for acceptance, indicating a clear consensus that the paper meets the standard for acceptance at MICCAI.

title: Test-Time Adaptation for Rare Surgical Phase Recognition: Bridging the Coverage-Gap Paradox
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors propose a test-time adaptation framework centered on an adaptive pseudo-label threshold that resolves the empty-pool failure of fixed thresholds, with temporal smoothing serving as a precision filter for downstream pseudo-label selection. The proposed method assigns phase numbers using the nearest neighbor algorithm and adaptively adjusts representative points at test time; its key feature is its low computational complexity. Among three representative surgical image datasets (MultiBypass140, Cholec80, and Cataract-101), the method demonstrates improved recognition performance for rare phases compared to conventional methods on two of these datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are numerous points where the presentation of experimental results and the discussion are insufficient, making it impossible to assess the effectiveness of the proposed method. In the experimental results for “Causal variants” in Section 4.2, only the results for Cholec80 are shown; results for the other two datasets are not presented. In Table 1, the experimental results for “Combined” and “Oracle” on the Cholec80 dataset are not shown. Furthermore, no reason is given for this omission. In Table 1, for the Cataract-101 dataset, the proposed method (Combined) achieves a 33.3-point improvement in accuracy over the Baseline for the rare phases, but a 10.8-point decrease in accuracy for the overall phases. Such a significant drop in accuracy for the overall phases appears to be a major issue, yet no discussion or explanation regarding this is provided. In Table 2, results for Cataract-101 are not shown. In Table 2, the experimental results for Cholec80 show a significant decline in “Ours (Combined)”, resulting in lower performance than the conventional methods; however, no discussion of this is provided.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed Test-Time Adaptation framework is exceptionally lightweight, requiring under 20,000 parameters and processing at less than 0.1 milliseconds per frame, making real-time intraoperative deployment highly feasible 2.Its shift from a standard fixed-confidence threshold to an adaptive q-th percentile threshold is a brilliant fix that guarantees rare-phase updates and acts as the primary driver of the model’s success.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the method improves rare-phase recognition, it causes a severe degradation in overall accuracy on the Cataract-101 dataset, dropping by up to 13.7 percentage points. The authors acknowledge this as a structural limitation for datasets with a high number of classes and overlapping clusters. 1.The framework relies on pseudo-labels that have very low precision, explicitly noted as 11-25% on the MB140 dataset. This means the prototypes are being updated with a large proportion of incorrect data, leaving theoretical convergence bounds an open question. 2.The ablation study used to justify hyperparameter choices is fragile, as it was conducted on only a single fold and a single random seed. The authors concede that values from a single seed can deviate from the true multi-seed means by up to 12 percentage points. 3.The study lacks a systematic evaluation of different foundation model choices, relying solely on LemonFM and DINOv2 for feature extraction. Because the “coverage-gap paradox” and the success of the Test-Time Adaptation framework fundamentally depend on the geometric properties of the embedding space, failing to benchmark across diverse foundation models leaves it unclear whether the observed baseline failures and subsequent accuracy gains are universal or merely artifacts of the specific embeddings used.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and under-addressed failure mode in surgical phase recognition: poor performance on rare or sparsely annotated phases. This is clinically meaningful because the paper is not merely optimizing overall accuracy, but focusing on phases that are easy to miss and often most affected by data scarcity. The paper clearly identifies and empirically characterizes a “coverage-gap paradox” linked to prototype dilution across multi-center surgical videos, a problem formulation that resonates with practical annotation scarcity and across-hospital heterogeneity. The central adaptive percentile threshold for class-conditional pseudo-label selection is simple, computationally negligible, and directly addresses empty-pool failures of fixed thresholds in rare classes. The framework integrates temporal precision filtering and a minimal-budget, auto-guided annotation strategy in a practical TTA pipeline (including a causal, real-time variant). Evaluation on three distinct surgical domains (gastric bypass, cholecystectomy, cataract) with multiple settings (within- and cross-center) demonstrates robustness. Factorial analysis isolates the contribution of the adaptive threshold (dominant driver, +22 pp on MB140) and shows interactions with temporal smoothing for precision improvements. Addresses a clinically relevant failure mode (rare, short phases with low label coverage) that conventional long-tail or class-balanced losses cannot resolve when video-level class coverage is lacking. The solution is practical: source-free, low-parameter, fast, and easily layered atop foundation-model features for deployment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The adaptive percentile pseudo-labeling idea, while effective, is conceptually modest and related to established class-wise confidence/percentile selection in UDA/self-training; the novelty is more in application to surgical rare-phase TTA than in core methodology. Prototype updating can adversely shift decision boundaries, substantially degrading overall accuracy in higher-class settings (e.g., Cat-101), indicating brittleness in complex feature geometries. The method presumes non-empty class-specific predicted pools to compute percentiles; a fallback strategy for empty-pool scenarios is not fully specified. Comparisons to strong temporal backbones (e.g., MS-TCN, Trans-SVNet, LoViT) under an adapted rare-label regime are not provided; only post-hoc smoothing and a TENT-style baseline are shown, potentially underestimating competitive strong baselines for rare phases. The paper cites SPA as complementary, but does not empirically compare against it. Given the paper’s framing around test-time adaptation for surgical phase recognition, the absence of a stronger surgical-specific adaptation baseline weakens the claim of state-of-the-art relevance. Reported overall accuracies are quite low on Cholec80 relative to the literature (owing to the label-masking regime and prototype classifier), making it hard to contextualize results versus established systems. Prior class-wise adaptive pseudo-labeling in source-free UDA/self-training (e.g., CBST and related class-conditional thresholding) is not cited or contrasted. Also, broader long-tailed action/phase literature and prototype-based adaptation work could be more comprehensively connected to the paradox and method. There is a meaningful trade-off with overall performance, especially on Cat-101, where rare-phase gains come with a large drop in overall accuracy. Since phase recognition systems are usually deployed for complete workflow understanding, this is not a minor issue. The paper describes it as structural, but the practical consequence is that the proposed method may improve the corner case while harming the full task. Finally, the “Combined” setting uses oracle annotation of B=5 frames, which is useful as an upper-bound/practical hybrid scenario, but it also means some of the most impressive gains partly rely on human input. That is not a flaw by itself, though the framing should remain careful when emphasizing adaptation performance.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer. We restrict the response to presentation amendments of existing results; algorithmic extensions are future work. A. Cat-101 overall-rare trade-off (shared). Under the Stage-4 oracle update, rare-class prototypes on Cat-101 drift toward boundary regions of the embedding space. This drift raises rare-recall but reduces the margin against neighboring common classes, costing -10.8 pp overall under Combined and -13.7 pp under Oracle (Tab. 1). The mechanism is the same in both cases: it is structural to the source-free regime with a frozen encoder on a 10-class topology (Sec. 4.2), not a missed hyperparameter. Anchoring each rare-class prototype to its base counterpart by bounding the cosine drift, or applying a confidence-margin gate at prediction time, both preserve the source-free guarantee and are a clearly scoped future direction. B. R1 - missing data and conditions. Cholec80 Combined/Oracle in Tab. 1.Cholec80 uses label masking: videos stay in training but rare-phase labels are masked. Oracle annotation re-introduces them, making “Combined/Oracle” semantically circular under this protocol. MB140 and Cat-101 use video-removal and are unaffected. Cholec80 Combined decline in Tab. 2.Same Stage-4 oracle-drift mechanism as in §A applies. Cat-101 in Tab. 2.The MV/TCN/GRU/TENT comparison was run on MB140 and Cholec80 only; the Base-vs-Temporal-vs-Combined analysis on Cat-101 in Tab. 1 supports the same claim that temporal post-processing alone cannot bridge the coverage gap. Cholec80 causal. Tab. 4 already reports causal results (71.2% vs. 70.8% bidirectional, w=15); the small gap supports cross-dataset extension as future work. Clarifications. w=15 means 15 frames at 1 fps; Self-Training is TENT-style entropy minimization on a prototype classifier with a fixed p=0.95 threshold; “structural embedding limitation” means the frozen-encoder representational ceiling under the source-free constraint. C. R2 - precision, ablation, FM diversity. 11-25% pseudo-label precision. The adaptive percentile is designed to prevent rare-class empty pools (factorial Tab. 3); we accept lower per-frame precision for guaranteed coverage. Temporal smoothing and prototype-centroid geometry recover precision downstream. “Single-seed” wording. The wording was misleading: the factorial in Tab. 3 in fact uses 5 seeds x 5 folds, matching the headline +22 pp claim. The “up to 12 pp deviation” note refers to a separate per-fold sub-analysis in the hyperparameter ablation. FM diversity. LemonFM (surgical) and DINOv2 (general) span two distinct families and TTA gains are consistent across both (Tab. 1); broader FM sweeps are future work. D. R3 - prior work, baselines, framing. CBST / class-conditional thresholding. Our method differs by being source-free TTA over fixed prototypes (no retraining), providing a per-class empty-pool guarantee via the adaptive percentile, and running at <0.1 ms/frame. Stronger temporal baselines. Tab. 2 already compares MV, TCN post-hoc, GRU-smooth, and TENT-style on the same features. MS-TCN and Trans-SVNet are full end-to-end retraining methods outside the source-free regime we target; our claim is that temporal post-processing alone cannot bridge the coverage gap (Sec. 4.3), which Tab. 2 evidences. “Classifier-agnostic” framing. We agree this overstates the result; the supported claim is “observed across three representative classifier families (k-NN, linear, prototype)” (Sec. 3.2). Combined uses oracle B=5.The Temporal rows in Tabs. 1-2 are the fully source-free results, and we will sharpen this distinction. Camera-ready amendments. Tab. 1 footnote on label masking; CBST (Zou 2018), SHOT, and SPA citations in Sec. 2; softened “classifier-agnostic” claim; sharper Combined-vs-Temporal distinction in Sec. 3.4; corrected Limitations note on factorial seed counts. We intend to extend our code release with reproducibility scripts upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): There are mixed reviews (2WA, 1WR). Reviewers are concerned with the presentation of experimental results and the limited discussion. It would be great to clarify them during rebuttal. | This paper explores improving recognition of rare or sparsely annotated phases. The main merit of the work is the proposed lightweight source-free test-time adaptation strategy based on adaptive percentile pseudo-labeling. The method directly targets the empty-pool failure of fixed confidence thresholds for rare classes. It looks computationally very efficient and is practical for real-time deployment. The evaluation across multiple surgical datasets and feature backbones provides useful evidence that the approach can improve rare-phase recognition in several settings. The rebuttal also clarified several important points, including the seed/fold setup and the role of the Combined versus Temporal settings. There are still remaining concerns, including performance degradation on more complex datasets and the reliance on low-precision pseudo-labels. Despite these limitations, I think the problem formulation and practical efficiency are sufficiently valuable for the MICCAI community. I would suggest accept. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the rebuttal letter and reviewers’ post-rebuttal comments, I recommend acceptance as the post-rebuttal largely addresses reviewers’ concerns. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The reviewers highlight concerns regarding insufficient experimental results and discussion, making it difficult to assess the method’s effectiveness. Key issues include missing baseline evaluations, lack of explanation for significant performance drops, reliance on fragile ablation studies, and limited benchmarking across diverse models or stronger baselines. Despite addressing concerns in the rebuttal, the core issues around robustness, novelty, and broader applicability remain unresolved.

title: Towards Unified Surgical Scene Understanding: Bridging Reasoning and Grounding via MLLMs
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel Unified Architecture: First to jointly model phase recognition, triplet reasoning, and entity grounding in a single MLLM-driven pipeline, addressing the fragmentation of prior surgical scene understanding methods. Well-Motivated Design: The [SEG] token bridge and temporal fusion explicitly tackle surgical video consistency and cross-task semantic alignment. Strong Empirical Results: Consistently achieves SOTA across all three tasks on CholecT45 (e. g. , APIVT +5.3%, mIoU 84.4%), with clear ablation validating joint optimization benefits. Valuable Community Resource: CholecT45-Scene provides dense pixel-level masks and structured reasoning narratives, filling a critical gap for unified surgical video analysis.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Baseline Fairness & Currency: Comparisons mainly include methods from 2021–2024 and omit recent reasoning-segmentation frameworks (e. g. , LISA, Sa2VA, VideoLISA, MEJO) that share the [SEG]-to-SAM paradigm. Performance gains may partially stem from backbone capacity (4B MLLM + SAM2-H) rather than architectural novelty. Clinical Deployment Feasibility Unaddressed: No inference latency, FPS, or memory analysis is provided. Given the computational cost of a 4B MLLM + SAM2-H pipeline, real-time intraoperative applicability remains unclear. Annotation QA Transparency: While manual auditing is mentioned, quantitative inter-annotator agreement, SAM2 correction rates, and handling of ambiguous target boundaries (e. g. , deformed gallbladder, omentum) are not reported. Mechanistic Validation of Mutual Promotion: Table 4 confirms joint training helps, but lacks gradient/attribution analysis or error-case studies demonstrating how grounding concretely corrects MLLM reasoning errors (or vice versa).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Dataset contribution. Extending CholecT45 with target masks fills a real gap — CholecTriplet-Seg provides instrument masks only, and target grounding for anatomical structures is exactly the piece needed to evaluate IVT grounding end-to-end. The reasoning narratives, while synthetic, enable a new supervision signal for the community. Task formulation. Unifying phase + triplet + pixel-level triplet-entity grounding in a single model is, to my knowledge, new at the pixel level. The ablations in Table 4 (w/o triplet, w/o phase, w/o grounding) provide meaningful evidence that the three objectives interact constructively rather than degrade one another. AP_IVT improvement. The +5.3 point gain on the primary triplet metric (40.7 → 46.0) over CurConMix is a meaningful step. Gains on AP_T (+10.9) and AP_IV (+22.2) suggest the grounding supervision genuinely helps IVT reasoning, which is a non-obvious and positive finding. Grounding numbers. 84.4 mIoU vs 65.8 for SurgSAM2 is a large margin, and the ablations indicate the per-frame [SEG] + residual fusion design contributes to this. Evaluation protocol. 5-fold CV with mean±std follows the established protocol, making the numbers comparable to prior work.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1: Overstated novelty of the “unified MLLM for surgical scene understanding” claim. The introduction and contribution list position this as the first unified MLLM framework, but this ignores GP-VLS (Schmidgall et al., 2024), which unifies phase, triplet, and tool recognition in a surgical VLM, and SurgVLM (2025) and EndoChat (MedIA 2026), which additionally incorporate bounding-box-level visual grounding alongside surgical reasoning. The contribution is more accurately described as the first MLLM framework to bridge structured triplet reasoning with pixel-level grounding of both instruments and targets via [SEG]-driven SAM2 decoding. The related work section and triplet-recognition baselines should be updated accordingly. At minimum, one surgical MLLM should appear in Table 2 — currently all triplet baselines are specialist classifiers, which makes the MLLM contribution look stronger than a head-to-head with a surgical VLM would. W2: Architectural novelty is limited and under-explained. The reasoning-to-grounding bridge reproduces the Sa2VA [26] architecture, which itself adapts LISA [13] to SAM2: expanding the LLM vocabulary with a [SEG] token, extracting its last-layer hidden state, projecting it through an MLP into SAM2’s sparse prompt embedding space, and training end-to-end with BCE + Dice + language modeling losses while fine-tuning only the SAM2 mask decoder. SurgMLLM adopts this pipeline, including the same InternVL2.5 backbone used in Sa2VA. The mechanistic contributions beyond Sa2VA appear to be the per-entity residual fusion over per-frame [SEG] tokens (Eq. 2) and the structured / reasoning format, but this inheritance is not acknowledged in either the related work or the method section. Beyond the novelty framing, the method section leaves several implementation details unspecified that are necessary to reproduce or correctly interpret the approach: (a) Which LLM representation is extracted at [SEG] positions (last hidden layer, pooled, or other)? (b) Is [SEG] a newly added vocabulary token, or a reused existing token? (c) Which SAM2 prompt slot (sparse prompt embeddings, dense embeddings, other) does the projected embedding replace or augment? (d) What does "entity u" in Eq. 2 actually group — the entity class across all frames (e.g., all occurrences of "grasper"), per triplet-slot position, or per instance? Each choice yields different fusion behavior and different handling of multiple simultaneous instances of the same class. (e) Do gradients from the mask losses flow back through the projection MLP into the LoRA adapters, or is the LLM trained purely from the language modeling and entity-aware losses? A clearer equation chain from LLM hidden state → projection → SAM2 prompt slot → mask, together with explicit positioning relative to Sa2VA and LISA, would substantially strengthen the paper. W3: The central claim that reasoning helps grounding is not ablated. The paper sells the ... block as enabling "explicit structured reasoning," but Table 4 does not contain an "answer-only" row. Without an ablation removing the CoT block while retaining phase + triplet + grounding supervision, readers cannot tell whether the reasoning narrative actually contributes to grounding quality or whether it is a stylistic wrapper on the GT labels that the Qwen3-generated supervision trained the model to reproduce. W4: mIoU in Table 3 does not reconcile with the reported IoUs. With IoU_I = 87.8 and IoU_T = 67.8, a simple mean is 77.8, not 84.4.Per-class averaging across the 6 instrument and 15 target categories would produce a different (likely pixel-frequency-weighted) aggregate. Since mIoU is the headline grounding metric, the exact definition must be stated in the manuscript. W5: Segmentation baselines are underspecified. Table 3 compares against SAM2-ZeroShot, SAM2-Adapter, and SurgSAM2, but what prompts are the baselines given? Points? Boxes? Text? If SurgMLLM receives LLM-derived entity-specific prompts while baselines receive weaker prompts, the comparison is not isolating the grounding method. W6: Multi-task vs. single-task baseline fairness. SurgMLLM benefits from phase + triplet + mask supervision simultaneously. Phase and triplet baselines receive only their own labels. The architectural contribution is not cleanly separated from the multi-task-supervision effect. W7: Circular GT for segmentation evaluation. CholecT45-Scene masks are generated by SAM2 + ~30 point prompts + temporal propagation + manual audit. SurgMLLM also uses SAM2.Systematic SAM2 failure modes are therefore baked into both the GT and the predictions, biasing IoU upward for SAM2-based methods. An externally annotated held-out subset, or cross-evaluation on CholecTriplet-Seg, would strengthen the claim. W8: AP computation from autoregressive text is not explained. Triplet AP requires per-class confidence scores. How are these derived from the LLM's text output — token logits at the entity position? Sampled probabilities? Rank-based? This is non-trivial and fundamentally affects comparability with AP-trained classifiers (RDV, TERL, CurConMix). W9: Cascaded recall is not analyzed. If the MLLM under-predicts N triplets, the missing entities are never segmented, and there is no way to separate reasoning errors from grounding errors. The grounding results would be more informative decomposed into (triplet recall) × (mask IoU \| triplet recalled). W10: No latency or compute reporting. The introduction motivates "context-aware computer-assisted intervention," implying near-real-time use. At minimum, GPU used and effective fps achieved should be stated. W11: Temporal consistency is claimed but not measured. Residual fusion is motivated as a temporal-consistency mechanism, but only frame-wise mIoU is reported. W12: L_ent is introduced as a contribution but never ablated, loss weights (λ_bce, λ_dice, λ_ent) are not reported, and the temporal fusion uses an unspecified number of frames T. The "lightweight MLP aggregation" is not described architecturally. W13: Reasoning narrative generation is under-described. The main text does not specify, the paper only references "Qwen3" in a figure caption. The specific model version, the prompt template, and any validation of factual correctness of generated narratives are missing. Given that the narratives are a named supervision signal, this is a reproducibility gap. W14: Dataset construction protocol is thin. Number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, audit sampling rate, rejection criteria, and the fraction of propagated masks that were corrected are not reported. The 90,489 → 64,299 frame reduction from CholecT45 to CholecT45-Scene is also unexplained and may introduce selection bias. W15: Ablations are single-fold (Fold 1) while main results are 5-fold. Single-fold ablations are noisy. The suspiciously low std on Phase Accuracy (0.6 vs 2.3–4.2 for baselines) is also worth explaining. W16: Results narrative is one-sided. The text claims consistent improvements across Table 2, but AP_I drops from 93.5 (TERL) to 89.9 and AP_V drops from 72.8 (TERL) to 71.0.These regressions deserve honest discussion. (AP_IVT is the primary metric and the +5.3 gain there is substantial, but the paper should discuss the component losses.)
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: (1) The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem. The unified formulation of phrase recognition, triplet recognition, and segmentation in a well-designed framework is clinically meaningful. (2) The proposed framework is well designed and conceptually coherent. The authors attempt to explicitly bridge high-level reasoning and low-level grounding. (3) The dataset contribution is valuable. The introduction of Cholec T45-Scene is a strong practical contribution to this paper. The dataset can be used to support future work on more integrated surgical video understanding. (4) The overall presentation is well organized. The problem setup, framework overview, and experimental sections are easy to read. The experimental evaluation is convincing.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) The unified surgical formulation is interesting, but I think the core design ideas are related to existing grounded reasoning and segmentation frameworks, such as LISA, GLAMM, and Sa2VA. These works also connect language-side reasoning with segmentation outputs. The authors overstate the methodological novelty rather than the surgical-specific integration of phase, triplet, and grounding tasks. (2) For the grounding task, the authors mainly compare with SAM2-ZeroShot, SAM2-Adapter, and SurgSAM2, but do not include direct comparison against the more task-relevant surgical works [1, 25] mentioned in the paper. (3) The new dataset is promising, but annotation details are somewhat limited. (4) The authors should provide an anonymized GitHub repository (or other anonymous project page) containing at least the evaluation protocol and annotation data samples for verification.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and the Area Chair for their constructive feedback. We appreciate the recognition of our well-motivated problem and sensible solution (R2&R3), timely unified framework for surgical scene understanding (R1&R4), and valuable CholecT45-Scene dataset that fills a real gap (R1-R4). We first address common questions (CQs), followed by point-by-point responses. (CQ1) Dataset annotation: Initial masks were generated by SAM2 using positive/negative point prompts, then audited by three expert surgeons with consensus correction. The audit-flag rate was 42.2%, and 32.7% of flagged frames were corrected after manual re-filtering/re-annotation. For ambiguous boundaries, prompts were used when regions were visually separable. For deformation, occlusion, or tissue overlap, annotations followed surgical semantic consistency rather than strict exclusive pixel ownership; thus, independent binary entity masks may overlap. (CQ2) Method Novelty: Our framework extends generic LISA/Sa2VA-style reasoning segmentation to surgery by unifying three surgical tasks with frame-wise per-entity [SEG] representations, temporal residual fusion, structured Phase-IVT reasoning, and surgical-entity-aware auxiliary supervision. Unlike existing surgical MLLMs (GP-VLS, SurgVLM, and EndoChat), which mainly address VQA, our method jointly performs Phase-IVT reasoning and pixel-level grounding for both instruments and targets. Generic Sa2VA provides only global video-level responses but lacks frame-wise per-entity modeling and structured Phase-IVT reasoning. We will clarify these surgery-specific contributions in the revision. (CQ3) Comparison with Other Baselines: On Fold 1, Sa2VA achieves 30.3 AP_IVT, compared with 46.4 AP_IVT by our method under the same backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of our surgery-specific design. Task-relevant surgical works [1,25] do not release code, making reproducible comparison infeasible. We therefore compare against stronger SAM-series models to provide a fair and rigorous evaluation of our framework. (R1 W1) Please see CQ2&3. (R1 W2) SurgMLLM runs at 2.8 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.We will explore lighter variants to improve real-time applicability in our extension work. (R1 W3) Please see CQ1. (R1 W4) Mask losses are not detached and back-propagate through projection, temporal fusion, and trainable LLM LoRA adapters. (R2 W1) Please see CQ2&3. (R2 W2) Please see CQ2 and (R1 W4). In Eq. 2, entity group u denotes the same grounded phrase across frames, e.g., “grasper” or “gallbladder”, based on phrase/entity-label consistency over frame-wise [SEG] embeddings, not persistent instance ID or triplet-slot position. (R2 W3) Removing ... while keeping the same phase, triplet, and grounding supervision yields 79.1/44.2/82.8 (Phase Acc./AP_IVT/mIoU), compared with 84.0/46.4/83.6 for the full model, showing structured reasoning effectiveness. (R2 W4) mIoU is the average IoU over all grounded entity masks, with instrument/target ratios of 0.83/0.17; IoU_I and IoU_T report the instrument and target subsets separately. (R2 W8) AP confidence is computed from the autoregressive generation logits. At each generated entity-token position, we apply softmax over the vocabulary logits and take the probability assigned to the generated token. (R3 W1) Please see CQ2. (R3 W2) Please see CQ3. (R3 W3) Please see CQ1. (R3 W4) We will release the code and annotations in the camera-ready version. (R4 W1) CholecT45 is the most representative dataset and is widely used in prior works [9–11]. We will include more datasets in the extension. (R4 W2) Please see CQ3. (R4 W3) We report only AP_IVT due to space limit and will include other metrics in the final version. (R4 W4) Please see CQ2. (R4 W5) Please see CQ3.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): SurgMLLM jointly produces phase prediction, IVT triplets, and pixel-level grounding via per-frame [SEG] tokens with residual temporal fusion, and releases CholecT45-Scene (64,299 frames with dual masks and reasoning narratives). Three of four reviewers vote weak-accept on the strength of substantial empirical gains (+5.3 AP_IVT over CurConMix; 84.4 vs. 65.8 mIoU vs. SurgSAM2), the dataset value, and meaningful ablation in Table 4.novelty relative to Sa2VA/LISA/GP-VLS/SurgVLM/EndoChat should be more clearly positioned, the block contribution should be ablated, the mIoU 84.4 should be reconciled with IoU_I=87.8/IoU_T=67.8, AP from autoregressive text must be specified, segmentation baseline prompts must be documented, and single-fold ablations should be reconciled with 5-fold main results.The authors should address these points in the camera-ready version.

title: Track2Map: Online Deformable SLAM with Motion-Aware Pose Optimization in Robotic Surgery
reviewer_1_strengths: Challenging problem and relevant for the community. Promising results and good comparison with other techniques. Simple yet effective model.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Lack of related works. Lack of important details and values to guarantee reproducibility.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The positive aspects of the paper are: Paper is in general well written and simple to follow Addresses a relevant subject for the MICCAI community and a critical limitation of current surgical reconstruction pipelines, which is the reliance on accurate camera pose priors The system-level design composed of motion-aware pose gating, track-guided deformation initialization, etc. make sense and is not straightforward the individual components of the system are not new, but their integration and procedural use in this context seems to be novel The experimental results and comparison with SOTA approaches are convincing, showing improvements in reconstruction quality and pose accuracy
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The negative aspects of the paper are: Limited dataset diversity: all reconstruction and SLAM evaluations are performed only on the StereoMIS dataset High dependence on 2D tracking quality (pose gating, pose init, deformation init), and robustness under tracking degradation is not explicitly evaluated motion gating thresholds is empirically selected and fixed the current implementation runs at approximately 6 seconds per frame on an NVIDIA V100 GPU, which is far from meeting the latency requirements of a realistic OR scenario. Although this limitation is explicitly acknowledged by the authors, it significantly weakens the practical interpretation of the method as “online”, especially when compared to existing real-time or near–real-time SLAM systems in surgical environments. As such, in its current form, the system appears more suited for offline analysis, and the paper’s positioning as a surgical-targeted solution should be interpreted accordingly.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in robotic surgery, where accurate pose information is often unavailable. The idea of motion-aware pose updates is interesting and practically relevant. The experimental results on StereoMIS show better 3D reconstruction and pose estimation over baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The main weakness is clarity: We don’t know in the abstract whether the method is based on monocular or stereo endoscope. Same comment in the first paragraphs of the introduction “Second, we use dense 2D point tracking to disentangle camera motion from tissue deformation.” in the introduction: the key idea on how this is achieved is not introduced. In the method: notations not defined for the scene represented as a set of Gaussains (their centers appear to be x in Section 2.2), and for the sparse set of control points (?). This makes the subsequent section hard to follow. The Section 2.2 is particularly hard to follow: in “which treats control-point offsets as free variables optimized per frame, we explicitly drive the deformation field using tracked anchor motion.”, what is the conceptual difference between “control-point offsets” and “tracked anchor motion”? In “its N nearest anchors”: are these anchors the control points? Additional justifications of the design of the “Motion-Aware Camera Update” module would be welcome: Why not using standard tools of epipolar geometry to detect dominant rigid motion (eg RANSAC + F or H estimation)? Why not using depth of the 2D correspondences at hand that provide additional information? If the endoscope is moving along its optical axis in a cavity, the optical flow should in general present a high circular standard deviation, and therefore associated to the “scene motion” mode which is opposed to the expected behavior. Missing references: EndoGaussian paper, and its follow up TMI paper “Foundation Model-Guided Gaussian Splatting for 4D Reconstruction of Deformable Tissues”. EndoNerf not cited (Neural Rendering for Stereo 3D Reconstruction of Deformable Tissues in Robotic Surgery)
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: [R1/R2/R3] Novelty/related work We agree deformable SLAM is not new. Our contribution is adopting it for 3DGS dense reconstruction of surgery scenes using priors specific to this context. We will add NRSfM/SLAM references and clarify the contribution. [R1/R3] Input modalities The proposed method uses stereo RGB. Depth is estimated from FoundationStereo. Pose input is optional. We will consistently refer to this as “stereo RGB video with optional pose prior”. In Table 1, we test a monocular version using the left RGB and depth from DepthAnything-V2.[R1] Reproducibility Implementation details were provided in the linked GitHub repo. We will add key values(e.g. w_depth=10, w_color=5, w_pose=0.25) to the paper [R2] Dataset diversity We agree that more datasets would be welcome. To our knowledge, StereoMIS is the only public robotic-surgery benchmark supporting Track2Map full evaluation: calibrated stereo, deformable tissue and tool interaction, metric depth, and camera trajectories for ATE/RPE evaluation. Other benchmarks lack requirements: SCARED is rigid, EndoNeRF/STIR/SurgT lacks poses. We will clarify this limitation. [R2] Robustness to tracking We tested perturbing 2D tracks with pixel-level Gaussian noise, leading to following changes (σ=1,2,4px): σ px PSNR SSIM LPIPS ATE m RPEt m RPEr deg 1 27.4 0.729 0.319 0.0276 0.0029 0.327 2 27.3 0.726 0.319 0.0288 0.0031 0.338 4 27.2 0.720 0.327 0.0290 0.0033 0.352 This suggests moderate robustness to track noise. If permitted, we will include this in the paper. [R3] Control-point vs. anchor Control-point offsets are learnable 3D deformation variables, while anchors provide track-derived 3D displacement measurements from 2D tracks lifted with stereo depth. Previous work[8] estimated them from photometric loss; in our work, control points are optimised with additional supervision of anchors. “N nearest anchors” refers to the spatially closest anchors used to interpolate displacement at each control point location. [R2] Kinematic pose reliability Camera kinematics have low relative pose errors, but large absolute pose errors. This is relevant in SLAM where camera and anatomy are in the same coordinate system. Hand-eye calibration error is a large contributor. This is documented e.g. in Ferguson, Comparing the Accuracy of the da Vinci Xi and da Vinci Si for Image Guidance and Automation, 2017 [R2] Online We use online in an algorithmic sense: frames are processed sequentially without future observations. It reduces memory/computation vs. existing offline pipelines that optimise over a full sequence simultaneously. We agree ⅙ fps is not real-time. We state this clearly and discuss how to address it in future work. [R2/R3] Camera/tissue motion Camera and tissue motion can happen at the same time. However, large tissue deformations are caused by tools while the endoscope is stationary (the da Vinci camera locks during tool motion and vice versa). We assume that during camera motion, tissue motion is much smaller (e.g. breathing) compared to direct tissue manipulation and thus constraining tissue deformation in these cases provides a fair approximation leading to better motion estimation. [R2/R3] Optical flow gating [R3] We agree using epipolar constraints with RANSAC would be a more principled approach for motion gating. Optical flow statistics is a simple solution that doesn’t require extensive sampling in high outlier environments. We verified experimentally that there is very good separation between the 2 motion modes (shown in the supplementary). We agree that optical-axis motion is a limitation of our simplification, which didn’t significantly affect performance as lateral motions are significantly more frequent in MIS after the initial camera insertion. [R2] Flow magnitude is not used during gating, but it is used during scene-flow and pose/deformation initialization, so small noisy motions do not contribute equally to large motions during optimisation. We will clarify this.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The submission received mixed reviews (2xWR, WA). The authors should prepare a rebuttal addressing the raised issues and in particular the issues raised by R1 and R2. | The rebuttal clarified several questions and persuaded R2 to recommend acceptance. Nevertheless the paper still has mixed scores 2xA + 1xR and many outstanding concerns remain namely on clarity and missing references. I will lean towards majority and support acceptance trusting that authors will fix many of the clarity issues in an eventual camera ready version: e.g. clarify input modality, state assumption to disambiguate camera from tissue motion and how it affect generality of method, discuss preference for optical flow statistics as opposed to epipolar geometry + RANSAC and inherent limitation when camera moves along optical axis. I also have no objections to the inclusion of the results that demonstrate moderate resilience to errors in tracking as this does not requrie a new dataset/experiment. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Note on additional experiments; Additional experiments were requested by reviewers, which should not have been done. Results from a noise sensitivity analysis were presented in the rebuttal, which I have excluded form my decision-making. This submission addresses an important problem in online deformable reconstruction for surgical SLAM. All reviewers agree that the method is relevant and shows promising empirical results on the StereoMIS dataset, with improvements over baseline approaches. R1 recommends weak accept, citing solid experimental results but noting incomplete related work coverage and missing reproducibility details. R2 initially recommended weak reject due to concerns about single-dataset evaluation, reliance on 2D tracking quality, heuristic design choices, and runtime limitations. author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback, with our point-to-point response below. 1.Novelty over prior DT work (R1,R4,MR): Our method differs from prior DT-based reasoning [23-26] in three ways. (a) Hierarchical temporal DT, specifically for surgical videos: prior methods build flat, per-frame representations; we introduce a three-level hierarchy (frame, temporal window, procedure), improving EM from 0.383 to 0.441 (Tab.3). (b) Probabilistic DT: prior DT representations are deterministic; we attach calibrated confidence scores and propagate them into the reward, improving EM to 0.584 with uncertainty-modulated reward. (c) Clinical validity reward: prior methods for DT use generic accuracy rewards; ours penalizes clinically implausible answers via LLM-as-judge, absent in general-domain DT work. We will add a dedicated comparison paragraph and temper novelty claims accordingly in revision (R4). 2.Missing DT baselines (R4,MR): We evaluated DT-R1 (state-of-the-art DT method) on REAL-Colon-Reason using the same surgical foundation models. DT-R1 (zero-shot): 0.298 EM; DT-R1 (fine-tuned on our data): 0.462 EM; Ours: 0.584 EM. The gap comes from DT-R1 lacking hierarchical temporal modeling, uncertainty calibration, and clinical reward. We will add these to Tab.1. 3.Comparison fairness (R4,MR): Our method intentionally accesses perception tools; the contribution is the framework orchestrating them via learned DT planning. Tab.3 provides controlled ablations on the same backbone: no DT 0.242 EM, flat DT 0.383, full framework 0.584.The SFT baseline with identical tool access achieves only 0.325 EM, confirming gains arise from RL-trained reasoning, not merely stronger perception. 4.Dataset sufficiency and clinician involvement (R1,MR): REAL-Colon-Reason builds on REAL-Colon (60 videos, 6 medical centers), one of the largest public colonoscopy datasets with frame-level annotations. Three annotators independently reviewed all 2000 QA pairs generated by GPT, correcting reasoning chains and verifying clinical accuracy (Cohen kappa: 0.82). We evaluate on three benchmarks (REAL-Colon-Reason, REAL-Colon-VQA, EndoVis18-VQA) spanning two procedure types (colonoscopy and nephrectomy) to validate cross-procedure generalization; these are the only publicly available surgical VideoQA benchmarks with temporal annotations suitable for our task. 5.Qualitative expert evaluation (R3,MR): Three annotators rated 50 randomly sampled answers from our method and the strongest baseline (Qwen3-VL-8B) on a 1-5 clinical correctness scale. Ours: 4.12 avg vs 3.28 for Qwen3-VL-8B, with the largest gap on Level 3 questions (3.85 vs 2.64). We will include this in revision. 6.Complex workflow and efficiency (R1): The query-adaptive DAG planning avoids invoking all foundation models uniformly; on average only 2.3 of 4 models are called per query. Per-clip inference takes approximately 12s for DT construction and 3s for LLM reasoning on a single 4090 GPU. While slower than end-to-end VLMs, the modular design allows each component to be independently upgraded or accelerated. 7.Experimental details (R4,MR): Standard deviations in Tab.1 are over 3 independent runs with different seeds. Frame-based baselines (SurgicalGPT, PitVQA) are adapted to video by per-frame inference with majority-vote aggregation. 8.Reproducibility/open-source (R1,R3,R4,MR): We will release the full codebase and REAL-Colon-Reason benchmark upon acceptance, an anonymous version: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/surgical_videoqa_dt/. 9.Figure 1 and typos (R4): We will restructure Fig.1 to clearly separate the four stages with explicit input/output annotations for each component. The “NVIDIA NVIDIA” repetition and other typos will be corrected.
